name: Burkitts Reef ("Greg's Reef")
year: Construction Feb 1997 (2 days on-reef excavator work); first council application 1982 [R4][R8][R1][R6]
type: Existing natural basalt boulder headland reef, reshaped in place — boulders broken down/relocated with a rented excavator, not a new engineered structure [R1][R3][R4][R6][R8]
purpose: Surfing only — remove/relocate hazardous boulders and old rail-track debris that made the point break dangerous and largely unsurfable [R1][R3][R6]
size: ~300 m3 of rock moved; at least 12 large basalt boulders relocated/broken down; ~2.5 m local tide swing exploited to work at low tide [R4][R8]
cost_usd_approx: ~USD $6,500-7,500 (rough 1997 FX estimate, not sourced from an FX reference)
financed_by: Greg Redgard personally, who mortgaged his house; approvals only (no funding) from the Beach Protection Authority of Queensland and Burnett Shire Council [R1][R6]
motivation: One local surfer's grassroots push, not a council/tourism/erosion program: Greg Redgard, a Bargara Boardriders Association member, first applied in 1982 and spent over a decade lobbying before approval landed in 1997 [R1][R3][R4][R6][R8]
designer: Greg Redgard, a local sugarcane cutter with no engineering background or formal reef modelling/scale testing [R1][R4][R6]
contractor: None named as a firm — Redgard and his mates did the work themselves using a rented Kobelco hydraulic excavator [R1][R4][R6]
status_now: Still standing and still surfed as of the most recent (2024) coverage, known locally as "Greg's Reef"; no reported repair, damage, or removal in nearly three decades [R1][R5]
hover_text: A Bargara sugarcane cutter spent AUD $10,000 of his own money (mortgaging his house) to have an excavator reshape a natural basalt reef in 1997, after a 15-year fight for approval — surfable days rose from a handful a year to about 30, and the reef still works, unrepaired, almost three decades later [R1][R4][R6][R8].
design_as_planned: No formal engineering design, wave model, or scale test — Redgard designed and built it by instinct, telling ABC "Not rocket science, really, when you think about it." The plan was simply to break down/relocate the boulders and discarded railway-track debris blocking the takeoff zone so a wave could "break over it," turning a hazard-strewn stretch into a rideable right-hand point break. No modelled promises about wave height, beach width, or ecological effect were made [R1][R5][R6][R8].
as_built_vs_design: Because there was no formal design, sources report little planned-vs-built gap: construction (completed February 1997) matched Redgard's simple intent. A Kobelco hydraulic excavator worked at low tide (using the ~2.5 m local tide range) to break down and reposition at least 12 large boulders, clearing a deep gutter that had split the wave into two disconnected sections, with gaps filled partly by hand — reportedly including carrying bricks out on a surfboard. Construction duration is reported two ways: R4/R8 describe the on-reef excavator work as "two days (~8 hours)," while ABC News (R1) describes the whole job as completed "within weeks" of approval — a genuine, unresolved cross-source discrepancy the dossier flags rather than silently resolving. Some of the large rocks removed from the takeoff zone were relocated to the shoreline rather than discarded, where locals still use them for fishing [R1][R4][R5][R6][R8].
outcome: Surfable days rose from "a handful" per year before the works to roughly 30 days a year afterward, with overhead (4+ ft) conditions on the order of 4 days a year, per researcher Andrew Pitt (SurfingRamps.com.au), cited independently via Raised Water Research and a Swellnet forum comment. Wave face height is reported at 2-6 ft (0.5-2 m), period 7-10 seconds, described as a consistent peeling face that occasionally barrels. Best swell window is November-April. The modification has held for nearly three decades with no reported maintenance, storm damage, or re-work. No coastal-protection outcome or ecological impact study was found (not a stated goal) [R1][R3][R4][R6][R8].
why_worked_or_failed: By the consensus of every source found, this is treated as a rare unambiguous success among artificial/enhanced surf reefs: (1) it reshaped an existing natural reef rather than importing new structure, unlike sandbag/geotextile reefs that must create a wholly new bathymetric feature; (2) it was a simple, low-risk intervention — removing hazards and gap-filling rather than engineering a specific wave shape, so there was little to go wrong structurally, unlike geotextile-bag reefs whose fabric tore, shifted, or sank; (3) a large natural tide range (~2.5 m) made the boulders workable at low tide with ordinary excavation equipment, without marine plant or diving contractors; (4) rock/boulder material is inherently more durable than sand-filled geotextile bags. No source reports a failure mode for this reef [R3][R4].
unexpected_results: Boulders cleared from the takeoff zone were relocated to the shoreline, where locals now use them as a fishing spot — an unplanned secondary benefit. The project was picked up by TIME magazine (per ABC) as the "world's first surf enhancement project" and resurfaced in Australian national media in January 2024 as a good-news/DIY-hero story. The same reef is independently marketed as a scuba/snorkel attraction ("Burkitts Reef Dive Site"), an example of one enhanced natural reef serving two recreational audiences. Redgard's daughter Tahlija, who grew up surfing the reef, became a professional surfer and credits it directly. No litigation, safety incident, localism/crowding conflict, or negative unexpected consequence was found in any source [R1][R5][R6][R10][R13].
could_be_better: None of the sources reviewed (including comparison pages that do critique other reefs' bag sizes, crest depths, and funding models) offer a specific critique of Burkitts Reef's execution — it is consistently used as the positive contrast case rather than a subject of critique. No critical surfer commentary was found. Sources suggest very little "could have been done better": if anything, some note it did not create "a world-class surf spot," only a modest, locally valued improvement — offered as a realistic-expectations lesson rather than a criticism [R3][R4][R8].
relevance_to_israel: Bargara's ~2.5 m tide swing is far larger than the Israeli Mediterranean coast's tide range (well under 0.5 m, micro-tidal) — Burkitts' construction method assumed tidal exposure that a Haifa-area site would not get, so similar reshaping there would likely need different plant (barge/crane, diver-assisted work) rather than simple low-tide excavator access. Bargara's 2-6 ft, 7-10 s point-break wave comes from a defined Coral Sea/Pacific swell season (Nov-Apr); Israeli Mediterranean wave climate is generally smaller and more wind-swell dominated with shorter period. The core transferable lesson is procedural/economic rather than technical: a modest, self-funded, reshape-what's-already-there approach (relocating existing boulders rather than importing new engineered material) achieved a multi-decade, apparently maintenance-free improvement for roughly AUD $10,000, in contrast to far more expensive professionally engineered geotextile-bag reefs elsewhere that have frequently failed or required costly renewal. For any Haifa/Israel natural reef or rock outcrop with existing hazards, a similarly minimal clear/reshape approach is the direct analogy worth testing, if geology and permitting allow [R4][R1].

reviews.role: builder, Bargara Boardriders Association member, sugarcane cutter
reviews.quote_or_summary: You really couldn't surf it, because you'd take off, go for about 2 or 3 metres and you would just run into rocks.
The wave could break over it. Not rocket science, really, when you think about it.
He took Burkitts Reef, redefined what was possible and made what was once unrideable an absolute playground.

Assessed the reef's before/after performance: surfable days rose from "a handful... every year" to about 30/year, with the wave changing from a hazard-split break into a smooth peeling lip with some barrel action.

reviews.quote_or_summary: Prior wave broke a few days/yr, now 30 days/yr plus overhead 4 days/yr — explicitly contrasted with failed professionally-designed reefs.

The surf break of Burkitts Reef at Bargara, in Queensland's Bundaberg region, was previously obstructed by large rocks. Then Greg Redgard and his mates turned the 'unrideable' beach into a surfers' playground.

footprint.name: Burkitts Reef ("Greg's Reef")
footprint.shape_type_notes: Not an engineered structure with a designed plan-view template -- Burkitts Reef is a natural basalt headland/rock shelf that was reshaped in place (existing boulders broken down and relocated with a rented excavator) rather than built from new imported material. None of V/delta/chevron/linear/crescent/L/mound describes a natural point/headland reef, so 'other' is used. The polygon below traces the visible natural rock/reef extent read off satellite imagery -- it is NOT a surveyed or designed footprint, and no such footprint has ever been published for this reef (confirmed against our own card, which already states 'No footprint length/width figure found', and against every source checked in this pass).
footprint.coords: metres; origin = shoreline point nearest the reef centroid (approx. the beach access point at the southern end of Bargara Beach, near Bill Fritz Park / Burkitt Street, Bargara); x = alongshore (positive toward north, approximate -- Bargara's coastline trends roughly N-S here; no source gives an exact shoreline azimuth); y = offshore (positive seaward, approximately east into the Coral Sea); shoreline approximated as the line y=0. Because the reef is an attached headland (not a detached structure), much of its landward edge lies at or near y=0.

crest_depth_m.datum: exposed dry basalt at low tide (the condition under which the 1997 excavator work was done); rises to roughly 2.5 m of water depth over the same rock at high spring tide

footprint.crest_depth_alt_note: This is not a single engineered crest depth -- Burkitts Reef is an intertidal rock platform whose water cover varies continuously with the tide. No source publishes a fixed crest elevation against a survey datum (e.g. LAT). The 0 m (dry) to ~2.5 m (submerged) range is our own inference from R4's stated ~2.5 m local tide swing, not a direct measurement. Corrected 2026-09-25: an earlier draft of this file also cited R8 for the ~2.5 m figure; R8 (Swellnet, re-fetched) corroborates the 1982/1997 timeline and before/after surf-day counts but does not itself restate a tide-swing number, so it has been removed from this citation. Gemini's file gives the same order-of-magnitude range (0.2-2.5 m) but does not tie it to either of its own two relevant sources.
footprint.orientation_notes: Attached headland/point at the southern end of Bargara Beach (near Bill Fritz Park / Burkitt Street) trending roughly NNE-SSW, with its rocky tip projecting seaward (east) into the Coral Sea. Consistently described as a 'right-hand point break' (R1,R3): the wave wraps the point and peels back toward the beach, putting the wave face on the surfer's right as they ride it, which is only possible with the seaward apex/densest boulder mass lying to the north/east of the main takeoff zone. No source gives a precise compass bearing or arm angle -- this description is drawn from (a) the plan shape visible in satellite imagery (see images_relied_on) and (b) Greg Redgard's own 1980 hand-drawn petition sketch, which labels a dense boulder mass 'BURKITTS REEF' at the seaward/outer end of a wedge-shaped point, shows a cleared 'swimmers passage' / 'boat passage' channel along the shoreward side, and marks hazard rocks with 'X' roughly midway along the point -- consistent with the satellite-imagery shape and with the Esplanade/houses/Basin/golf-course landmarks also visible on today's satellite imagery.
footprint.materials: Natural volcanic basalt boulders (existing headland rock), reshaped in place -- not new material. ~300 m3 of rock relocated, at least 12 large boulders broken down/repositioned, gaps hand-packed with bricks; some old discarded railway-track iron was also present in the rock and cleared [R1][R3][R4][R6][R8] (all figures already in the verified card; not re-derived here).

footprint.crest_label: 0 m: rock exposed at low tide

name: Cable Station Reef (Cables Reef)
year: 1999 (construction Feb-Dec 1999; site studies from 1988; design/feasibility report to WA govt 1994) [R2][R5]
type: Granite boulders (over 10,000 tons, boulders up to 3 m) placed on existing natural limestone reef/bedrock; one source (ICM) and another (The Inertia, quoting the Committee) instead describe the placed rock as limestone rather than granite — sources disagree [R1][R2][R4][R5][R6]
purpose: Surf-only enhancement: create a more consistent, higher-quality surfing spot with left- and right-hand waves and a 'gently barreling' face for intermediate surfers, for swells 0.5-3.5 m at a peel angle of ~45°; not designed as a coastal-protection structure [R1][R2][R5]
size: Length ~140 m (north-south), max width ~70 m, ~275 m offshore, water depth 3-6 m, reef crest 1-3 m below average tide (~1.5 m below lowest tide per a 2009 review); volume of rock ~3,500 m3 per Wikipedia vs ~5,000 m3 per Coastal Management (ICM) - sources disagree [R1][R2][R4][R5]
cost: Approximately AUD $2 million for study, design and construction combined [R2][R5]
cost_usd_approx: Roughly US$1.3-1.4 million; this is the agent's own arithmetic conversion using a typical 1999 AUD/USD rate of ~0.63-0.67, not a figure taken from any cited source
financed_by: Western Australia Department of Sport and Recreation [R2]
motivation: The site was a natural point break, Cable Station reef, surfed since the late 1940s and regarded highly through the 1950s-1980s, which local surfers (per Len Dibben) believed had been degraded by nearby coastal engineering works (Cottesloe Groyne, Dutch Inn Groyne and others) [R3]. This fed the WA Surf Rider Association's 1975 'Build a Reef' campaign (surfers John Balgarnie and Geoff Berry), carried through to the 1999 build by Cottesloe surfers John Balgarnie and Keith Campbell working with the Perth Artificial Surfing Reef Committee [R3][R6], with site-selection (M. Crawford, 1988) and a 1994 engineering feasibility report to the WA government preceding construction [R2][R5]
designer: Client/advocacy body: Perth Artificial Surfing Reef Committee, driven by Cottesloe surfers John Balgarnie and Keith Campbell [R3][R6]. Site selection: M. Crawford (1988) [R2]. Design sketches enabling funding: Andrew Pitt, founder of SurfingRamps.com.au [R2]. Engineering studies: WA Department of Marine and Harbours and the University of Western Australia, reporting to the WA government in 1994 [R5]. Physical-model design work (random-wave flume, 1:40-scale model in a 40 m x 40 m wave basin, optimum bed slope 1:20, final 'boomerang-shaped' reef) documented in Hutt et al., 'Design Studies for an Artificial Surfing Reef: Cable Station, Western Australia' [R8]
contractor: WA Limestone, using a barge-based cycle of transporting and placing the granite boulders onto the limestone bedrock [R2][R5]
status_now: No removal or dismantling reported in any source found; the granite/limestone construction is repeatedly described as structurally durable ('stood the test of time,' better shape-retention than geotextile-bag reefs elsewhere) as of the most recent sources reviewed (2023-2024) [R2][R3][R5]. Wave-frequency consistency remains disputed among surfers
hover_text: A 140 m x 70 m granite-boulder reef built in 1999 for about AUD $2 million (state-government funded) to improve surfing off Cottesloe/Leighton, Perth; it proved structurally durable (unlike sand-filled geotextile-bag reefs elsewhere) but its wave frequency remains disputed, with a 2009 assessment finding only a handful of good surf days per month against the original design target [R1][R2][R5].
design_as_planned: The Perth Artificial Surfing Reef Committee's design goal was a reef generating consistent left- and right-hand waves with a 'gently barreling' face, working across a 0.5-3.5 m swell range at a ~45° peel angle suited to intermediate surfers [R1][R2][R5]. Physical-model testing (random-wave flume; 1:40-scale model in a 40 m x 40 m wave basin) found an optimum bottom slope of 1:20 (matching the site's natural bed slope and slopes recorded at many surf breaks worldwide); several reef shapes were tested and a 'boomerang-shaped' form that minimised fill volume and merged with the existing natural reef was selected as final [R8]. Placing rock directly on the existing limestone bedrock (rather than a sand-filled geotextile-bag structure on sand) was explicitly meant to avoid sinking and remove the need for sand cover [R2][R5]
as_built_vs_design: Construction began February 1999, reached ~90% completion by May 1999, but was not fully finished until December 1999 [R2][R5]. WA Limestone used a cyclical barge-transport-and-placement process, placing over 10,000 tons of quarried granite boulders (up to 3 m across) on the limestone bedrock [R2][R5]. One documented mid-project change: once it became clear the rock-on-bedrock method needed no sand cover and prevented sinking, that realisation 'led to an extension of the reef's southern end' beyond the original footprint [R5] — a design-to-built change, though no source gives a size or cost figure for the extension. No cost-overrun figure was found in any source reviewed
outcome: Early academic monitoring was positive: Stacey Bancroft's 1999 study found peel angles closely matched the ~45° design target and surfable days exceeded predicted values across three measurement methods [R2][R5][R9]; Charitha Pattiaratchi's 1999-2001 monitoring concluded the reef was 'performing according to its design and... as well or better than predicted,' citing roughly four to six months of good conditions in 2000-2001, though the paper itself notes this 'has been disputed by some members of the local surfing population' [R9][R2]. A 2009 assessment by Andrew Pitt found the reef 'only provides a "few surfable days per month"' and does not reliably break chest-high waves, attributing this to the crest depth (~1.5 m below lowest tide) and the site's position in the swell shadow of Rottnest Island and other outer reefs, which block a significant share of incoming wave energy [R2][R5]. Wikipedia similarly notes performance is 'hampered by the presence of offshore islands and reefs which block a significant fraction of the wave energy' [R1]. Two conflicting headline frequency figures exist across sources: some describe ~150 rideable days per year, others (Pitt, 2009) describe only a handful of good days per month — this dossier could not resolve which is more current [R2][R5][R6]. Structurally the reef has proven durable, with better shape-retention than geotextile-bag reefs built elsewhere in the same era [R2][R5]. No coastal-protection outcome (beach widening/salient formation) was reported, consistent with the reef never being designed for that purpose [R2]
why_worked_or_failed: Cable Station Reef is repeatedly cited (with Burkitts Reef and Palm Beach Reef) as one of the few artificial surf reefs built from solid rock rather than sand-filled geotextile bags, and one of the few that did not structurally fail [R6][R7]. Surf scientist Shaw Mead told Newsroom (NZ) that 'while the structures have failed (except for Cable Station (limestone), Borth (rock), Palm Beach (rock) and Narrowneck (sandbags maintained)), all have created surfing waves that have replicated the designs' [R7]. The engineering logic: geotextile sand-filled containers fail because losing sand from even one bag changes the whole structure's shape, whereas rock placed directly on hard limestone bedrock does not sink, needs no sand cover, and keeps its shape under wave attack [R2][R5][R6]. It under-delivers on wave frequency because (1) the reef crest sits too deep for smaller/moderate swells to break reliably, against a 0.5 m minimum-swell design target [R2][R5]; and (2) the site lies in the lee of Rottnest Island and other offshore reefs which absorb/block a meaningful share of incoming swell energy [R1][R2][R5]
unexpected_results: Access to the site has caused dune erosion, as surfers cross the cliff face on foot to reach the break [R2][R5]. Positively, Bancroft's monitoring found significant biological recolonisation of the placed rock surfaces, an ecological benefit not central to the original surf-only design brief [R2][R5]. No reports of increased fishing pressure, dangerous rips, drowning incidents, or litigation tied specifically to Cable Station Reef were found in the sources reviewed
could_be_better: Andrew Pitt's 2009 assessment recommended making the reef shallower and extending its seaward 'nose' further offshore, to intercept more swell before it is blocked by Rottnest Island and the outer reefs, and to allow smaller swells to break as originally designed [R2][R5]. Surfers' recurring complaint across sources is consistency, not quality — they 'appreciate the quality of the wave when it breaks' but see 'lack of frequency as the biggest problem' [R1][R2][R5][R6]
relevance_to_israel: Cable Station's core engineering lesson — build in solid rock placed directly on hard substrate rather than sand-filled geotextile bags on a sandy bed — removes tide-driven sand-burial risk as a failure mode, directly relevant to any Israeli reef design [R2][R5][R6]. Its real-world problem was insufficient swell energy reaching too-deep a crest, not excess swell [R1][R2][R5]; Lior's own field measurements at the Shikmona buoy off Haifa define the 'minimum surfable wave' window there as 0.45-0.6 m significant wave height (0.6-0.8 m maximum), with swell approach ~284-294 deg (WNW) and peak periods ~5.7-6.2 s — a substantially smaller, more marginal wave climate than Cable Station's 0.5-3.5 m design range [R15]. The transferable lesson is that a low-energy site like Haifa/Shikmona faces exactly Cable Station's failure mode (crest set too deep to reliably break the smaller end of the local swell range) if the crest is not kept shallow — the same design lever Pitt recommended for Cable Station, and the same one Lior's own 'Light Construction' concept sketch addresses by placing its crest near the natural Wave Breaking Depth line [R15]. A government/community-driven, surfer-advocated funding model (WA Dept of Sport and Recreation, after a 24-year advocacy campaign from 1975-1999) is also a plausible funding-model precedent for an Israeli project pursued via local surfer/NGO advocacy [R2][R3]

sections.title: Quick facts
sections.html_or_text:
NameCable Station Reef (Cables Reef)
PlaceLeighton / Cottesloe, Perth, Western Australia
CountryAustralia
Year1999 (construction Feb-Dec 1999; site studies from 1988; design/feasibility report to WA govt 1994) [R2][R5]
TypeGranite boulders (over 10,000 tons, boulders up to 3 m) placed on existing natural limestone reef/bedrock; one source (ICM) and another (The Inertia, quoting the Committee) instead describe the placed rock as limestone rather than granite — sources disagree [R1][R2][R4][R5][R6]
PurposeSurf-only enhancement: create a more consistent, higher-quality surfing spot with left- and right-hand waves and a 'gently barreling' face for intermediate surfers, for swells 0.5-3.5 m at a peel angle of ~45°; not designed as a coastal-protection structure [R1][R2][R5]
SizeLength ~140 m (north-south), max width ~70 m, ~275 m offshore, water depth 3-6 m, reef crest 1-3 m below average tide (~1.5 m below lowest tide per a 2009 review); volume of rock ~3,500 m3 per Wikipedia vs ~5,000 m3 per Coastal Management (ICM) - sources disagree [R1][R2][R4][R5]
CostApproximately AUD $2 million for study, design and construction combined [R2][R5]
Cost (approx. USD)Roughly US$1.3-1.4 million; this is the agent's own arithmetic conversion using a typical 1999 AUD/USD rate of ~0.63-0.67, not a figure taken from any cited source
Financed byWestern Australia Department of Sport and Recreation [R2]
DesignerClient/advocacy body: Perth Artificial Surfing Reef Committee, driven by Cottesloe surfers John Balgarnie and Keith Campbell [R3][R6]. Site selection: M. Crawford (1988) [R2]. Design sketches enabling funding: Andrew Pitt, founder of SurfingRamps.com.au [R2]. Engineering studies: WA Department of Marine and Harbours and the University of Western Australia, reporting to the WA government in 1994 [R5]. Physical-model design work (random-wave flume, 1:40-scale model in a 40 m x 40 m wave basin, optimum bed slope 1:20, final 'boomerang-shaped' reef) documented in Hutt et al., 'Design Studies for an Artificial Surfing Reef: Cable Station, Western Australia' [R8]
ContractorWA Limestone, using a barge-based cycle of transporting and placing the granite boulders onto the limestone bedrock [R2][R5]
Status nowNo removal or dismantling reported in any source found; the granite/limestone construction is repeatedly described as structurally durable ('stood the test of time,' better shape-retention than geotextile-bag reefs elsewhere) as of the most recent sources reviewed (2023-2024) [R2][R3][R5]. Wave-frequency consistency remains disputed among surfers
Verdictmixed

sections.title: Motivation & who pushed for it
sections.html_or_text: The site was a natural point break, Cable Station reef, surfed since the late 1940s and regarded highly through the 1950s-1980s, which local surfers (per Len Dibben) believed had been degraded by nearby coastal engineering works (Cottesloe Groyne, Dutch Inn Groyne and others) [R3]. This fed the WA Surf Rider Association's 1975 'Build a Reef' campaign (surfers John Balgarnie and Geoff Berry), carried through to the 1999 build by Cottesloe surfers John Balgarnie and Keith Campbell working with the Perth Artificial Surfing Reef Committee [R3][R6], with site-selection (M. Crawford, 1988) and a 1994 engineering feasibility report to the WA government preceding construction [R2][R5]

sections.title: Design as planned
sections.html_or_text: The Perth Artificial Surfing Reef Committee's design goal was a reef generating consistent left- and right-hand waves with a 'gently barreling' face, working across a 0.5-3.5 m swell range at a ~45° peel angle suited to intermediate surfers [R1][R2][R5]. Physical-model testing (random-wave flume; 1:40-scale model in a 40 m x 40 m wave basin) found an optimum bottom slope of 1:20 (matching the site's natural bed slope and slopes recorded at many surf breaks worldwide); several reef shapes were tested and a 'boomerang-shaped' form that minimised fill volume and merged with the existing natural reef was selected as final [R8]. Placing rock directly on the existing limestone bedrock (rather than a sand-filled geotextile-bag structure on sand) was explicitly meant to avoid sinking and remove the need for sand cover [R2][R5]

sections.title: As built vs design
sections.html_or_text: Construction began February 1999, reached ~90% completion by May 1999, but was not fully finished until December 1999 [R2][R5]. WA Limestone used a cyclical barge-transport-and-placement process, placing over 10,000 tons of quarried granite boulders (up to 3 m across) on the limestone bedrock [R2][R5]. One documented mid-project change: once it became clear the rock-on-bedrock method needed no sand cover and prevented sinking, that realisation 'led to an extension of the reef's southern end' beyond the original footprint [R5] — a design-to-built change, though no source gives a size or cost figure for the extension. No cost-overrun figure was found in any source reviewed

sections.title: Outcome
sections.html_or_text: Early academic monitoring was positive: Stacey Bancroft's 1999 study found peel angles closely matched the ~45° design target and surfable days exceeded predicted values across three measurement methods [R2][R5][R9]; Charitha Pattiaratchi's 1999-2001 monitoring concluded the reef was 'performing according to its design and... as well or better than predicted,' citing roughly four to six months of good conditions in 2000-2001, though the paper itself notes this 'has been disputed by some members of the local surfing population' [R9][R2]. A 2009 assessment by Andrew Pitt found the reef 'only provides a "few surfable days per month"' and does not reliably break chest-high waves, attributing this to the crest depth (~1.5 m below lowest tide) and the site's position in the swell shadow of Rottnest Island and other outer reefs, which block a significant share of incoming wave energy [R2][R5]. Wikipedia similarly notes performance is 'hampered by the presence of offshore islands and reefs which block a significant fraction of the wave energy' [R1]. Two conflicting headline frequency figures exist across sources: some describe ~150 rideable days per year, others (Pitt, 2009) describe only a handful of good days per month — this dossier could not resolve which is more current [R2][R5][R6]. Structurally the reef has proven durable, with better shape-retention than geotextile-bag reefs built elsewhere in the same era [R2][R5]. No coastal-protection outcome (beach widening/salient formation) was reported, consistent with the reef never being designed for that purpose [R2]

sections.title: Why it worked / failed
sections.html_or_text: Cable Station Reef is repeatedly cited (with Burkitts Reef and Palm Beach Reef) as one of the few artificial surf reefs built from solid rock rather than sand-filled geotextile bags, and one of the few that did not structurally fail [R6][R7]. Surf scientist Shaw Mead told Newsroom (NZ) that 'while the structures have failed (except for Cable Station (limestone), Borth (rock), Palm Beach (rock) and Narrowneck (sandbags maintained)), all have created surfing waves that have replicated the designs' [R7]. The engineering logic: geotextile sand-filled containers fail because losing sand from even one bag changes the whole structure's shape, whereas rock placed directly on hard limestone bedrock does not sink, needs no sand cover, and keeps its shape under wave attack [R2][R5][R6]. It under-delivers on wave frequency because (1) the reef crest sits too deep for smaller/moderate swells to break reliably, against a 0.5 m minimum-swell design target [R2][R5]; and (2) the site lies in the lee of Rottnest Island and other offshore reefs which absorb/block a meaningful share of incoming swell energy [R1][R2][R5]

sections.title: Unexpected results
sections.html_or_text: Access to the site has caused dune erosion, as surfers cross the cliff face on foot to reach the break [R2][R5]. Positively, Bancroft's monitoring found significant biological recolonisation of the placed rock surfaces, an ecological benefit not central to the original surf-only design brief [R2][R5]. No reports of increased fishing pressure, dangerous rips, drowning incidents, or litigation tied specifically to Cable Station Reef were found in the sources reviewed

sections.title: What could have been done better
sections.html_or_text: Andrew Pitt's 2009 assessment recommended making the reef shallower and extending its seaward 'nose' further offshore, to intercept more swell before it is blocked by Rottnest Island and the outer reefs, and to allow smaller swells to break as originally designed [R2][R5]. Surfers' recurring complaint across sources is consistency, not quality — they 'appreciate the quality of the wave when it breaks' but see 'lack of frequency as the biggest problem' [R1][R2][R5][R6]

sections.title: Relevance to Israel / Haifa
sections.html_or_text: Cable Station's core engineering lesson — build in solid rock placed directly on hard substrate rather than sand-filled geotextile bags on a sandy bed — removes tide-driven sand-burial risk as a failure mode, directly relevant to any Israeli reef design [R2][R5][R6]. Its real-world problem was insufficient swell energy reaching too-deep a crest, not excess swell [R1][R2][R5]; Lior's own field measurements at the Shikmona buoy off Haifa define the 'minimum surfable wave' window there as 0.45-0.6 m significant wave height (0.6-0.8 m maximum), with swell approach ~284-294 deg (WNW) and peak periods ~5.7-6.2 s — a substantially smaller, more marginal wave climate than Cable Station's 0.5-3.5 m design range [R15]. The transferable lesson is that a low-energy site like Haifa/Shikmona faces exactly Cable Station's failure mode (crest set too deep to reliably break the smaller end of the local swell range) if the crest is not kept shallow — the same design lever Pitt recommended for Cable Station, and the same one Lior's own 'Light Construction' concept sketch addresses by placing its crest near the natural Wave Breaking Depth line [R15]. A government/community-driven, surfer-advocated funding model (WA Dept of Sport and Recreation, after a 24-year advocacy campaign from 1975-1999) is also a plausible funding-model precedent for an Israeli project pursued via local surfer/NGO advocacy [R2][R3]

footprint.coords: metres; origin = shoreline point nearest the reef centroid; x = alongshore (positive toward north, per R2's 'from north to south' length description — no source states which specific end/arm is the northern one, treated as a stated but not surveyed convention); y = offshore (positive seaward); shoreline approximated as the line y=0

footprint.orientation_notes: Plan shape is a 'V'/chevron ('boomerang') mound with two unequal arms (left-hand ride 30-40 m, right-hand ride 50-80 m per S1) meeting at a single apex. Whether the apex points offshore (toward the incident swell) or onshore (toward the beach) could not be conclusively read from the only available plan-view figures (S1 Figures 4 and 7, low-resolution 1999 photocopies with illegible scale bars). This file assumes apex-offshore (the standard configuration for point-break-style chevron surf reefs, and consistent with S1's text describing the fill as 'extending the existing 3 m depth contour offshore' while the arms merge with the natural reef inshore) - flagged low confidence. The reef's overall alongshore axis runs north-south per R2; no source gives which arm is north. Design-era swell assumption (S1): 'predominantly from the west' - no specific compass bearing for the final built structure's orientation was found in any source (Gemini's precise '240-270 deg WSW' figure is unverified/unsourced).
footprint.materials: Granite boulders, more than 10,000 tons, individual boulders up to 3 m across, placed on the existing natural limestone reef/bedrock [R1][R2][S1]; two other sources (card's R4/R6) instead describe the placed rock as limestone - unresolved disagreement, carried from the verified card. Volume of rock: 3,500 m3 (Wikipedia, R1) vs ~5,000 m3 (ICM, R4) - also unresolved.

disagree.ours: 275 (final) / 250 (original site estimate)
disagree.why_ours: Both R2 ('about 275 meters') and S1 ('250 m') are well above Gemini's 170 m; R2 is again Gemini's own cited source and directly contradicts Gemini's figure.

disagree.gemini: 6200 gross / 5222 net (84% net/gross ratio per Gemini's own audit)
disagree.ours: ~2,300 (illustrative, low confidence)
disagree.why_ours: No source publishes an area for Cables, so neither number is truly 'sourced' - but Gemini's own 84% net/gross fill ratio is implausibly high for a thin rubble-mound V built by extending natural-reef depth contours (S1 Figure 4 shows a narrow hatched V, not a filled block); even Gemini's own figures for genuinely broad GSC reefs (Boscombe 59%, Mount Maunganui 51%) are thinner than 84%.

open_issues: Apex-vs-arms orientation (offshore-facing vs onshore-facing V) could not be conclusively read from S1's low-resolution 1999 figures (4 and 7); 'apex offshore' was adopted as a working assumption only - low confidence.

No source publishes a crest width, plan-view footprint area, or exact compass bearing for the arms; the 12 m crest-width assumption and resulting ~2,300 m2 area are this file's own illustrative estimate, not a published figure.

The card's R8 reference attributes the Cable Station design-studies paper to 'Hutt et al.' (from a blocked ResearchGate snippet); the full paper located this pass (S1) lists Charitha Pattiaratchi as sole author on its title page - a likely small attribution correction for the card, not made here (out of this task's scope).
Granite-vs-limestone material naming and the 3,500 m3-vs-5,000 m3 volume disagreement remain unresolved, carried over unchanged from the verified card.

The 250 m (S1, pre-final-design) vs 275 m (R2, final) offshore-distance figures may reflect the card's already-documented mid-construction southern-end extension, but no source explicitly connects the two numbers - an inference, not a confirmed explanation.

name: Narrowneck Reef (Gold Coast Reef)
year: Construction began August 1999, completed by December 2000 [R2][R8]; renewed/topped up with 84 more containers June 2018 [R2][R9][R14].
type: Submerged multi-purpose artificial reef (MPR) built from sand-filled geotextile containers ("mega sandbags"), placed on the seabed by split-hull barge with GPS positioning [R1][R2][R3][R9].
purpose: Primary: coastal/erosion protection for the Narrowneck isthmus, where only ~100 m of land separates the Nerang River from the ocean [R2][R14]. Secondary ("multi-purpose"): surfing amenity, folded in partly for public-relations value in a surf-centric region [R2]. A tertiary, unplanned outcome was ecological habitat creation [R1][R3][R8][R9].
size: Volume approx. 70,000 m3 of sand (the largest multi-purpose reef ever built at the time), from approx. 400 geotextile containers each approx. 20 m long, 3-4.5 m diameter [R1][R9][R3]. Footprint reported as 350 m x 600 m, split "V" shape, 200 m offshore, bags 1-10 m below sea level [R9]; a second source directly states the reef "measures 450 meters long by 250 meters wide" [R8] -- the two footprint figures disagree and both are given per the reference rule. Crest lowered 1 m before construction, landing about 1.5 m below the low-tide waterline [R2][R3]; by 2017 low-tide depth over the reef measured 2.5-2.6 m, i.e. the crest had sunk/settled deeper than designed [R2].
cost: Original 1999 build: AUD $2.3 million (approx. AUD $30/m3) per one source [R3], and separately "roughly $2.1 million AUD... over the first 10 years" per another [R5] -- both given since they disagree on scope (one-off build vs. 10-year total). Lior's own notes and a Hebrew-language source both give "$2.5 million," currency unspecified [R19][R20] -- not reconciled with the figures above. 2017-2018 renewal: approx. AUD $2 million per Mayor Tom Tate, as reported by the Gold Coast Bulletin via The Inertia [R10].
cost_usd_approx: Very rough conversions by this report (not sourced): original build AUD $2.3M (1999 AUD~USD 0.65) approx. USD $1.5M; 2017-2018 renewal AUD $2M (2018 AUD~USD 0.75) approx. USD $1.5M.
financed_by: Gold Coast City Council, as part of its Northern Gold Coast Beach Protection Strategy [R1][R2][R9][R13]. No private or state/federal co-funding found in any source.
motivation: Erosion problem predates the reef by decades: a 1971 Delft University of Technology report, commissioned by the Queensland Government, recommended a groyne at Narrowneck [R9][R13]. Training walls built at the Spit in 1985 helped erosion further north but not at Narrowneck itself, and Cyclone Nancy (1990) eroded the beach back to the boulder wall protecting the Nerang River [R2]. Gold Coast City Council chose an artificial reef instead of the recommended groyne, branding it a "Multi-Purpose Reef" so that surfing amenity could be folded into the PR case in a surf-centric city [R2][R9][R13]. No evidence found of state/federal political involvement or a single named political champion for the original 1999 project; Mayor Tom Tate became the public face of the 2017-2018 renewal [R10].
designer: Original 1999 design: Prof. Kerry Black and Shaw Mead (University of Waikato, NZ; later founders of coastal-engineering firm ASR) [R11]. ICM (International Coastal Management, Gold Coast) separately credits its founder Angus Jackson with leading the project as part of the wider Northern Gold Coast Beach Protection Strategy [R3] -- the two attributions disagree on lead designer; both given. The 2017-2018 renewal's coastal-engineering consultant was reported by Swellnet as ICM [R2].
contractor: Not named for the 1999 build beyond "Gold Coast City Council" as project owner [R2][R9]. For the 2017-2018 renewal, the placement barge was the split-hull dredger Faucon, whose skipper gave on-record comments to Swellnet [R2].
status_now: Still in place and monitored by Gold Coast City Council as of the most recent sources found (2019 monitoring, 2026 commentary) [R12][R14]. As of January 2026, the Gold Coast mayor announced plans to "fast-track" a separate, new rockwall/groyne structure immediately south of Narrowneck -- not a rebuild of the existing reef -- contested by local surfer/environmental group Save Our Spit Alliance; a live, unresolved controversy, not a completed project [R12].
hover_text: A 70,000 m3 sand-filled geotextile reef built 1999-2000 for about AUD $2.3M to protect Narrowneck's isthmus; it worked well for coastal protection but a last-minute 1-metre crest-lowering decision left the promised surf underperforming, while the reef became an unplanned ecological hotspot whose fishing traffic then tore the bags with boat anchors, forcing a 2017-2018 renewal [R1][R2][R3][R9][R11].
design_as_planned: Designed by Kerry Black (University of Waikato) and Shaw Mead, using refraction-diffraction (WBEND) and Boussinesq wave modelling, checked against a 1:50-scale physical model at the UNSW Water Research Laboratory [R5][R11]. Stated targets: widen the beach 20-30 m in the reef's lee and produce surfable waves under defined conditions [R5]. A 2007 performance report (cited by Swellnet) noted the reef needed "long period, clean swell" to replicate the modelled wave shape, and that "larger swells, lower tides, and offshore winds have the potential to produce hollow, plunging breakers" [R2] -- the promised surf was explicitly conditional. The original design was a split "V" shape for both left- and right-hand rides with a paddling channel between the arms [R3][R9].
as_built_vs_design: The most consequential change was a late, last-minute council decision to lower the reef's crest by 1 metre before construction -- "the change would have no effect on sand accretion but was terminal to Narrowneck becoming a good surfing reef," per Swellnet [R2]. Otherwise the built reef followed the approx. 400-container, approx. 70,000 m3 design, placed via split-hull barge with GPS [R1][R3][R9]. By approx. 2011 an underwater survey found several containers missing or damaged and seaward containers buried by sand [R4]. By 2017 the bags had "settled further into the sand" over 17 years, deeper than as-built [R2]. Designer Shaw Mead later attributed geotextile-bag failures across his firm's projects worldwide to specific causes per site, identifying boat anchors as the Gold Coast failure mechanism: "The containers failed due to a number of reasons including anchors (Gold Coast), debris strikes (Kovalam), during construction with over-filling (Mount Reef), propellor strike (Boscombe)" [R11].
outcome: Coastal protection: judged successful by the council and most independent sources; an 11-year monitoring study (Jackson et al., ICCE proceedings) found 2009 storm erosion "was accommodated within the wider beach created in 1999," with gradual post-storm recovery producing a mild groyne effect [R4]. A 2019 City statement described continued sand-volume increases, but specifically in offshore sandbars rather than the upper beach -- contradicting earlier (2010-era) reports of a 30-50 m salient, which Google Earth historical imagery does not corroborate [R14]. Wikipedia (citing Turner 2006) gives an independently monitored beach-widening figure of approx. 20 m, lower than the 30-50 m figure elsewhere [R1][R14]; both given per the reference rule. Surfing: consistently underperforming versus expectations -- "disappointing in its secondary objective to improve surfing" [R9]; surfers "seldom surf the reef," persisting after the 2017-2018 renewal [R14]. An earlier study (via ecoshape.org) reported the reef broke waves "roughly 50% of the time," faces 0.7-2.0 m, average ride 150-200 m / 30 s, "fun, but not hollow, in average conditions" [R5]. Ecology: widely reported as an unplanned success -- popular fishing/diving/snorkelling site with macro-algae, fish and reported turtle activity on the geotextile substrate [R1][R3][R8][R9]; the 2011 survey found "high abundance and biodiversity" despite sand-burial and container damage [R4].
why_worked_or_failed: Coastal protection worked primarily because the reef's core hydraulic function -- dissipating wave energy offshore and trapping sediment in the nearshore sandbar system -- does not depend on precise crest depth or bag integrity to the same degree surf-wave shaping does; even a degraded, buried or partially damaged reef still perturbs the sand-transport regime [R4][R14]. Surfing underperformed for a documented, specific reason: the council's last-minute 1-metre crest-lowering decision, made for reasons unrelated to surf quality, put the structure too deep for consistent wave-breaking under normal swell/tide/wind combinations [R2]. Compounding this, geotextile bags are inherently fragile: Shaw Mead stated that losing even a single sand-filled container changes the seabed shape and degrades wave quality, and that Gold Coast's containers specifically failed due to boat anchors [R11]. Mead's broader verdict: he "no longer believes in the viability of geotextile bags for artificial reef construction," having led a critical industry review approximately a decade after Narrowneck "which led to the change to traditional rock construction methods of the most recent MPRs built" [R11].
unexpected_results: Ecological colonisation and the resulting fishing/anchor-damage cycle: the reef's unplanned success as a fish habitat drew recreational fishing traffic, whose boat anchors are identified as the specific mechanism that tore the geotextile containers [R11] -- an ecological win directly causing the structural failure that required the 2017-2018 renewal. "Moving the goalposts" on beach-widening claims: early (2010-era) monitoring described a clear 30-50 m salient; by 2019 the City's official position shifted to say a salient was "never expected" and sand build-up was always meant to be offshore -- flagged by multiple Swellnet commenters as inconsistent with what residents were originally told [R14]. A 2026 political sequel: 27 years after Narrowneck was built to avoid a conventional groyne, the Gold Coast mayor proposed fast-tracking a new rockwall/groyne immediately adjacent to it, prompting the same updrift/downdrift erosion-displacement objections coastal engineers raise about hard groynes generally [R12]. Depth-measurement uncertainty: the City's post-renewal survey data claims no settlement of the new containers, directly contradicting anecdotal local reports that the new bags were already breaking less often and appeared to be settling [R14].
could_be_better: Experts'/engineers' view: Shaw Mead, the reef's original designer, has publicly stated (in a critical review conducted roughly a decade after Narrowneck was built) that sand-filled geotextile containers should not be used for multi-purpose reef construction at all, and that the industry has since moved to rock construction [R11]. Swellnet's 2017 reporting singles out the crest-lowering decision as the single design change most responsible for the surf underperformance, implying a purely surf-focused crest depth would have produced a better wave without necessarily compromising protection [R2]. Surfers'/locals' view: commenters were blunter -- one ("warddy," 2019) called it an "absolute waste of money" and suggested rock construction instead; another ("the-spleen_2") noted "beach widening" had originally been "the core of the project" as pitched by Griffith University, and found it "funny to see how the idea has changed over time" toward the offshore-sandbar framing [R14].
relevance_to_israel: Narrowneck's central lesson for a Haifa or other Israeli Mediterranean project is the crest-depth-versus-tide-range trade-off: the reef's surf underperformance is traced by an independent source specifically to a council decision to change crest depth relative to the tide datum, made for reasons unrelated to surfing, which then dominated wave-breaking outcomes [R2]. The Gold Coast has a meaningful astronomical tide range (crest explicitly set "1.5 m below the low tide waterline") [R2][R3] -- a variable a designer must actively engineer around, since a fixed crest depth performs differently at high versus low tide. Lior's own draft outreach material argues the Mediterranean's smaller tidal range at Haifa is an advantage for reef stability and maintenance ("the tide conditions here allow high stability and natural long-term maintenance") [R18] -- this is Lior's own hypothesis, not an independently sourced engineering conclusion, and no numeric Haifa/Mediterranean tide-range figure was found in the sources fetched for this dossier. If correct, a Haifa reef would face a smaller version of Narrowneck's tide-datum problem, making crest-depth choice a one-time design decision rather than a chronic multi-condition compromise. Separately, Narrowneck's identified failure mechanism -- boat anchors tearing geotextile bags that had become a popular fishing spot [R11] -- is directly transferable: any Israeli geotextile-based reef that succeeds ecologically should expect the same anchor-damage risk and may want to restrict anchoring or use more anchor-resistant materials such as rock, per Mead's own post-Narrowneck design shift [R11].

sections.title: Quick facts
sections.html_or_text:
NameNarrowneck Reef (Gold Coast Reef)
PlaceNarrowneck, Gold Coast, Queensland
CountryAustralia
YearConstruction began August 1999, completed by December 2000 [R2][R8]; renewed/topped up with 84 more containers June 2018 [R2][R9][R14].
TypeSubmerged multi-purpose artificial reef (MPR) built from sand-filled geotextile containers ("mega sandbags"), placed on the seabed by split-hull barge with GPS positioning [R1][R2][R3][R9].
PurposePrimary: coastal/erosion protection for the Narrowneck isthmus, where only ~100 m of land separates the Nerang River from the ocean [R2][R14]. Secondary ("multi-purpose"): surfing amenity, folded in partly for public-relations value in a surf-centric region [R2]. A tertiary, unplanned outcome was ecological habitat creation [R1][R3][R8][R9].
SizeVolume approx. 70,000 m3 of sand (the largest multi-purpose reef ever built at the time), from approx. 400 geotextile containers each approx. 20 m long, 3-4.5 m diameter [R1][R9][R3]. Footprint reported as 350 m x 600 m, split "V" shape, 200 m offshore, bags 1-10 m below sea level [R9]; a second source directly states the reef "measures 450 meters long by 250 meters wide" [R8] -- the two footprint figures disagree and both are given per the reference rule. Crest lowered 1 m before construction, landing about 1.5 m below the low-tide waterline [R2][R3]; by 2017 low-tide depth over the reef measured 2.5-2.6 m, i.e. the crest had sunk/settled deeper than designed [R2].
CostOriginal 1999 build: AUD $2.3 million (approx. AUD $30/m3) per one source [R3], and separately "roughly $2.1 million AUD... over the first 10 years" per another [R5] -- both given since they disagree on scope (one-off build vs. 10-year total). Lior's own notes and a Hebrew-language source both give "$2.5 million," currency unspecified [R19][R20] -- not reconciled with the figures above. 2017-2018 renewal: approx. AUD $2 million per Mayor Tom Tate, as reported by the Gold Coast Bulletin via The Inertia [R10].
Cost (approx. USD)Very rough conversions by this report (not sourced): original build AUD $2.3M (1999 AUD~USD 0.65) approx. USD $1.5M; 2017-2018 renewal AUD $2M (2018 AUD~USD 0.75) approx. USD $1.5M.
Financed byGold Coast City Council, as part of its Northern Gold Coast Beach Protection Strategy [R1][R2][R9][R13]. No private or state/federal co-funding found in any source.
DesignerOriginal 1999 design: Prof. Kerry Black and Shaw Mead (University of Waikato, NZ; later founders of coastal-engineering firm ASR) [R11]. ICM (International Coastal Management, Gold Coast) separately credits its founder Angus Jackson with leading the project as part of the wider Northern Gold Coast Beach Protection Strategy [R3] -- the two attributions disagree on lead designer; both given. The 2017-2018 renewal's coastal-engineering consultant was reported by Swellnet as ICM [R2].
ContractorNot named for the 1999 build beyond "Gold Coast City Council" as project owner [R2][R9]. For the 2017-2018 renewal, the placement barge was the split-hull dredger Faucon, whose skipper gave on-record comments to Swellnet [R2].
Status nowStill in place and monitored by Gold Coast City Council as of the most recent sources found (2019 monitoring, 2026 commentary) [R12][R14]. As of January 2026, the Gold Coast mayor announced plans to "fast-track" a separate, new rockwall/groyne structure immediately south of Narrowneck -- not a rebuild of the existing reef -- contested by local surfer/environmental group Save Our Spit Alliance; a live, unresolved controversy, not a completed project [R12].
Verdictmixed

sections.title: Motivation & who pushed for it
sections.html_or_text: Erosion problem predates the reef by decades: a 1971 Delft University of Technology report, commissioned by the Queensland Government, recommended a groyne at Narrowneck [R9][R13]. Training walls built at the Spit in 1985 helped erosion further north but not at Narrowneck itself, and Cyclone Nancy (1990) eroded the beach back to the boulder wall protecting the Nerang River [R2]. Gold Coast City Council chose an artificial reef instead of the recommended groyne, branding it a "Multi-Purpose Reef" so that surfing amenity could be folded into the PR case in a surf-centric city [R2][R9][R13]. No evidence found of state/federal political involvement or a single named political champion for the original 1999 project; Mayor Tom Tate became the public face of the 2017-2018 renewal [R10].

sections.title: Design as planned
sections.html_or_text: Designed by Kerry Black (University of Waikato) and Shaw Mead, using refraction-diffraction (WBEND) and Boussinesq wave modelling, checked against a 1:50-scale physical model at the UNSW Water Research Laboratory [R5][R11]. Stated targets: widen the beach 20-30 m in the reef's lee and produce surfable waves under defined conditions [R5]. A 2007 performance report (cited by Swellnet) noted the reef needed "long period, clean swell" to replicate the modelled wave shape, and that "larger swells, lower tides, and offshore winds have the potential to produce hollow, plunging breakers" [R2] -- the promised surf was explicitly conditional. The original design was a split "V" shape for both left- and right-hand rides with a paddling channel between the arms [R3][R9].

sections.title: As built vs design
sections.html_or_text: The most consequential change was a late, last-minute council decision to lower the reef's crest by 1 metre before construction -- "the change would have no effect on sand accretion but was terminal to Narrowneck becoming a good surfing reef," per Swellnet [R2]. Otherwise the built reef followed the approx. 400-container, approx. 70,000 m3 design, placed via split-hull barge with GPS [R1][R3][R9]. By approx. 2011 an underwater survey found several containers missing or damaged and seaward containers buried by sand [R4]. By 2017 the bags had "settled further into the sand" over 17 years, deeper than as-built [R2]. Designer Shaw Mead later attributed geotextile-bag failures across his firm's projects worldwide to specific causes per site, identifying boat anchors as the Gold Coast failure mechanism: "The containers failed due to a number of reasons including anchors (Gold Coast), debris strikes (Kovalam), during construction with over-filling (Mount Reef), propellor strike (Boscombe)" [R11].

sections.title: Outcome
sections.html_or_text: Coastal protection: judged successful by the council and most independent sources; an 11-year monitoring study (Jackson et al., ICCE proceedings) found 2009 storm erosion "was accommodated within the wider beach created in 1999," with gradual post-storm recovery producing a mild groyne effect [R4]. A 2019 City statement described continued sand-volume increases, but specifically in offshore sandbars rather than the upper beach -- contradicting earlier (2010-era) reports of a 30-50 m salient, which Google Earth historical imagery does not corroborate [R14]. Wikipedia (citing Turner 2006) gives an independently monitored beach-widening figure of approx. 20 m, lower than the 30-50 m figure elsewhere [R1][R14]; both given per the reference rule. Surfing: consistently underperforming versus expectations -- "disappointing in its secondary objective to improve surfing" [R9]; surfers "seldom surf the reef," persisting after the 2017-2018 renewal [R14]. An earlier study (via ecoshape.org) reported the reef broke waves "roughly 50% of the time," faces 0.7-2.0 m, average ride 150-200 m / 30 s, "fun, but not hollow, in average conditions" [R5]. Ecology: widely reported as an unplanned success -- popular fishing/diving/snorkelling site with macro-algae, fish and reported turtle activity on the geotextile substrate [R1][R3][R8][R9]; the 2011 survey found "high abundance and biodiversity" despite sand-burial and container damage [R4].

sections.title: Why it worked / failed
sections.html_or_text: Coastal protection worked primarily because the reef's core hydraulic function -- dissipating wave energy offshore and trapping sediment in the nearshore sandbar system -- does not depend on precise crest depth or bag integrity to the same degree surf-wave shaping does; even a degraded, buried or partially damaged reef still perturbs the sand-transport regime [R4][R14]. Surfing underperformed for a documented, specific reason: the council's last-minute 1-metre crest-lowering decision, made for reasons unrelated to surf quality, put the structure too deep for consistent wave-breaking under normal swell/tide/wind combinations [R2]. Compounding this, geotextile bags are inherently fragile: Shaw Mead stated that losing even a single sand-filled container changes the seabed shape and degrades wave quality, and that Gold Coast's containers specifically failed due to boat anchors [R11]. Mead's broader verdict: he "no longer believes in the viability of geotextile bags for artificial reef construction," having led a critical industry review approximately a decade after Narrowneck "which led to the change to traditional rock construction methods of the most recent MPRs built" [R11].

sections.title: Unexpected results
sections.html_or_text: Ecological colonisation and the resulting fishing/anchor-damage cycle: the reef's unplanned success as a fish habitat drew recreational fishing traffic, whose boat anchors are identified as the specific mechanism that tore the geotextile containers [R11] -- an ecological win directly causing the structural failure that required the 2017-2018 renewal. "Moving the goalposts" on beach-widening claims: early (2010-era) monitoring described a clear 30-50 m salient; by 2019 the City's official position shifted to say a salient was "never expected" and sand build-up was always meant to be offshore -- flagged by multiple Swellnet commenters as inconsistent with what residents were originally told [R14]. A 2026 political sequel: 27 years after Narrowneck was built to avoid a conventional groyne, the Gold Coast mayor proposed fast-tracking a new rockwall/groyne immediately adjacent to it, prompting the same updrift/downdrift erosion-displacement objections coastal engineers raise about hard groynes generally [R12]. Depth-measurement uncertainty: the City's post-renewal survey data claims no settlement of the new containers, directly contradicting anecdotal local reports that the new bags were already breaking less often and appeared to be settling [R14].

sections.title: What could have been done better
sections.html_or_text: Experts'/engineers' view: Shaw Mead, the reef's original designer, has publicly stated (in a critical review conducted roughly a decade after Narrowneck was built) that sand-filled geotextile containers should not be used for multi-purpose reef construction at all, and that the industry has since moved to rock construction [R11]. Swellnet's 2017 reporting singles out the crest-lowering decision as the single design change most responsible for the surf underperformance, implying a purely surf-focused crest depth would have produced a better wave without necessarily compromising protection [R2]. Surfers'/locals' view: commenters were blunter -- one ("warddy," 2019) called it an "absolute waste of money" and suggested rock construction instead; another ("the-spleen_2") noted "beach widening" had originally been "the core of the project" as pitched by Griffith University, and found it "funny to see how the idea has changed over time" toward the offshore-sandbar framing [R14].

sections.title: Relevance to Israel / Haifa
sections.html_or_text: Narrowneck's central lesson for a Haifa or other Israeli Mediterranean project is the crest-depth-versus-tide-range trade-off: the reef's surf underperformance is traced by an independent source specifically to a council decision to change crest depth relative to the tide datum, made for reasons unrelated to surfing, which then dominated wave-breaking outcomes [R2]. The Gold Coast has a meaningful astronomical tide range (crest explicitly set "1.5 m below the low tide waterline") [R2][R3] -- a variable a designer must actively engineer around, since a fixed crest depth performs differently at high versus low tide. Lior's own draft outreach material argues the Mediterranean's smaller tidal range at Haifa is an advantage for reef stability and maintenance ("the tide conditions here allow high stability and natural long-term maintenance") [R18] -- this is Lior's own hypothesis, not an independently sourced engineering conclusion, and no numeric Haifa/Mediterranean tide-range figure was found in the sources fetched for this dossier. If correct, a Haifa reef would face a smaller version of Narrowneck's tide-datum problem, making crest-depth choice a one-time design decision rather than a chronic multi-condition compromise. Separately, Narrowneck's identified failure mechanism -- boat anchors tearing geotextile bags that had become a popular fishing spot [R11] -- is directly transferable: any Israeli geotextile-based reef that succeeds ecologically should expect the same anchor-damage risk and may want to restrict anchoring or use more anchor-resistant materials such as rock, per Mead's own post-Narrowneck design shift [R11].

footprint.name: Narrowneck Reef (Gold Coast Reef)
footprint.shape_type_notes: Dual-arm split-V / chevron: two separate wishbone-shaped reef units ('north arm' and 'south arm' in this report's own labelling) set side by side alongshore, joined by a narrow central channel across which a small submerged weir (two containers) was added in 2004. Confirmed by text and four plan-view figures in the primary monitoring paper (Jackson et al. 2012, [R4]). This is NOT an inshore/offshore concentric-lobe arrangement (see gemini_comparison).
footprint.coords: metres; origin = shoreline point nearest the reef centroid; x = alongshore (positive toward north -- the Narrowneck isthmus trends roughly N-S per general regional geography, no source gives an exact shoreline azimuth); y = offshore (positive seaward); shoreline approximated as the line y=0.
footprint.polygon_components_notes: polygons_m[0] = north arm (x>0), polygons_m[1] = south arm (x<0, mirror image of the north arm in x). Both closed and non-self-intersecting (checked with shapely: is_valid=True, is_simple=True for both). No solid polygon is given for the central channel/waist (x approx -50 to 50) since it is open water crossed only by a small 2-container weir added in 2004, not a filled structure -- see md derivation/'Polygon construction'.
footprint.bbox_alt_note: A second source [R8] gives a conflicting 450 m (long) x 250 m (wide) for this same reef; not reconciled with the 600x350 [R9] figure used for this file's bounding box and polygon scaffold. Both are retained per the project reference rule.
footprint.area_m2_notes: Net area of the two schematic arm polygons above (shoelace formula: 57,475 m^2 each), NOT a published or surveyed figure -- it is a geometric consequence of this report's own illustrative vertex placement (see md 'Polygon construction'). Gross bounding-box area (600x350) = 210,000 m^2. Not directly comparable to Gemini's gross (75,000) or net (42,650) figures since Gemini's underlying shape (inshore/offshore lobes) differs from the alongshore-split shape used here.

crest_depth_m.datum: below low tide waterline (approx. LAT), as stated in sources -- design/2012 value

footprint.crest_depth_alt_note: Crest depth is time-varying and this single value should not be used without noting its date: as designed/1999 and as of the 2012 primary-source survey, crest was 'about 1-1.5m below low tide' [R4 p.13, also R2][R3]; by 2017, before the 2018 renewal, it had settled to 2.5-2.6 m below low tide [R2]; the 2018 renewal added 84 containers to raise the crest again but no source gives a specific post-renewal number.

distance_offshore_m.measured_from: shoreline -- treated as the reef's shoreward/inner edge; no source specifies exactly which point 'X m offshore' is measured to

footprint.orientation_notes: Two arms (north/south) run alongshore either side of a central channel/weir, matching the card's pre-existing 'split V shape... paddling channel between the arms' language [R3][R9]. The reef is understood to face the Gold Coast's predominant E-ESE swell (general regional geography, open east-facing coast), consistent with (though not independently confirmed to the same precision as) Gemini's claimed 090-120 deg incident swell direction -- no source found by either this report or Gemini states a precise degree figure. Alongshore axis 'north' is this report's own convention, not a sourced compass bearing.
footprint.materials: Sand-filled non-woven geotextile containers ('mega sandbags'), approx. 450 placed by 1999-2006 (arithmetic per [R4] p.3/Fig.4: ~408 from the original 1999-2000 construction + top-up, plus 42 in three later maintenance campaigns 2002-2006 [Fig.4 table: 10+15+17=42] = 450 total; R9 separately and independently gives a rounded 'more than 400' for the original build, consistent with ~408 but not an exact match to a card-invented '400') + 84 more added June 2018 [R9][R14]; each container approx. 20 m long, 3.0-4.8 m diameter [R1/R9 exact figure; corrected this pass from an earlier '3-4.5 m' rounding].

With the alongshore-split topology used here, there is no separate 'outer ridge' 300-380m out; the reef's full cross-shore extent (200-550m in this report's schematic) comes from each arm's own outer horn, not a second, more-offshore reef ring.

open_issues: No plan-view figure with a legible printed scale bar was found for this reef in any source consulted (primary paper, ICM webpage, or the card's image list); the polygon vertices in this file are a documented schematic, not a survey-grade digitization.
The card's own pre-existing footprint disagreement (350x600m [R9] vs. 450x250m [R8]) remains unreconciled; no third, tie-breaking source was found.

This report assumes north/south mirror symmetry between the two arms for the schematic polygon; Jackson et al. 2012 Fig. 4 suggests the two arms may not be perfectly identical, but source resolution does not support characterizing the actual asymmetry.

The exact shoreline azimuth at Narrowneck (to convert 'alongshore = positive north' into a true compass bearing) was not found in any source consulted; the isthmus's roughly N-S trend is inferred from general regional geography, not a stated figure.

Crest depth is genuinely time-varying (~1.0-1.5m as designed/2012 -> ~2.5-2.6m by 2017 settled -> an unstated, presumably shallower figure after the 2018 renewal); any single crest-depth number used elsewhere for this reef should specify which date/state it refers to.
The central channel's width (~100m, used to space the two arms in the schematic polygon) is this report's own unsourced assumption, not a published figure.

(Added 2026-09-25 verification pass) R9's exact text is an unordered pair '350 x 600 m' with no stated axis; this file's 600=alongshore/350=cross-shore assignment (used in bbox_m and the polygon construction) is this report's own inference, not sourced.

name: Pratte's Reef (permit name: Chevron Reef)
place: Dockweiler State Beach / El Segundo, California
year: 2000-2001 built (Phase I fall 2000, 110 bags; Phase II spring 2001, +90 bags); removed 2008-2010
type: Submerged artificial surf reef (ASR), sand-filled geotextile bags in a V/chevron layout
purpose: Surfing — court/permit-mandated legal mitigation for a surf break lost to a 1984 Chevron rock groin
size: ~200 geotextile bags total, ~1,400-1,600 m3 built volume (vs. ~3,800 m3 / 5,000 yd3 in the original 1997 proposal); crest ~0.9-2.4 m below low-tide sea level (sources disagree)
cost: $300,000 Chevron construction payment + $200,000-250,000 California Coastal Conservancy grant + $50,000 Surfrider add-on + ~$300,000 anonymous donation for removal; Surfline's cumulative headline figure is $850,000 over 2000-2008
financed_by: Chevron Corporation (construction, as legal mitigation), California Coastal Conservancy (construction top-up), Surfrider Foundation (added funds + anonymous-donor-funded removal)
motivation: Court/permit-mandated mitigation for loss of the surfable Grand Avenue break, caused by Chevron's 1984 rock groin built to stop beach erosion threatening its El Segundo refinery's offshore oil-pipeline terminal [R1][R7]
contractor: Placed by barge-mounted crane (builder not separately named in sources); removal directed by Coastal Frontiers Corporation, with American Marine Corporation (dive crew) and Morrissey Construction Company (onshore handling/disposal) [R3][R6][R10]
status_now: Removed. Phase I removal fall 2008 (Sept 30-Oct 17, 2008); Phase II removal fall 2010, coinciding with expiry of the original 10-year experimental permit. First-ever removal of a purpose-built artificial surfing reef [R3][R6][R9][R10]
hover_text: ~200 sand-filled geotextile bags (~1,400-1,600 m3) built 2000-2001 for roughly $550,000-$850,000, funded by Chevron as legal mitigation for a lost surf break; never produced a consistently surfable wave in 8 years and was removed in 2008-2010, the first-ever removal of a purpose-built artificial surfing reef [R1][R7][R6].
design_as_planned: The original 1997 CEQA filing by Surfrider Foundation (via the LA Dept. of Parks & Recreation) described '10-20 large geo-textile fabric bags containing approx. 5,000 cubic yards of sand' [R8]. As engineered by Skelly Engineering, the built design called for a V-shaped (delta/chevron) reef with arms at roughly 45 degrees to the predominant swell, meant to focus and peel incoming waves like a natural point break, cresting close to the low-tide waterline for consistent breaking [R4]. The goal was purely restoring a lost surfing amenity at the Grand Avenue break, not beach nourishment or ecological habitat creation [R4][R1].
as_built_vs_design: Construction proceeded in two funded phases instead of one: 110 bags in fall 2000 (using the initial $300,000 Chevron payment), then ~90 more bags in spring 2001 once the Coastal Conservancy added $200,000-250,000, for roughly 200 bags total [R1][R7]. Even after that expansion, the built reef was far smaller than the 1997 proposal's ~5,000 yd3 (~3,800 m3) target: built volume is reported at only ~1,400-1,600 m3 [R2][R4] — under half the size first proposed, and by Surfrider's own later accounting roughly one-seventh the volume of Mount Maunganui and one-tenth to one-thirtieth the volume of Narrowneck [R7]. Individual bags were also markedly smaller (~8 m3 each) than Narrowneck's containers (140-320 m3 each) [R2]. Chad Nelsen (Surfrider): 'we probably should have said $300,000 is not enough' [R7].
outcome: Wikipedia states the reef 'had very little effect on the surfing conditions at Dockweiler Beach and ... no measurable effect on the shoreline morphology' [R1][R2]. Surfline's 2008 feature: over 'eight plus years, Pratte's Reef was as useless as useless gets' and 'it never produced a consistently surfable wave' [R7]. Diver surveys found bags had moved, sunk, and been buried by sand, with the black polypropylene material visibly deteriorating — 'largely disintegrated' within about two years [R4][R2]. No coastal-protection or ecological benefit is reported anywhere in the sources found. The reef was removed over two phases (fall 2008, fall 2010), the first-ever removal of a purpose-built artificial surfing reef [R3][R6][R7][R9][R10].
why_worked_or_failed: Undersized for its budget and site: a $300,000-$550,000 construction budget bought a reef roughly 1/7 the size of Mount Maunganui's and 1/10-1/30 the size of Narrowneck's [R7]. Crest-depth mismatch: on big swells the crest was too deep to trigger breaking, so waves broke outside the reef [R1][R7]. Pre-existing degraded beach: the Chevron groin had already straightened/steepened the beach and buried the original Grand Avenue break in trapped sand, conditions a small mitigation reef could not reverse [R7]. Material/structural failure: sand-filled fabric bags resting on a sandy, mobile seabed with no rigid foundation settled, sank, and were buried, and the polypropylene fabric deteriorated within roughly two years [R4][R2]. Insufficient pre-construction monitoring: Nelsen said more monitoring of sand bars and beach conditions beforehand 'would have told us the reef was too small before we even put it in' [R7].
unexpected_results: No fishing-pressure or ecological side effects are reported for Pratte's Reef in any source found, unlike Narrowneck (Gold Coast), whose geotextile containers were colonized by macro-algae, benthos and pelagic fish and became popular for local (spear-)fishing, diving and snorkeling, though also flagged as vulnerable to vessel/anchor damage as a design risk [R17]. The project's most consequential outcome may have been legal/political: the 1984 mitigation condition Tom Pratte secured is credited by Surfrider as the first case in which the California Coastal Commission formally recognized a surf break as a protectable coastal recreational resource, a precedent Surfrider says later helped protect Trestles from development [R7]. Surfrider itself updated its institutional policy on artificial reefs after this project, moving toward protecting existing surf breaks rather than promising to recreate lost ones: 'I don't think we should ever trade a surf spot for the promise of building something else' (Chad Nelsen) [R7]. No litigation was found in any source reviewed.
could_be_better: Surfrider's Chad Nelsen (2008 Surfline retrospective): should have told Chevron up front that $300,000 was not enough to build a working reef; more monitoring of sand bars and beach conditions before construction would have revealed the reef was undersized before it was built; more broadly, mitigation itself is often 'a false promise', and protecting existing surf breaks is preferable to engineering replacements after the fact [R7]. Named Surfline commenters (2008): depth/tide design was wrong ('Andrew': should have been 'nearly dry on a negative tide to be legit', not 8 feet deep at zero tide); distance from shore was wrong, though commenters disagreed on direction ('Randy Wright': 'simply too far away from the shore'; Dr. Jose Borrero, quoted elsewhere: 'too small and too close to shore'); cruder/cheaper materials might have worked as well ('prattes is a joke': rocks or 'smashed up cars'); lack of surfer input in the engineering process ('evan') [R7][R4].
relevance_to_israel: Tidal range is the single most transferable engineering lesson: Pratte's Reef's crest depth was wrong for the local tide swing (too deep to break big swells; ~8 ft/2.4 m deep even at zero/low tide per a Surfrider-sourced figure) [R7]. Santa Monica Bay has a mean tidal range of ~1.4-1.7 m [R12], versus Haifa's ~0.3-0.4 m [R13], consistent with the Mediterranean's generally small tides [R11] — a crest depth calibrated for Haifa's ~0.3-0.4 m swing is a much smaller, more predictable engineering target than one spanning ~1.5 m, supporting Lior's thesis that Israel's small tidal range is a structural advantage for reef stability [R15]. Budget-driven undersizing is a transferable governance/funding risk, not a site-specific one, relevant to any small pilot reef Israel might build on a limited budget. Material degradation (UV/wave abrasion of polypropylene bags within ~2 years) is a warning for any low-cost geotextile design proposed for the Israeli coast, including Lior's own 'cheap & light materials... for fast deployment and removal' sketch [R15]. Israel has no directly comparable built ASR yet — its only confirmed built geotextile project is the Ashkelon Geotube, a shore-protection structure, not a surf reef [R14].

videos.title: Pratte's Reef
videos.relevance_evidence: Title is the reef's name and the description names Chevron USA, Surfrider and Tom Pratte. About 13 of the 30 minutes (roughly 14:00-27:00) are the reef itself: its purpose, designer Dave Skelly explaining the planned geotextile-bag chevron layout, and a Tom Pratte tribute. It is a PRE-construction documentary (closing line says the wave 'remains to be seen'); the spoken track contains nothing about the built reef. Earlier frame checks (2026-09-24) found no footage of the actual reef; whether the picture shows plans/animation is not verifiable from the transcript.
