videos.date: 2016-04-18 (upload date; content/interviews are contemporaneous with the 1998-2000 project run-up, before construction)
videos.what_it_shows: A ~30-minute documentary about the origin of Pratte's Reef: the 1983-84 El Nino storm damage and Chevron groin construction, Tom Pratte's Coastal Commission mitigation condition, the earlier failed 'Hoppy's Reef' attempt near Redondo Beach, and on-camera interviews with reef designer Dave Skelly (Skelly Engineering) explaining the planned V/chevron-shaped geotextile-bag design, plus commentary from Surfrider/local surfers and a tribute to Tom Pratte (d. 1994). Confirmed to be specifically about this site via its title, description, and content (references the El Segundo/Chevron groin, Dave Skelly, and the Surfrider/Chevron agreement).
key_quotes: [00:14:30] "We settled on Dave Skelly engineering... he was very enthusiastic about the project... would building this reef destroy something the locals value?"
[00:15:21] Dave Skelly: "It's actually a submerged breakwater... this project is kind of the dream of every surfer."

[00:18:36] Dave Skelly, describing the design: "My concept is to put out gigantic sand bags — a nice bag weighs about 12 to 14 tons, that's a rather large bag. Geotextile fabrics... have been used on the Mississippi River to control bank erosion... these bags will last probably at least two decades and possibly longer."

[00:19:04] Dave Skelly: "Construction in the surf zone is really difficult, and out here at El Segundo we have a 10-foot tide range, a mobile bottom, and waves that come from different directions. The formation that we're placing these bags in is a chevron shape formation, or v-shaped, and hopefully that will create a good right break and a good left break."

[00:23:56] Unnamed interviewee, on Tom Pratte: "Tom basically held a big company accountable for the destruction of a wave. The man was definitely ahead of his time, was a visionary — the whole project really is because of his foresight... it's Tom's reef, period."
[00:26:03] Narrator (closing): "An object lesson to see what happens... whether the crest of the perfect wave will ever rise from the waters off El Segundo remains to be seen."

sections.title: Motivation & who pushed for it
sections.html_or_text: Court/permit-mandated mitigation for loss of the surfable Grand Avenue break, caused by Chevron's 1984 rock groin built to stop beach erosion threatening its El Segundo refinery's offshore oil-pipeline terminal [R1][R7]

sections.title: Design as planned
sections.html_or_text: The original 1997 CEQA filing by Surfrider Foundation (via the LA Dept. of Parks & Recreation) described '10-20 large geo-textile fabric bags containing approx. 5,000 cubic yards of sand' [R8]. As engineered by Skelly Engineering, the built design called for a V-shaped (delta/chevron) reef with arms at roughly 45 degrees to the predominant swell, meant to focus and peel incoming waves like a natural point break, cresting close to the low-tide waterline for consistent breaking [R4]. The goal was purely restoring a lost surfing amenity at the Grand Avenue break, not beach nourishment or ecological habitat creation [R4][R1].

sections.title: As built vs design
sections.html_or_text: Construction proceeded in two funded phases instead of one: 110 bags in fall 2000 (using the initial $300,000 Chevron payment), then ~90 more bags in spring 2001 once the Coastal Conservancy added $200,000-250,000, for roughly 200 bags total [R1][R7]. Even after that expansion, the built reef was far smaller than the 1997 proposal's ~5,000 yd3 (~3,800 m3) target: built volume is reported at only ~1,400-1,600 m3 [R2][R4] — under half the size first proposed, and by Surfrider's own later accounting roughly one-seventh the volume of Mount Maunganui and one-tenth to one-thirtieth the volume of Narrowneck [R7]. Individual bags were also markedly smaller (~8 m3 each) than Narrowneck's containers (140-320 m3 each) [R2]. Chad Nelsen (Surfrider): 'we probably should have said $300,000 is not enough' [R7].

sections.title: Outcome
sections.html_or_text: Wikipedia states the reef 'had very little effect on the surfing conditions at Dockweiler Beach and ... no measurable effect on the shoreline morphology' [R1][R2]. Surfline's 2008 feature: over 'eight plus years, Pratte's Reef was as useless as useless gets' and 'it never produced a consistently surfable wave' [R7]. Diver surveys found bags had moved, sunk, and been buried by sand, with the black polypropylene material visibly deteriorating — 'largely disintegrated' within about two years [R4][R2]. No coastal-protection or ecological benefit is reported anywhere in the sources found. The reef was removed over two phases (fall 2008, fall 2010), the first-ever removal of a purpose-built artificial surfing reef [R3][R6][R7][R9][R10].

sections.title: Why it worked / failed
sections.html_or_text: Undersized for its budget and site: a $300,000-$550,000 construction budget bought a reef roughly 1/7 the size of Mount Maunganui's and 1/10-1/30 the size of Narrowneck's [R7]. Crest-depth mismatch: on big swells the crest was too deep to trigger breaking, so waves broke outside the reef [R1][R7]. Pre-existing degraded beach: the Chevron groin had already straightened/steepened the beach and buried the original Grand Avenue break in trapped sand, conditions a small mitigation reef could not reverse [R7]. Material/structural failure: sand-filled fabric bags resting on a sandy, mobile seabed with no rigid foundation settled, sank, and were buried, and the polypropylene fabric deteriorated within roughly two years [R4][R2]. Insufficient pre-construction monitoring: Nelsen said more monitoring of sand bars and beach conditions beforehand 'would have told us the reef was too small before we even put it in' [R7].

sections.title: Unexpected results
sections.html_or_text: No fishing-pressure or ecological side effects are reported for Pratte's Reef in any source found, unlike Narrowneck (Gold Coast), whose geotextile containers were colonized by macro-algae, benthos and pelagic fish and became popular for local (spear-)fishing, diving and snorkeling, though also flagged as vulnerable to vessel/anchor damage as a design risk [R17]. The project's most consequential outcome may have been legal/political: the 1984 mitigation condition Tom Pratte secured is credited by Surfrider as the first case in which the California Coastal Commission formally recognized a surf break as a protectable coastal recreational resource, a precedent Surfrider says later helped protect Trestles from development [R7]. Surfrider itself updated its institutional policy on artificial reefs after this project, moving toward protecting existing surf breaks rather than promising to recreate lost ones: 'I don't think we should ever trade a surf spot for the promise of building something else' (Chad Nelsen) [R7]. No litigation was found in any source reviewed.

sections.title: What could have been done better
sections.html_or_text: Surfrider's Chad Nelsen (2008 Surfline retrospective): should have told Chevron up front that $300,000 was not enough to build a working reef; more monitoring of sand bars and beach conditions before construction would have revealed the reef was undersized before it was built; more broadly, mitigation itself is often 'a false promise', and protecting existing surf breaks is preferable to engineering replacements after the fact [R7]. Named Surfline commenters (2008): depth/tide design was wrong ('Andrew': should have been 'nearly dry on a negative tide to be legit', not 8 feet deep at zero tide); distance from shore was wrong, though commenters disagreed on direction ('Randy Wright': 'simply too far away from the shore'; Dr. Jose Borrero, quoted elsewhere: 'too small and too close to shore'); cruder/cheaper materials might have worked as well ('prattes is a joke': rocks or 'smashed up cars'); lack of surfer input in the engineering process ('evan') [R7][R4].

sections.title: Relevance to Israel / Haifa
sections.html_or_text: Tidal range is the single most transferable engineering lesson: Pratte's Reef's crest depth was wrong for the local tide swing (too deep to break big swells; ~8 ft/2.4 m deep even at zero/low tide per a Surfrider-sourced figure) [R7]. Santa Monica Bay has a mean tidal range of ~1.4-1.7 m [R12], versus Haifa's ~0.3-0.4 m [R13], consistent with the Mediterranean's generally small tides [R11] — a crest depth calibrated for Haifa's ~0.3-0.4 m swing is a much smaller, more predictable engineering target than one spanning ~1.5 m, supporting Lior's thesis that Israel's small tidal range is a structural advantage for reef stability [R15]. Budget-driven undersizing is a transferable governance/funding risk, not a site-specific one, relevant to any small pilot reef Israel might build on a limited budget. Material degradation (UV/wave abrasion of polypropylene bags within ~2 years) is a warning for any low-cost geotextile design proposed for the Israeli coast, including Lior's own 'cheap & light materials... for fast deployment and removal' sketch [R15]. Israel has no directly comparable built ASR yet — its only confirmed built geotextile project is the Ashkelon Geotube, a shore-protection structure, not a surf reef [R14].

Card's other cited sources give two additional, conflicting as-surveyed/as-reported figures on different datums: -0.9 m MLLW (R4) and ~2.4 m/8 ft at zero tide (R7, Surfrider-sourced, quoted by a Surfline commenter) - not resolved here, likely partly a datum (MSL vs MLLW vs 'zero tide') difference.

distance_offshore_m.measured_from: shoreline (approximate; card's R1 states only '~100 yards/100 m off the beach', not a precise engineering survey; ~100 yards = 91.4 m)

footprint.orientation_notes: The reinforced central 'spine' block (where the two arms of bags converge) is the most-offshore point of the structure and faces the 'WAVE DIRECTION' arrow drawn on the Skelly Engineering plan view, i.e. the apex points seaward into the incident swell, consistent with the card's design narrative ('arms at roughly 45 degrees to the predominant swell, meant to focus and peel incoming waves'). The drawing's own 45-degree angle annotation (measured from a vertical reference line to one arm) and this file's pixel-geometry check (~92 degrees between the two arms, i.e. ~46 degrees each side of the wave-direction axis) agree closely. The two arms are markedly ASYMMETRIC: ~44 m from spine to one tip, ~33 m to the other (a ~25% difference) - a refinement on Gemini's near-symmetric 9-vertex polygon. No compass bearing for the wave-direction axis, and no indication of which arm points which alongshore (e.g. north vs south) direction, could be determined from the design drawing itself (no north arrow). Gemini's specific '260-280 deg, W-WNW' bearing is plausible for a Santa Monica Bay/El Segundo south-/west-facing beach but is not confirmed in any source in our card or found in this pass.
footprint.materials: ~200 sand-filled geotextile (described as polyester/black polypropylene) bags total, built in two phases: 110 bags fall 2000 (this drawing's exact bag count) + ~90 more bags spring 2001; individual bags ~14 tons (R4) or ~14,000 lb (R7) - sources disagree ~2x; bag footprint 3 m x 1.2 m per the Raised Water Research bag-size diagram (R4) [R1][R2][R4][R7].

open_issues: This file's Skelly-drawing-based measurements (R4) describe the Phase I design only (110 bags + up to 30 'optional' bags = up to 140), matching the fall-2000 as-built count exactly. No plan-view drawing was found anywhere in our references for the spring-2001 Phase II addition (~90 more bags, bringing the total to ~200 built) - the FINAL as-built footprint (2001-2008) may have been somewhat larger than reported here, by an unknown amount.

The arm cross-section width (4 m) and spine-block size (8x6 m) used to turn the drawing's bag-chain centrelines into a closed polygon are this file's own estimate (from the bag-size diagram and visual inspection), not a published figure - area_m2 (324.1) should be read as order-of-magnitude only, not a precise footprint.

No compass bearing or north arrow appears on the Skelly drawing; this file's alongshore (x) axis direction is an arbitrary, stated-but-unverified convention (same limitation flagged in the parallel cables-reef-wa.md file for that reef).

The card's own two pre-existing crest-depth figures (-0.9 m MLLW per R4's text vs ~2.4 m/8 ft at zero tide per R7) remain unresolved; this file's new '-6 ft MSL' (1.83 m) reading from the drawing itself is a third data point, close to but not identical to either, plausibly a datum (MSL vs MLLW vs 'zero tide') difference rather than a genuine conflict - not resolved here.

All pixel measurements come from a low-resolution (308x385 px) scanned engineering drawing; scale-bar tick-mark reading, bag-corner anti-aliasing, and line thickness contribute an estimated +/-10% uncertainty to every length/width/area figure derived from it.

name: Mount Maunganui Beach Reef ("Mount Reef")
year: 2005-2008 (construction started Feb/Nov 2005 — sources disagree on month — finished June 2008) [R2][R3][R4][R12]
purpose: Multipurpose: improve surfing wave quality (primary, per designer), plus hoped-for coastal-protection and public-amenity/tourism benefits [R13][R1]
size: Designed volume ~5,000 m3 [R1] or 6,000 m3 [R2] (sources disagree); built/actual volume only 2,800 m3 [R2]. Footprint 50 m wide x 100 m long (perpendicular to shore), containers up to 60 m long x 5 m diameter, per [R2]; an earlier (Nov 2005, pre-completion) account describes a V-shaped layout of two 70 m x 30 m arms sited 240 m offshore [R8]
cost: NZ$1.5 million (~US$1 million at the time), per most sources [R2][R6][R7][R12]; one source (Wikipedia's Mount Maunganui page) instead gives an initial estimate of ~NZ$500,000 escalating to ~NZ$800,000 [R10]. Removal cost NZ$87,000 per [R2], vs "~NZ$60,000" per [R3][R4]
financed_by: Public donations plus community funding groups via the Mount Maunganui Reef Trust: TECT NZ$250,000, Pub Charity NZ$200,000, Bay Trust NZ$80,000 [R6][R4]
motivation: The Mount Maunganui Reef Trust obtained resource consent in August 2000 for a pilot offshore submerged reef, conceived partly as ongoing University of Waikato surf-reef research and partly as a community/tourism project to give the town "a superior surf break" and attract surfing visitors [R4]. The Reef Trust argued the reef would "return more than 30 times its cost through visitor spending," an economic-development pitch used to solicit the public donations and community-funding-group grants that ultimately paid for it [R8][R6]. It was explicitly framed by its designer, ASR Ltd/Kerry Black, as a wave-quality project rather than a coastal-protection project: "Like Cable Station, the Mount Reef was designed purely to improve surfing wave quality" [R1].
designer: Dr Kerry Black / ASR Ltd (Raglan, NZ); design/concept paper co-authored by Black and Mead [R2][R8][R4][R9]. Master-list-cited design paper: "Black, S.M.; Kerry, A. 1999, Coastal Manag. 27:355-365" [R13] — author-name order looks like a transcription slip for Black, K.P. & Mead, S.T.
contractor: Local Tauranga-area contractors managing construction (not named in sources found); ASR Ltd as design/engineering lead [R4]
status_now: Partially removed 2014 (large geotextile containers taken out, 25 September-10 November 2014); resource consent had lapsed in 2010 [R3][R4][R6]. Remnant geotextile fabric was still washing ashore as late as January 2023, confirming the reef was not fully cleared [R12]
hover_text: A submerged geotextile-container reef built 2005-2008 for NZ$1.5 million (~US$1m) via public/community-trust funding, aimed at improving surf quality; it was built to only about half its designed sand volume, produced rideable waves only rarely, worsened rip currents near a popular swimming beach, and was partially removed by the regional council in 2014 after its consent lapsed — with debris still washing ashore in 2023 [R1][R2][R3][R6][R7][R12].
design_as_planned: The design, credited to Kerry Black and ASR Ltd (design/concept paper Black & Mead, cited by the project master list as "Black, S.M.; Kerry, A. 1999, Coastal Manag. 27:355-365" [R13]), called for a reef built from large sand-filled geotextile containers, sized larger than the earlier Narrowneck (Gold Coast) units, for a total design volume reported as approximately 5,000 m3 by one source [R1] and 6,000 m3 by another [R2]. The design promised world-class, high-quality peeling waves able to host up to 50 surfers at once [R4], plus (implicitly, from the "multipurpose" framing used across the sources) some coastal-protection and amenity value [R13]. An early construction-phase account (Nov 2005) describes a V-shaped layout of two 70 m x 30 m arms set 240 m offshore [R8], while the reef as intended in its final form is described elsewhere as a 50 m x 100 m submerged footprint using containers up to 60 m long and 5 m in diameter [R2]. No crest-depth figure, sand/rock split, or hydrodynamic wave-height model output was found in any source fetched for this dossier. Design and construction details from the paper by the designers: design waves 1-3 m height, 5-13 s period (optimum 11 s), optimal approach 50 +-20 degrees True; the 2004 final "Delta" reef is symmetrical about its axis with peel of 50-65 m each way, an offshore focus zone sloping 1:20-1:50 backed by a horseshoe "wedge" breaking zone at 1:20-1:10 [R16]. A 1:20 physical model showed a barrel of only about 30 m and a crest too narrow, so the wedge was widened, and the shape could not be built from sand-filled containers; a 1:21 plastic-tube model followed; best waves were at mid tide with 1.5-2 m swell and the reef closes out above about 3 m [R16]. It was built by the "reef assembled onshore" method (sewn webbing, geomat under the bags against differential settling, geo-containers, straps) in two halves of 12 containers each, from 50 x 7.2 x 3.2 m high (filled) down to 30 x 1.5 x 1.0 m; each half is about 80 x 30 m and was winched into the sea in 3.5 hours, then filled in situ with sand pumped from the nearby seabed (8/6 Warman submersible pump), with manta anchors at surveyed positions and bi-monthly surveys [R16]. The wedge version (87.6 m overall, 75.1 m wide) was a design only and was never built [R16].
as_built_vs_design: Construction was repeatedly delayed by bad weather and equipment failure [R1], stretched over roughly three years (2005-2008) instead of a single season, and never reached the designed volume: the finished structure held only about 2,800 m3 of sand-filled geotextile against a design target of 5,000-6,000 m3 [R1][R2] — i.e. built at roughly half the intended volume. Construction proceeded in halves: the left/western side began in November 2005, and by 8 March 2006 was already producing "quick, head-high, left-hand barrels" on a small windswell even while incomplete [R2]. The right side was reported "nearly to specifications" by October 2006, but final construction did not finish until June 2008 [R2][R7] — a multi-year gap the sources attribute to weather, funding, and construction snags rather than a single design change [R1][R2]. ASR Ltd, the reef's designer, later went into liquidation; the company was also separately criticised for its Boscombe (Dorset, UK) surf reef, which suffered comparable geotextile-container degradation within about two years of construction according to a peer-reviewed evaluation of that reef [R4][R9]. Mead & Borrero (2011) give the design volume as 6,500 m3 and say it was never fully completed to specification: construction began in November 2005 and suffered delays, overruns, ruptured geo-containers, unsealed ports that lost sand, and plant failure [R17]. By late October 2006 the right-hander was close to design and gave hollow tubing waves, but one of the largest containers was damaged beyond repair and removed; it took about nine months to replace it, and meanwhile an adjacent container slumped into the 60 x 6 m gap (a crest about 1 m lower at the offshore end) and sand was lost from the lower containers, so "only 2,800 m3 of the 6,500 m3 design volume" was in place (their Fig. 3) [R17]. At the time of the 2007 paper the reef was about 70 % complete, the main focus area was unfilled and many bags were not full; an October 2006 bathymetric survey (Fig. 12) shows the gap [R16]. The reef was built about 50 m closer to shore than designed, at the limit of the Port of Tauranga nearshore dredge-disposal grounds, so it lies inside the surf zone in large waves [R17].
outcome: When it worked, surfers reported the reef producing "quick barreling waves similar to what you might find at a ledge like the Box but smaller," with ride lengths of 20-40 m [R2]; the very first days of surf on the partially built reef (Sunday, per an article dated 21-22 December 2005, i.e. most likely 18 December 2005) were described as short, sharp, chest-to-shoulder-high waves that mostly "disappeared before making the link" to the inner beach, more suited to bodyboarders than standing surfers at that stage [R5]. But usable conditions were rare: long-time local surfer and former surf-shop owner Derek Winter said rideable surf occurred only "three or four times since the surf reef was completed" and called it "pretty pathetic" [R7]. ASR's Dr Shaw Mead conceded the reef was "over-sold and under-delivered" and was "a fickle break" that needed precise swell/tide alignment [R7]. Coastal-protection performance was mixed: one source reports the beach in the reef's lee grew "up to 20 m wider than sections of the beach away from the reef" [R1] (an unreferenced-elsewhere, single-source claim). Safety outcomes were negative: the reef caused scouring, "unexpected holes in adjacent sand," and "increased rip currents," raising lifeguard call-out rates and drawing a "dangerous flop" verdict from lifeguards [R2][R3][R4]. The five-year resource consent lapsed in 2010, an independent specialist report assessed status-quo/removal/repair options, and the Bay of Plenty Regional Council opted for (partial) removal, executed 25 September-10 November 2014 at a reported cost of NZ$87,000 [R2] (vs "~NZ$60,000" in two other accounts [R3][R4]), described by council staff as completed "on time and within budget" [R6]. Removal was only partial — large sections of geotextile fabric, "likely" from this reef "given the large size of the geotextile fabric," washed ashore near Sutherland Ave on 18 January 2023, prompting a fresh council clean-up and safety advisory [R12]. Mead & Borrero (2011) judge the reef "a failure in terms of surfing": it breaks only in a very confined set of conditions; they also note that, being inside the surf zone in large waves, it was counter-productive for coastal protection (citing Ranasinghe, Turner and Symonds, 2006, Coastal Engineering 53:589-611), that more than 30 theses and peer-reviewed papers came from it, and (citing Weppe et al., 2009, Proc. 19th Australasian Coasts and Ports) that the beach widened by about 25 m with a positive influence along about 150 m of beach south-east of the reef [R17].
why_worked_or_failed: The core engineering failure identified across sources is a volume shortfall: the reef was built to roughly half its designed sand volume (2,800 m3 actual vs. 5,000-6,000 m3 designed) [R1][R2], which the sources link to construction delays from weather and equipment failure rather than a documented deliberate redesign [R1]. This under-delivery meant the structure could not reliably reproduce the wave shape the design promised, leaving it "fickle" and dependent on rare, precisely-aligned swell and tide conditions [R7]. On the coastal-process side, the reef altered nearshore currents in ways that were not the intended benefit: it produced localised scour holes and intensified rip currents near the structure, which lifeguard services flagged as an escalating safety hazard rather than an amenity [R2][R3][R4]. The comparable Boscombe reef (same designer, ASR Ltd) showed geotextile containers physically degrading within about two years in a shallow marine setting, pointing to a possible generic durability weakness in ASR's geotextile-container approach beyond Mount Maunganui alone [R9].
unexpected_results: The reef's most consequential unexpected effect was safety-negative rather than safety-positive: instead of the hoped-for amenity, it measurably worsened rip-current frequency and intensity near a popular swimming beach, to the point that Bay of Plenty Regional Council deputy chief executive Eddie Grogan stated "the reef's expected positive effects have not been realised. It's also generated some unforeseen effects, including creating a large scour hole which affects waves and currents, increasing the frequency and intensity of rips which pose a serious risk to swimmers in the popular Tay Street area" [R3]. Mount Lifeguard Service and Omanu Surf Lifesaving Club both had to increase monitoring in the area because of this [R6]. Local surf lifesaving bodies ultimately called the project a "white elephant" that caused "more headaches than success stories" [R6]. A second unexpected result was the reef's very slow, incomplete "removal": geotextile fabric attributable to the structure was still surfacing and washing onto the beach nearly a decade after the 2014 removal project was declared complete, in January 2023 [R12].
could_be_better: Council staff and the independent specialist report that Bay of Plenty Regional Council commissioned before deciding on removal framed the core problem as a structure that could not deliver its promised benefits while actively creating a new hazard (rips), concluding removal was the only responsible option [R3]. ASR's own Dr Shaw Mead acknowledged the project had been "over-sold and under-delivered" [R7]. Veteran local surfer Derek Winter framed it as a trust-and-value failure rather than a purely technical one — that the community "were sold a con or a lemon" [R7]. No source fetched gives a specific engineering fix in Mount Maunganui's own case; the closest is the implicit conclusion, drawn by comparing design (5,000-6,000 m3) to built (2,800 m3), that finishing construction to the full designed volume was the design team's and Trust's own unmet target [R1][R2].
relevance_to_israel: Tauranga/Mount Maunganui is a micro-tidal to low-meso-tidal harbour coast: the tide-table data source shows high tides ranging roughly 1.5-2.1 m and lows ranging roughly -0.1-0.6 m over a monthly cycle [R11]. This is a genuinely tidal environment — meaningfully larger than the near-zero, sub-0.5 m Mediterranean tidal range at Haifa/Israel that Lior's own outreach material argues is an advantage for reef stability [R14]. What transfers directly to Israel is not the tide range but the two failure modes documented here: (1) under-building relative to design volume (only ~47-56% of the designed sand volume was actually placed [R1][R2]) as a root cause of underperformance, and (2) a geotextile-container reef's capacity to unintentionally amplify rip currents near a public swimming beach [R2][R3][R4] — a safety risk that would need explicit hydrodynamic modelling before any similar structure is proposed for an Israeli beach. The fact that Mount Maunganui's higher tidal range did not save the project from failure (the failure was volume/construction-driven, not tide-driven) is itself a useful data point against overstating Israel's low-tide advantage as sufficient on its own.

hover.outcome: A submerged geotextile-container reef built 2005-2008 for NZ$1.5 million (~US$1m) via public/community-trust funding, aimed at improving surf quality; it was built to only about half its designed sand volume, produced rideable waves only rarely, worsened rip currents near a popular swimming beach, and was partially removed by the regional council in 2014 after its consent lapsed — with debris still washing ashore in 2023 [R1][R2][R3][R6][R7][R12].

sections.title: Motivation & who pushed for it
sections.html_or_text: The Mount Maunganui Reef Trust obtained resource consent in August 2000 for a pilot offshore submerged reef, conceived partly as ongoing University of Waikato surf-reef research and partly as a community/tourism project to give the town "a superior surf break" and attract surfing visitors [R4]. The Reef Trust argued the reef would "return more than 30 times its cost through visitor spending," an economic-development pitch used to solicit the public donations and community-funding-group grants that ultimately paid for it [R8][R6]. It was explicitly framed by its designer, ASR Ltd/Kerry Black, as a wave-quality project rather than a coastal-protection project: "Like Cable Station, the Mount Reef was designed purely to improve surfing wave quality" [R1].

sections.title: Design as planned
sections.html_or_text: The design, credited to Kerry Black and ASR Ltd (design/concept paper Black & Mead, cited by the project master list as "Black, S.M.; Kerry, A. 1999, Coastal Manag. 27:355-365" [R13]), called for a reef built from large sand-filled geotextile containers, sized larger than the earlier Narrowneck (Gold Coast) units, for a total design volume reported as approximately 5,000 m3 by one source [R1] and 6,000 m3 by another [R2]. The design promised world-class, high-quality peeling waves able to host up to 50 surfers at once [R4], plus (implicitly, from the "multipurpose" framing used across the sources) some coastal-protection and amenity value [R13]. An early construction-phase account (Nov 2005) describes a V-shaped layout of two 70 m x 30 m arms set 240 m offshore [R8], while the reef as intended in its final form is described elsewhere as a 50 m x 100 m submerged footprint using containers up to 60 m long and 5 m in diameter [R2]. No crest-depth figure, sand/rock split, or hydrodynamic wave-height model output was found in any source fetched for this dossier. Design and construction details from the paper by the designers: design waves 1-3 m height, 5-13 s period (optimum 11 s), optimal approach 50 +-20 degrees True; the 2004 final "Delta" reef is symmetrical about its axis with peel of 50-65 m each way, an offshore focus zone sloping 1:20-1:50 backed by a horseshoe "wedge" breaking zone at 1:20-1:10 [R16]. A 1:20 physical model showed a barrel of only about 30 m and a crest too narrow, so the wedge was widened, and the shape could not be built from sand-filled containers; a 1:21 plastic-tube model followed; best waves were at mid tide with 1.5-2 m swell and the reef closes out above about 3 m [R16]. It was built by the "reef assembled onshore" method (sewn webbing, geomat under the bags against differential settling, geo-containers, straps) in two halves of 12 containers each, from 50 x 7.2 x 3.2 m high (filled) down to 30 x 1.5 x 1.0 m; each half is about 80 x 30 m and was winched into the sea in 3.5 hours, then filled in situ with sand pumped from the nearby seabed (8/6 Warman submersible pump), with manta anchors at surveyed positions and bi-monthly surveys [R16]. The wedge version (87.6 m overall, 75.1 m wide) was a design only and was never built [R16].

sections.title: As built vs design
sections.html_or_text: Construction was repeatedly delayed by bad weather and equipment failure [R1], stretched over roughly three years (2005-2008) instead of a single season, and never reached the designed volume: the finished structure held only about 2,800 m3 of sand-filled geotextile against a design target of 5,000-6,000 m3 [R1][R2] — i.e. built at roughly half the intended volume. Construction proceeded in halves: the left/western side began in November 2005, and by 8 March 2006 was already producing "quick, head-high, left-hand barrels" on a small windswell even while incomplete [R2]. The right side was reported "nearly to specifications" by October 2006, but final construction did not finish until June 2008 [R2][R7] — a multi-year gap the sources attribute to weather, funding, and construction snags rather than a single design change [R1][R2]. ASR Ltd, the reef's designer, later went into liquidation; the company was also separately criticised for its Boscombe (Dorset, UK) surf reef, which suffered comparable geotextile-container degradation within about two years of construction according to a peer-reviewed evaluation of that reef [R4][R9]. Mead & Borrero (2011) give the design volume as 6,500 m3 and say it was never fully completed to specification: construction began in November 2005 and suffered delays, overruns, ruptured geo-containers, unsealed ports that lost sand, and plant failure [R17]. By late October 2006 the right-hander was close to design and gave hollow tubing waves, but one of the largest containers was damaged beyond repair and removed; it took about nine months to replace it, and meanwhile an adjacent container slumped into the 60 x 6 m gap (a crest about 1 m lower at the offshore end) and sand was lost from the lower containers, so "only 2,800 m3 of the 6,500 m3 design volume" was in place (their Fig. 3) [R17]. At the time of the 2007 paper the reef was about 70 % complete, the main focus area was unfilled and many bags were not full; an October 2006 bathymetric survey (Fig. 12) shows the gap [R16]. The reef was built about 50 m closer to shore than designed, at the limit of the Port of Tauranga nearshore dredge-disposal grounds, so it lies inside the surf zone in large waves [R17].

sections.title: Outcome
sections.html_or_text: When it worked, surfers reported the reef producing "quick barreling waves similar to what you might find at a ledge like the Box but smaller," with ride lengths of 20-40 m [R2]; the very first days of surf on the partially built reef (Sunday, per an article dated 21-22 December 2005, i.e. most likely 18 December 2005) were described as short, sharp, chest-to-shoulder-high waves that mostly "disappeared before making the link" to the inner beach, more suited to bodyboarders than standing surfers at that stage [R5]. But usable conditions were rare: long-time local surfer and former surf-shop owner Derek Winter said rideable surf occurred only "three or four times since the surf reef was completed" and called it "pretty pathetic" [R7]. ASR's Dr Shaw Mead conceded the reef was "over-sold and under-delivered" and was "a fickle break" that needed precise swell/tide alignment [R7]. Coastal-protection performance was mixed: one source reports the beach in the reef's lee grew "up to 20 m wider than sections of the beach away from the reef" [R1] (an unreferenced-elsewhere, single-source claim). Safety outcomes were negative: the reef caused scouring, "unexpected holes in adjacent sand," and "increased rip currents," raising lifeguard call-out rates and drawing a "dangerous flop" verdict from lifeguards [R2][R3][R4]. The five-year resource consent lapsed in 2010, an independent specialist report assessed status-quo/removal/repair options, and the Bay of Plenty Regional Council opted for (partial) removal, executed 25 September-10 November 2014 at a reported cost of NZ$87,000 [R2] (vs "~NZ$60,000" in two other accounts [R3][R4]), described by council staff as completed "on time and within budget" [R6]. Removal was only partial — large sections of geotextile fabric, "likely" from this reef "given the large size of the geotextile fabric," washed ashore near Sutherland Ave on 18 January 2023, prompting a fresh council clean-up and safety advisory [R12]. Mead & Borrero (2011) judge the reef "a failure in terms of surfing": it breaks only in a very confined set of conditions; they also note that, being inside the surf zone in large waves, it was counter-productive for coastal protection (citing Ranasinghe, Turner and Symonds, 2006, Coastal Engineering 53:589-611), that more than 30 theses and peer-reviewed papers came from it, and (citing Weppe et al., 2009, Proc. 19th Australasian Coasts and Ports) that the beach widened by about 25 m with a positive influence along about 150 m of beach south-east of the reef [R17].

sections.title: Why it worked / failed
sections.html_or_text: The core engineering failure identified across sources is a volume shortfall: the reef was built to roughly half its designed sand volume (2,800 m3 actual vs. 5,000-6,000 m3 designed) [R1][R2], which the sources link to construction delays from weather and equipment failure rather than a documented deliberate redesign [R1]. This under-delivery meant the structure could not reliably reproduce the wave shape the design promised, leaving it "fickle" and dependent on rare, precisely-aligned swell and tide conditions [R7]. On the coastal-process side, the reef altered nearshore currents in ways that were not the intended benefit: it produced localised scour holes and intensified rip currents near the structure, which lifeguard services flagged as an escalating safety hazard rather than an amenity [R2][R3][R4]. The comparable Boscombe reef (same designer, ASR Ltd) showed geotextile containers physically degrading within about two years in a shallow marine setting, pointing to a possible generic durability weakness in ASR's geotextile-container approach beyond Mount Maunganui alone [R9].

sections.title: Unexpected results
sections.html_or_text: The reef's most consequential unexpected effect was safety-negative rather than safety-positive: instead of the hoped-for amenity, it measurably worsened rip-current frequency and intensity near a popular swimming beach, to the point that Bay of Plenty Regional Council deputy chief executive Eddie Grogan stated "the reef's expected positive effects have not been realised. It's also generated some unforeseen effects, including creating a large scour hole which affects waves and currents, increasing the frequency and intensity of rips which pose a serious risk to swimmers in the popular Tay Street area" [R3]. Mount Lifeguard Service and Omanu Surf Lifesaving Club both had to increase monitoring in the area because of this [R6]. Local surf lifesaving bodies ultimately called the project a "white elephant" that caused "more headaches than success stories" [R6]. A second unexpected result was the reef's very slow, incomplete "removal": geotextile fabric attributable to the structure was still surfacing and washing onto the beach nearly a decade after the 2014 removal project was declared complete, in January 2023 [R12].

sections.title: What could have been done better
sections.html_or_text: Council staff and the independent specialist report that Bay of Plenty Regional Council commissioned before deciding on removal framed the core problem as a structure that could not deliver its promised benefits while actively creating a new hazard (rips), concluding removal was the only responsible option [R3]. ASR's own Dr Shaw Mead acknowledged the project had been "over-sold and under-delivered" [R7]. Veteran local surfer Derek Winter framed it as a trust-and-value failure rather than a purely technical one — that the community "were sold a con or a lemon" [R7]. No source fetched gives a specific engineering fix in Mount Maunganui's own case; the closest is the implicit conclusion, drawn by comparing design (5,000-6,000 m3) to built (2,800 m3), that finishing construction to the full designed volume was the design team's and Trust's own unmet target [R1][R2].

sections.title: Relevance to Israel / Haifa
sections.html_or_text: Tauranga/Mount Maunganui is a micro-tidal to low-meso-tidal harbour coast: the tide-table data source shows high tides ranging roughly 1.5-2.1 m and lows ranging roughly -0.1-0.6 m over a monthly cycle [R11]. This is a genuinely tidal environment — meaningfully larger than the near-zero, sub-0.5 m Mediterranean tidal range at Haifa/Israel that Lior's own outreach material argues is an advantage for reef stability [R14]. What transfers directly to Israel is not the tide range but the two failure modes documented here: (1) under-building relative to design volume (only ~47-56% of the designed sand volume was actually placed [R1][R2]) as a root cause of underperformance, and (2) a geotextile-container reef's capacity to unintentionally amplify rip currents near a public swimming beach [R2][R3][R4] — a safety risk that would need explicit hydrodynamic modelling before any similar structure is proposed for an Israeli beach. The fact that Mount Maunganui's higher tidal range did not save the project from failure (the failure was volume/construction-driven, not tide-driven) is itself a useful data point against overstating Israel's low-tide advantage as sufficient on its own.

footprint.name: Mount Maunganui Beach Reef ("Mount Reef")
footprint.coords: metres; origin = shoreline point (Tay St / Marine Parade waterline) nearest the reef centroid; x = alongshore (positive toward north, matching the sourced "northern arm" / "southern arm" naming in S1/Mead 2011 - exact compass bearing of this axis is not stated in any source, only the relative north/south naming of the two arms); y = offshore (positive seaward); shoreline approximated as the line y=0

crest_depth_m.datum: below Chart Datum (~ Lowest Astronomical Tide, LAT); DESIGN target was 0.4 m below LAT/Chart Datum; the most recent surveys (to 2013) found the MAJORITY of the as-built crest at 0.8-1.0 m below Chart Datum. S1 s2.1 separately states that 'at its highest point, the reef is approximately 0.2 m below chart datum, or approximately 0.1 m below the lowest astronomical tide' -- this is ONE point expressed in two datums (not a 0.1-0.2 m range), and S1's text does NOT say which arm it is on [CORRECTED 2026-09-25 verification pass: the original text here wrongly attributed this point to 'the northern arm crest', a detail invented by the prior pass and not present in S1's own text]. S1 s4.3.2.1 separately, and explicitly, states an isolated shallow spot on the SOUTHERN arm at 0.2-0.4 m below Chart Datum (July 2013 survey) -- given the similar depth and shared 'most recent survey' framing, this may be the same feature as the unattributed s2.1 point, but S1 never states this equivalence, so both are kept as separate, uncombined source statements. The single 0.9 m value here is our own midpoint of the reported 0.8-1.0 m 'majority of the reef' figure, not itself a directly quoted number.

distance_offshore_m.notes: Convergent across five independent-ish accounts: R12 (NZ Herald 2023) states 250 m directly; S1 (BoPRC consent-application text) gives 250-300 m; S4 (NZ Geographic 2006, quoting designer Kerry Black) gives 250 m; R2 (raisedwaterresearch.com) explains the reef was DESIGNED for 300 m but built ~50 m closer due to Port of Tauranga dredge-disposal-area constraints, i.e. ~250 m as sited; R8 (NZ Herald, Nov 2005, pre-completion) gives 240 m. We treat 250 m as the best-supported as-sited figure and 300 m as the superseded original design target.

footprint.orientation_notes: DESIGN intent (S4, NZ Geographic 2006, quoting designer Kerry Black): 'the apex of the V points seaward and the structure thickens towards the base' - i.e. a symmetric, seaward-pointing V/delta-wing widening toward the shore. AS-BUILT (per S1's multibeam survey figures, Jan 2007 at 70% complete and July 2013): the realised structure is NOT a clean symmetric V - it is a bent, asymmetric two-arm shape (a 'northern arm' and a 'southern arm' meeting near a central apex/focus point, per S1's own terminology, e.g. 'the focus structure at the apex'), with the northern arm's containers rendered as a roughly shore-parallel band and the southern arm's containers rendered as a roughly cross-shore band, meeting at an angle visually closer to ~90 degrees than to the narrow symmetric V shown in the ASR/raisedwaterresearch.com CAD rendering (R2's 'Mount Reef' design image). This asymmetry is consistent with, and likely a direct consequence of, the well-documented staged/incomplete construction (western/northern side built and surfable from Nov 2005-Mar 2006; eastern/southern side still 'nearly to specifications' by Oct 2006; final completion not until mid-2008) and the ~47% volume shortfall. The polygon in this file models the AS-BUILT bent shape (two separate arm rectangles under polygons_m), not the idealised symmetric design V.

volume_m3.notes: As-built volume, per Mead (2011) as cited in S1 and independently corroborated by R2 (2,800 m3). Design volume was 6,000 m3 per S1/S4 (R2 and R1 separately give 6,000 and ~5,000 m3 respectively for the design target - sources disagree on the exact design figure, see card).

footprint.materials: Sand-filled non-woven geotextile 'megacontainers' on a securing mesh/web lattice pulled to the seabed [R2][R8][S1][S4]. Design called for up to 24 large cylindrical bags [S4] (the largest 3.5 m high x 50 m long, holding 660 m3 each [S4]; alternatively described elsewhere as bags 'up to 60 m long x 5 m diameter' [R2] - these two bag-size descriptions do not match each other and neither source reconciles the difference, see open_issues). As-built, S1 (citing Mead 2011) instead describes 6 containers per arm (3 large crest containers + 3 smaller base containers per side, 12 total design, with the as-built base containers substituted for shorter units) - a third, different container-count description that also does not reconcile with S4's '24 bags' figure.

[CORRECTED 2026-09-25 verification pass: the original text here claimed this figure 'does not by itself reconcile arithmetically with S1's later as-built 80x70 bounding envelope under a simple symmetric-V geometry' and that 'no single symmetric half-angle satisfies both' -- this was checked by direct computation (python, sweeping the half-angle) and is WRONG: a symmetric V with two 70x30 m arms at a half-angle of approximately 22 degrees from the shore-normal axis produces an 80.05 x 70.54 m bounding envelope, matching S1's stated 80x70 m almost exactly. Treat individual arm lengths as +/-15 m uncertain; the overall bounding envelope (from S1's own stated 80x70 m) is much more reliable than our specific vertex placement.

gemini_values.shape_type: Swept-Wing Inverted Y / Chevron with Central Ridge
gemini_values.area_m2: 4800.0 gross (Gemini's own audit separately computes a net arm area of 2,455 m2)
sources_cited_by_gemini: Black, S.M. & Kerry, A. (1999). Coastal Manag. 27:355-365.
Mead, S. et al. (2007). Mount Maunganui Reef Monitoring Report. ASR Ltd.
Tauranga City Council: Tay Street Reef Removal Dossier (2014).

agree: Distance offshore (~250 m): matches our own best-supported figure exactly, and both are independently corroborated by multiple sources on our side (R12, S1, S4, R2's derivation) - genuine agreement, not coincidence.

General shape family ('chevron' / V-with-two-arms): Gemini's 'chevron' classification and our own (also 'chevron', built from two named arms) agree at the topology level, even though the specific polygon coordinates and gross/net dimensions disagree substantially (see below).

Net footprint/arm area (~2,455 m2 Gemini vs our 2,497 m2): close numerical agreement, though reached by very different methods and starting bounding dimensions - we treat this as a loose corroboration at best, not confirmation, given how differently each figure was derived.

Design crest depth in the same ballpark: Gemini's own footprint-notes mention 'Designed for -0.5m LAT', close to our sourced 0.4 m below LAT design target [S1] - a genuine partial match on the DESIGN figure specifically.

disagree.quantity: overall gross bounding dimensions (alongshore x cross-shore)
disagree.gemini: 95 m x 75 m (gross 4,800 m2 bounding envelope)
disagree.ours: 80 m x 70 m as-built [S1, directly stated], cross-checked at 79 m x 67 m by an independent academic thesis [S2, via S1's footnote]
disagree.why_ours: S1 is an official Bay of Plenty Regional Council-commissioned engineering assessment report that gives this figure as a direct, plainly-stated measurement ('As finally built, the structure is approximately 80 m in shore-parallel length and about 70 m in cross-shore width'), independently cross-checked against an academic PhD thesis survey (Scarfe 2008, 79x67 m) cited in the same report's own footnote. Gemini's 95x75 m has no source we could locate that states it directly; its own cited 'Mead et al. 2007 Mount Maunganui Reef Monitoring Report' could not be found by us anywhere (see open_issues) - the real, analogous document we found and read in full is Mead's 2011 assessment, cited via S1, which does NOT contain a 95x75 figure anywhere in the text we extracted. Gemini's 95x75 is closer to the DESIGN-stage target reported in S4 (75 m apex-to-base x ~100 m across the base) than to the as-built figure, which raises the possibility Gemini's number is a garbled/rounded version of the design figure rather than an as-built measurement - but even then, its own axis labels (95 alongshore, 75 cross-shore) have length and width swapped relative to S4's apex-to-base(75, i.e. cross-shore)/across-base(~100, i.e. alongshore) framing.

disagree.gemini: 2.2 m (with the underlying reef_footprints.json giving a range of -1.8 to -2.4 m LAT for the 'constructed' crest)
disagree.ours: 0.8-1.0 m below Chart Datum for the majority of the as-built crest, with an isolated point at 0.1-0.2 m [S1, directly stated from bathymetric survey data through 2013]
disagree.why_ours: S1 is the only source either of us appears to have found that gives a specific as-built crest-depth range, and it is a directly-quoted figure from an official survey-based assessment report, not an estimate. Gemini's 1.8-2.4 m figure would mean the crest sits roughly 1-1.5 m deeper than what S1's own bathymetric surveys (2008 and 2013) actually record; we could not find Gemini's cited 'Mead et al. 2007' monitoring report anywhere to check where this number might have come from, and it directly contradicts the one authoritative source we could locate and read in full.

disagree.quantity: ambient (pre-reef) seabed depth at the site
disagree.ours: 3.7-4.6 m (consent application) / 3-5 m (Scarfe 2008 survey) / 4.5 m (NZ Geographic, quoting the designer) [S1, S4]
disagree.why_ours: Three broadly consistent figures from two independent primary-ish sources (an official council report citing the original consent application and an academic thesis survey, plus a magazine feature directly quoting the designer) versus Gemini's single unsourced 6.2 m, which is 30-70% deeper than any of our three figures.

disagree.quantity: shape topology ("inverted Y" vs bent two-arm chevron)
disagree.gemini: "Swept-Wing Inverted Y / Chevron with Central Ridge" - implying three distinct members (a central ridge/stem plus two swept wings) and a broadly symmetric layout, per Gemini's own 10-vertex polygon
disagree.ours: Two arms only (northern, southern per S1/Mead 2011's own naming), no separate central ridge/stem member, meeting at a single apex/focus point at a bend that visual inspection of S1's own survey figures puts closer to ~90 degrees than to a narrow symmetric V or a three-limbed Y
disagree.why_ours: S1 (an official report directly describing the physical structure from diver inspections and repeated multibeam surveys) consistently describes exactly TWO arms ("6 geotextile containers on each side", "the northern arm", "the southern arm") plus a single shared "apex" - never a third, separate "central ridge" component. We could not find any source describing a distinct central-ridge member, and Gemini's own reef_footprints.json gives no image or figure citation for this specific claim beyond its own hand-built polygon.

open_issues: The polygons_m vertex coordinates are our own estimate: the overall bounding envelope (80x70 m / 67.8x72.9 m as modelled) is well-sourced [S1, cross-checked by S2], but the specific bend angle (~90 degrees) and the arm-length split (55 m northern / 45 m southern) used to place individual vertices were read qualitatively off S1's survey figures, not measured to a calibrated scale - we could not extract a reliable metres-per-pixel scale from the rendered PDF page images for Figure 3. Treat individual vertex positions as +/-15 m uncertain even though the overall envelope is high-confidence.

Three different, mutually inconsistent design-volume figures now exist across sources: ~5,000 m3 [R1], 6,000 m3 [R2, S4], and 6,500 m3 [S1] - none of the sources reconciles this with the others; all describe the same 'design' stage, not different stages.

Two different, mutually inconsistent container/bag-size and bag-count descriptions exist: S4 describes 24 bags total, the largest 3.5 m high x 50 m long holding 660 m3 each; R2 describes bags 'up to 60 m long and 5 m in diameter'; S1 (via Mead 2011) instead describes 6 containers per arm (12 total in the base design: 3 large crest + 3 smaller base containers per side). No source reconciles these three accounts, and it is unclear whether they describe the same design stage, different design revisions, or a reporting error.

Gemini's three cited sources ('Black, S.M. & Kerry, A. 1999' - already in our own reference list as R13/design-paper citation; 'Mead, S. et al. 2007 Mount Maunganui Reef Monitoring Report, ASR Ltd'; 'Tauranga City Council: Tay Street Reef Removal Dossier 2014') could not be independently located by us. The 1999 design paper is the same one our card already cites via Lior's notes [R13] and we did not find an accessible copy of it either (a design paper WITH plan-view figures and precise original design dimensions, if locatable, would likely be the single best remaining source to check against both our and Gemini's numbers - flagged for a possible future pass, not pursued further here as it is not yet in either project's accessible reference set).

Exact real-world compass bearing of the shoreline / the alongshore (x) axis at Mount Maunganui Beach is not stated in any source we accessed; we used the sourced 'northern arm' / 'southern arm' naming [S1] to fix positive-x = north, which is better-grounded than a fully arbitrary convention but still does not give an exact bearing in degrees.

The as-built shape shown in S1's July 2013 survey (5 years after 2008 completion, after documented bag deflation/sand-leakage damage 'near the apex of the structure') may itself have degraded/settled somewhat from the as-completed-in-2008 geometry; we did not find an earlier, immediately-post-completion (2008) survey figure to check against, only the January 2007 (70%-complete) and July 2013 figures.
Crest_depth_m.value (0.9 m) is our own midpoint of a stated 0.8-1.0 m range, not itself a directly quoted single figure - see the derivation table row and the crest_depth_m field's own notes.

[ADDED 2026-09-25 verification pass] A direct pixel-level zoom into S1's Figure 3 (July 2013 survey) shows a small, separate reddish-orange (shallow) blob near the apex/junction of the two arms, detached from both main limbs by a deeper (blue) gap. No source text names a distinct third feature here - S1/Mead 2011 consistently describe exactly two arms plus a shared apex - so this is recorded only as our own unsourced visual observation, of uncertain origin (possibly the repaired/replaced T4 bag documented near the apex, a small isolated remnant, or bathymetric noise), not as a basis for revising shape_type. It is noted here only because it is the one respect in which Gemini's 'with Central Ridge' framing is not obviously wrong, even though Gemini's own specific description (a swept-back three-limbed Y) does not match what is visible either.

verification.item: S1 (BoPRC 2014 report) -- every quoted figure
verification.evidence: Downloaded the actual PDF (curl, browser user-agent; WebFetch itself got a TLS cert error on this host) and extracted full text with PyMuPDF (fitz). Verbatim-confirmed on the live document: 'As finally built, the structure is approximately 80 m in shore-parallel length and about 70 m in cross-shore width' (p6); footnote 'Scarfe (2008, p271) gives the reef dimensions as 79 m by 67 m' (p7); original 'wedge' dimensions 'approximately 50 m in width ... and just less than 100 m in length' (p6); consent-application siting 'approximately 250-300 metres from the shoreline' and pre-reef depth '3.7-4.6 m' (p6); Scarfe's baseline survey depth 'approximately 3-5 m' (p6); design crest '0.4 m depth (below lowest astronomical tide ... equivalent to Chart Datum)' (p6); July 2013 survey 'shallowest areas ... most typically in the range of 0.8-1 m below Chart Datum ... isolated area on the southern arm ... as shallow as 0.2-0.4 m below Chart Datum' (p22, s4.3.2.1); as-built vs design volume '2,800 m3 ... significantly less than the design volume (6,500 m3)' (p29); 6 geotextile containers per side, 3 large crest + 3 smaller base containers (p7).

verification.item: S1 Figure 3 (p23) and Figure 4 (p26) -- shape/topology, arm naming, section/page numbers

verification.evidence: The pre-verification JSON attributed the isolated 0.1-0.2 m shallow point (S1 s2.1, 'at its highest point, the reef is approximately 0.2 m below chart datum, or approximately 0.1 m below the lowest astronomical tide') to 'the northern arm crest'. Re-reading S1's full extracted text: this sentence does NOT name an arm at all -- the arm attribution was an unsupported addition not present in the source. Corrected in crest_depth_m.notes to remove the invented attribution and clarify this is one point in two datums, not a range; also flagged that it may (unconfirmed) be the same feature as S1 s4.3.2.1's explicitly-named 'isolated area on the southern arm ... 0.2-0.4 m below Chart Datum'.

verification.item: 70x30 m (R8) vs 80x70 m (S1) 'does not reconcile under a symmetric geometry' claim
verification.evidence: The pre-verification JSON asserted 'no single symmetric half-angle satisfies both the 70x30 per-arm figures and the 80x70 overall envelope simultaneously'. This was checked by direct computation (Python, sweeping the half-angle from 0-90 degrees in 0.01-degree steps): a symmetric V with two 70x30 m arms at a half-angle of ~21.9 degrees from the shore-normal axis produces an 80.05 x 70.54 m bounding envelope -- matching S1's stated 80x70 m almost exactly. The original claim was mathematically wrong and has been corrected in the derivation table's uncertainty field. This does NOT overturn the file's as-built-asymmetry conclusion, which rests on independent, directly-viewed visual evidence (S1 Figures 3 and 4; R2's 'Mount Reef Installed' bathymetric image), not on this arithmetic argument.

verification.item: Gemini comparison table -- fairness of Gemini's own numbers as represented
verification.evidence: Read Gemini's own reef_footprints.json 'mount_maunganui' entry, reef_footprint_scale_analysis.md, and scale_sketch_photo_alignment_audit.md directly. Every Gemini figure attributed to it in this file's gemini_comparison (95x75 m, 4,800 m2 gross / 2,455 m2 net, crest_depth_m 2.2 / '-1.8 to -2.4m LAT' / 'Designed for -0.5m LAT', ambient_seabed_depth_m 6.2, shape_typology 'Swept-Wing Inverted Y / Chevron with Central Ridge', the three named sources, and Gemini's own audit note flagging the gross-vs-net area gap) is an accurate, unedited representation of what Gemini's files actually contain. No unfairness found.

verification.item: Shape topology vs Gemini's 'Inverted Y / Chevron with Central Ridge' (3-member claim)
verification.evidence: Direct pixel-level zoom into S1 Figure 3 shows a small, separate reddish-orange blob near the apex/junction, detached from the two main limbs by a blue (deeper) gap -- visually consistent with a third, smaller high point. Its origin is NOT established (could be a repaired/replaced bag near the documented apex damage, a small isolated remnant, or bathymetric noise) and NO source text describes a distinct third 'central ridge' member; S1/Mead 2011 consistently describe exactly two arms plus a shared apex/focus point. This is recorded as an open issue (this file's own independent visual observation, not sourced to any text) rather than a basis for changing the two-arm shape_type or agreeing with Gemini's specific 3-member topology.

name: Opunake Surf Reef
year: Planned for March 2006 construction start [R3]; most retrospective sources say started 2006 [R2][R4]; one 2021 source says 2005 [R1] — disputed
type: Submerged multi-purpose reef, sand-filled geotextile ("geo-container") bags — 27 bags in place by 2009 [R2][R4]
purpose: Increase surfable days at Opunake from an estimated 1-in-8 to 1-in-3, to draw tourism and jobs to a South Taranaki district with a slowly declining population; not designed for coastal-erosion protection [R2][R3][R4]
size: North reef only (the larger south reef was never built): footprint ~90 m long x 20 m wide, designed for a right-hand wave 1.8-2.5 m high, rideable for about 100 m [R2][R3][R4]
cost: North reef costed at ~NZ$1.3 million before construction [R3]; council actually allocated NZ$1.1 million [R2][R4]; spending had exceeded NZ$1.7 million by 2009 with a further NZ$400,000 sought [R1][R2][R4]; council separately wrote off a NZ$400,000 loan to the Trust in 2011 [R2][R4]
cost_usd_approx: No sourced USD conversion found in any reference; a rough unsourced conversion at ~0.65 NZD:USD puts the ~NZ$1.7m spend at roughly US$1.1m — Claude's own estimate, not a citable fact
financed_by: South Taranaki District Council (initial NZ$1.1M allocation plus a later NZ$400,000 loan) and the Opunake Artificial Surf Reef Trust, a local community trust [R1][R2][R4]
motivation: Tourism and economic development for a declining South Taranaki town, via more frequent good surfing conditions; explicitly not a coastal-protection project [R2][R3][R4]
designer: Dr Kerry Black / Artificial Surf Reefs (ASR) Ltd, Raglan, NZ, with surf-science design input from ASR co-founder Shaw Mead before he left the company in 2011 [R1][R2][R3][R4][R5]
contractor: ASR Ltd (Raglan, NZ) — no separate named construction contractor found [R2][R3][R4]
status_now: Failed: never produced the promised rideable waves. The Trust sued ASR in 2011; the council wrote off its debt as unrecoverable; ASR itself was liquidated in 2012. No source found reports formal removal or dismantling of the structure [R1][R2][R4]
hover_text: A ~90x20 m submerged sand-bag reef off Opunake Beach, Taranaki, planned for ~NZ$1.3 million from 2006 but ending up costing over NZ$1.7 million by 2009 [R1][R2][R3][R4] — it never produced the rideable waves it was designed for, and the project ended in litigation, a written-off council loan, and the designer's liquidation in 2012 [R1][R2][R4].
design_as_planned: Two reefs were planned: a cheaper north reef (built first) costed at ~NZ$1.3 million across a 90x20 m footprint, designed for a right-hand wave 1.8-2.5 m high rideable for ~100 m; and a larger, never-built south reef meant to deliver a 200 m ride on waves up to 3.6 m high. ASR tested the design in a small-scale wave pool at its Raglan facility. Kerry Black publicly expected the north reef to be finished within about two months of construction starting [R2][R3][R4].
as_built_vs_design: Only the cheaper north reef was ever attempted; the south reef was never built. Construction, planned for ~2 months, instead dragged on for years: by 2009 all 27 geotextile bags were reportedly in place but still needed "fine tuning" (more sand, closing gaps between bags), while spending had already passed NZ$1.7 million against the NZ$1.1 million council allocation. A 2009-10 proposal to cap the geo-containers with rock (est. NZ$150,000) was pledged by ASR's new part-owner Sealutions LLC as part of a sale agreement but was never honoured. In 2010 seabed changes were reported to be causing uneven performance across the reef. By August 2011 the council, Trust and ASR relationship had broken down entirely, ending in litigation [R2][R4].
outcome: No source found gives a measured/instrumented surf-quality outcome for Opunake (no wave-height, peel-angle or ride-length monitoring data, unlike Narrowneck) — "not found". Qualitatively, every source agrees the reef never produced the promised rideable waves; a 2021 investigative piece states flatly the reef "didn't produce the expected waves" [R1]. The reef did attract fish and other sea-life, but the structure itself began to break apart, with pieces washing ashore [R1]. No coastal-protection outcome is reported because none was designed in [R3]. No removal/dismantling is documented in any source found [R1][R2][R4].
why_worked_or_failed: It failed. Contributing causes across sources: chronic under-budgeting and repeated funding shortfalls (the NZ$1.1-1.3M allocation proved far short of the NZ$1.7M+ actually spent, and later top-up requests of NZ$400,000, NZ$150,000 and NZ$133,000 were each unmet or only partly met) [R1][R2][R4]; the intrinsic durability problem of sand-filled geotextile bags, which ASR co-founder Shaw Mead later called the technology's "fatal flaw" — a single torn bag loses sand and changes the whole structure's shape [R5]; seabed changes over time causing uneven performance across the reef by 2010 [R2][R4]; and corporate instability at ASR (majority sale to Sealutions LLC, an unhonoured completion pledge, and ASR's own liquidation in 2012) that removed any prospect of finishing the fix [R1][R2][R4]. Because the reef was designed purely for surfing with no coastal-protection goal, there was no secondary benefit to justify the sunk cost once the surf failed to materialise [R3].
unexpected_results: The reef attracted fish and other sea-life even as it failed to produce surf [R1]. Pieces of the failed structure washed ashore over time [R1], a pattern echoed more dramatically at the related Mount Maunganui and Boscombe ASR reefs [R1]. The dispute escalated beyond an engineering failure into litigation: the Trust sued ASR in 2011, and the council wrote off first a NZ$400,000 loan and then its whole claim as unrecoverable [R1][R2][R4]. No source found documents fishing pressure, swimmer-safety/rip-current incidents, or tourism data specific to Opunake — "not found" [R1][R5].
could_be_better: ASR co-founder Shaw Mead concluded the geotextile-bag construction method itself was the core weakness and said it led him to shift subsequent multi-purpose-reef designs to traditional rock construction [R5]; he separately called the sandbag approach "an evolutionary deadend" in an email to Newsroom [R1]. At Opunake specifically, ASR's own 2009-10 fix proposal was to cap the geo-containers with rock rather than keep tuning bags with sand, but the funding for that fix was never delivered [R2][R4]. Surfrider Foundation CEO Jim Moriarty argued more broadly that ocean-based artificial-reef attempts as a class have "absolutely horrible" results and that effort should go into protecting natural breaks instead [R6]. NZ Surfing Magazine editor Cory Scott was blunter still: "not one artificial reef has created a wave of any quality, despite claims to the contrary" [R1]. Process-wise, the repeated pattern of underestimating both time (2 months expected; it ran years) and cost (three separate unmet top-up requests) suggests firmer contingency budgeting and a completion-guarantee contract with the builder would have been needed to finish the job at all [R1][R2][R4].
relevance_to_israel: Tide range is the biggest physical contrast: Opunake's open New Zealand coast shows a sample tidal range on the order of ~2.5 m (high 2.94 m / low 0.47 m) [R7], versus well under half a metre at Haifa on Israel's virtually tideless Mediterranean coast (~0.36-0.40 m high / ~0.00-0.07 m low) [R12]. A geotextile-bag reef at Opunake has to keep working across that ~2.5 m swing in water depth every tide cycle — a substantially harder crest-depth design problem than any Israeli Mediterranean site would present, which is a point in Israel's favour for a similar reef proposal. However, the dominant documented failure modes at Opunake — chronic under-budgeting, repeated shortfalls in "finishing" funding, corporate instability at the design/construction firm, and the durability problem of sand-filled geotextile bags (tear -> sand loss -> shape change -> wave-quality loss) [R1][R2][R4][R5] — are not tide-dependent and would transfer directly to any Israeli geotextile-bag project, including the Ashkelon geotube project already logged in this project's master list, which itself suffered partial construction failure and higher-than-expected maintenance costs. The clearest transferable lesson is financial and material: secure full contingency funding and a completion-guarantee contract before committing to a geotextile-bag structure, and weigh rock-based construction (which ASR's own co-founder ultimately endorsed over bags) given the technology's poor track record on sand-bag durability [R1][R2][R4][R5][R7][R12].

footprint.orientation_notes: No plan-view figure, survey drawing or compass bearing for the Opunake reef was found in any accessible source (R1-R12 in the card, nor Gemini's cited-but-inaccessible 'Mead & Black 2007 Design Dossier' / 'Taranaki Regional Council Monitoring Records 2010'). The polygon here is a SCHEMATIC placeholder only: a symmetric isosceles wedge with its 20 m base at the shoreward (inshore) end and its apex pointing offshore (seaward), by direct analogy to the one Opunake-designer reef whose plan geometry IS described in a primary source in our reference list — Mount Maunganui, built by the same firm (ASR Ltd) around the same time, explicitly described as having its 'apex... point[ing] seaward and the structure thicken[ing] towards the base' [R3]. Opunake's own sources (R2, R4) state only that the reef's bags 'cover an area around 90m long and 20m wide' with no shape description; R2/R4 also both note the design was for a single 'right-hand wave' (one peel direction), unlike Mount Maunganui's two-directional wave off a symmetric V — meaning the real Opunake reef almost certainly had an ASYMMETRIC wedge/arm (like the 'asymmetric polygonal wedge' shape of the comparable Cables Reef), not the symmetric triangle drawn here. We chose the symmetric schematic deliberately rather than inventing a specific asymmetric skew, because no source gives which flank was the long peeling shoulder or the arm's angle to the shoreline. Distance offshore and crest depth are both low-confidence estimates (see derivation) since neither figure is published for Opunake specifically in any source we could access.

Opunake's own bag fabric composition is not published in any source we could access.
