name: Boscombe Surf Reef
year: Construction began June 2008; officially opened 19 November 2009 [R1][R4].
type: Submerged multi-purpose artificial surf reef built from large sand-filled geotextile containers ("geobags"), not rock [R1][R4][R7].
purpose: Coastal-town regeneration and surf tourism: create a reliable, higher-quality wave to roughly double good surfing days (from ~77 to ~154/yr) and double annual surf-related beach visits (from ~5,000 to ~10,000); marketed as Europe's/the Northern Hemisphere's first artificial surf reef [R1][R3][R4].
size: ~55 geotextile containers, each ~2–3 m high and ~60 m long; total sand-fill volume ≈13,000 m³; footprint ≈1 hectare (2.5 acres); positioned 220 m from the seawall base, ~240 m east of the pier [R4][R7].
cost: £3–3.2 million actually spent on the reef structure itself, against an original 1999–2003-era estimate of £1.4 million; the wider Boscombe seafront/pier regeneration scheme (reef + pier refurbishment + seafront) totalled ≈£11 million [R1][R2]. One New Zealand outlet states the cost as "more than NZD $6 million," over a year behind schedule — not corroborated by any UK source [R8].
cost_usd_approx: £3.2M ≈ US $5.1M at 2009 average GBP/USD rates (~1.59); NZD $6M ≈ US $4.2M at 2010 average NZD/USD rates (~0.70) — rough conversions, not sourced from any single article [R1][R2][R8].
financed_by: Bournemouth Borough Council, funded via sale of a car park (on which Barratt Developments built the Honeycombe Chine Flats) and sale of beach "pods" as part of the Overstrand seafront building [R1][R4].
motivation: Boscombe was a rundown 20th-century seaside suburb of Bournemouth in need of regeneration; the reef was one plank of a wider council-led seafront renewal that also refurbished Boscombe Pier and built new beachfront "pods" and flats [R1][R10]. A feasibility study was approved in 1999 and detailed plans approved in March 2003, with construction not starting until 2008 [R6][R1]. Financing was structured opportunistically around unrelated seafront property sales rather than a dedicated capital grant [R1][R4].
designer: Dr Kerry Black (oceanographer, ex-University of Waikato/NIWA, co-founder of ASR Ltd) did the wave-science/concept design; Shaw Mead (ASR co-founder) is credited as design/surf-science lead [R8][R7].
contractor: ASR Ltd (Artificial Surf Reefs Ltd), a New Zealand company; managing director Nick Behunin [R1][R4][R6].
status_now: Permanently closed to surfing since 31 March/April 2011 after storm and boat-propeller damage; ASR Ltd went into liquidation September 2012; rebranded and reopened in stages (2014, then 2017) as a "Coastal Activity Park" for diving, snorkelling, windsurfing/kitesurfing and other non-surf water activities; by 2018 described as largely forgotten/neglected; debris from the structure was still washing ashore as late as Boxing Day 2017 [R1][R3][R4][R8].
hover_text: A ~1-hectare, 13,000 m³ sand-filled geotextile-bag surf reef opened November 2009 for £3–3.2M (Bournemouth Borough Council, funded via land/beach-pod sales); a boat-propeller strike and storm damage forced permanent closure to surfing by 2011, ASR Ltd liquidated in 2012, and the site was rebranded a non-surf "Coastal Activity Park" from 2014 [R1][R2][R4][R8].
design_as_planned: The reef was designed as a submerged, angled ramp of stacked geotextile sand containers that would intercept the dominant swell direction and reshape it into rideable peeling waves, rather than "creating" waves from nothing. ASR director Shaw Mead described the mechanism directly: "The reef doesn't actually create waves. It's angled to catch the mean wave direction, and it acts as a ramp which changes the way the waves break" [R10]. The design target was a "Grade 5" wave under good swell conditions, producing rides of roughly 75 m to the right and 35 m to the left, suited to bodyboarders and surfers [R10]. Eleven specific design/performance objectives were set, including materially increasing surf-day frequency (from ~77 to ~154 good surf days/yr) and beach-visit numbers (from ~5,000 to ~10,000/yr) [R1][R2].
as_built_vs_design: The structure eventually installed — 55 sand-filled geotextile bags forming a ~1-hectare submerged mound ~13,000 m³ in volume — matched the general geotube concept, but construction ran roughly a decade behind the original 1999–2003 planning timeline and cost more than double the original £1.4 million estimate, landing at £3–3.2 million for the reef alone [R1][R2][R6]. Construction was repeatedly delayed and beset by "setbacks during building works" before the reef finally opened in November 2009 [R1]. Shaw Mead later blamed the outcome on "wrangling over funds, political in-fighting and bad project management decisions," distancing his own design/surf-science role from those problems [R8].
outcome: A University of Plymouth interim evaluation (Dr Mark Davidson, published May 2010) found the reef met only 4 of its 11 original design objectives, stating: "The wave length is rather too intense and challenging [and it] is not quite as consistent as it should be" [R1][R2]. This evaluation is credited solely to Dr Mark Davidson in every source found; a claim (raised during a Gemini-survey cross-check) that the evaluation was co-authored by "Reeve" and "Medina" is not confirmed anywhere and is rejected — the only genuine Davidson co-authored paper found online is the separate, later Rendle & Davidson (2012, ICCE Proceedings) study on structural degradation, with a different co-author [R1]. In practice the reef worked best around low tide, with rides largely limited to steep, short sections, mainly ridden by bodyboarders rather than the standup surfers it was marketed to [R1]. A routine inspection in March 2011 found "substantial changes" to the reef's profile; it was closed for safety on 31 March 2011 [R1]. In April 2011 further damage was found, with one geo-container removed and another repaired, apparently after an unidentified boat's propeller struck the reef [R1][R9]. Repairs begun in August 2011 were suspended for winter and never satisfactorily completed [R1][R7]. ASR Ltd went into liquidation in September 2012 (one source: November 2012), owing the council roughly £14,800–£15,000; the council obtained a £306,531 insurance settlement in 2013 [R1][R4][R6]. A 2012 plan to repurpose the site as a dive/snorkel trail was itself abandoned [R5]. The site was rebranded in 2014 and again in 2017 as a "Coastal Activity Park," with surfing dropped as a priority [R1][R6]. Debris from the decaying structure was reported washing ashore as late as Boxing Day 2017 [R8].
why_worked_or_failed: Shaw Mead's own later analysis concluded sand-filled geotextile bags were a structural dead end: "the sandbags were an evolutionary dead-end," and "as soon as even a single sand-filled container broke and lost sand, the whole structure changed shape due to the fluid nature of sand" — a design fundamentally vulnerable to point-impact damage [R8][R9]. The proximate damage cause was a boat-propeller strike, a mechanism Geosynthetics Magazine groups with damage at other ASR reefs elsewhere (anchor damage at Gold Coast, debris strikes at Kovalam, over-filling at Mount Maunganui) as evidence of a general geotextile-reef vulnerability pattern [R9]. Even before the propeller strike, the University of Plymouth's Davidson evaluation had already found the reef meeting only 4 of 11 design objectives, indicating the wave-shaping design itself, not only later physical damage, fell short [R1][R2]. Shaw Mead's own explanation for the broader project's failure also emphasises non-engineering causes — "wrangling over funds, political in-fighting and bad project management decisions" during a near-decade gap between 2003 planning approval and 2008 construction start [R8][R6][R1].
unexpected_results: The project drew media coverage in an estimated 60 countries around its 2009 opening, and local Boscombe hospitality businesses reported a real economic uplift regardless of the reef's technical shortcomings [R2]. Some media coverage carried headlines setting expectations the reef's actual short, steep, low-tide-only wave could not meet [R9]. The site was closed in 2011 over safety concerns involving hazardous undercurrents and gaps in the deteriorating structure, serious enough that local surfer/photographer Chris Skone-Roberts warned "it is just a question of time before someone dies" [R2]. Loose material and debris from the decaying geotextile bags continued washing ashore for years after closure, documented as late as Boxing Day 2017 [R8]. Dolphins were reported investigating the new structure shortly after construction, an unplanned/unmeasured ecological footnote [R10].
could_be_better: Shaw Mead (ASR co-designer) concluded the material choice itself was wrong — sand-filled geotextile bags are "an evolutionary dead-end" for a structure that must survive years of surf-zone wave energy and occasional impacts — and moved ASR's subsequent multi-purpose-reef designs to rock construction instead [R8]. Geosynthetics Magazine's review implies the fix is structural redundancy: a single ruptured bag should not be able to reshape the whole reef, pointing toward either more failure-tolerant bag engineering or abandoning fabric containers for point-impact-prone sites like a boat channel [R9]. The University of Plymouth's own evaluation implies the wave-shaping geometry needed further hydrodynamic refinement even independent of material failure, since only 4 of 11 objectives were met while the structure was still intact [R1][R2]. Local critics, including councillor Ben Grower, framed the entire project as a governance and money failure rather than a fixable engineering detail [R2][R5].
relevance_to_israel: Boscombe's tidal range is modest by UK Atlantic-coast standards (same-day check showed roughly 0.9–1.1 m high-to-low, illustrative only) [R12]; Haifa's Mediterranean coast is effectively micro-tidal, though no sourced numeric tidal-range figure for Haifa was found in this research [R14]. What transfers directly: Boscombe's central lesson is that geotextile-sandbag construction is vulnerable to point-impact damage (boat strikes, anchors, debris) and to cascading shape-change once any single bag ruptures, regardless of tidal regime [R8][R9]. Haifa's proposed reef site is assessed against real Shikmona-buoy wave data (significant wave height 0.45–0.8 m in the surfable window, occasional peaks to ~1.2 m), a much gentler wave-energy environment than the UK Channel/Atlantic-influenced south coast that shaped Boscombe's design — meaning less storm-wave loading, but underscoring that any Israeli project should still plan explicitly for boat-strike/anchor exposure in a working coastal-shipping and fishing environment [R14].

sections.title: Quick facts
sections.html_or_text:
NameBoscombe Surf Reef
PlaceBoscombe, Bournemouth, Dorset
CountryUnited Kingdom
YearConstruction began June 2008; officially opened 19 November 2009 [R1][R4].
TypeSubmerged multi-purpose artificial surf reef built from large sand-filled geotextile containers ("geobags"), not rock [R1][R4][R7].
PurposeCoastal-town regeneration and surf tourism: create a reliable, higher-quality wave to roughly double good surfing days (from ~77 to ~154/yr) and double annual surf-related beach visits (from ~5,000 to ~10,000); marketed as Europe's/the Northern Hemisphere's first artificial surf reef [R1][R3][R4].
Size~55 geotextile containers, each ~2–3 m high and ~60 m long; total sand-fill volume ≈13,000 m³; footprint ≈1 hectare (2.5 acres); positioned 220 m from the seawall base, ~240 m east of the pier [R4][R7].
Cost£3–3.2 million actually spent on the reef structure itself, against an original 1999–2003-era estimate of £1.4 million; the wider Boscombe seafront/pier regeneration scheme (reef + pier refurbishment + seafront) totalled ≈£11 million [R1][R2]. One New Zealand outlet states the cost as "more than NZD $6 million," over a year behind schedule — not corroborated by any UK source [R8].
Cost (approx. USD)£3.2M ≈ US $5.1M at 2009 average GBP/USD rates (~1.59); NZD $6M ≈ US $4.2M at 2010 average NZD/USD rates (~0.70) — rough conversions, not sourced from any single article [R1][R2][R8].
Financed byBournemouth Borough Council, funded via sale of a car park (on which Barratt Developments built the Honeycombe Chine Flats) and sale of beach "pods" as part of the Overstrand seafront building [R1][R4].
DesignerDr Kerry Black (oceanographer, ex-University of Waikato/NIWA, co-founder of ASR Ltd) did the wave-science/concept design; Shaw Mead (ASR co-founder) is credited as design/surf-science lead [R8][R7].
ContractorASR Ltd (Artificial Surf Reefs Ltd), a New Zealand company; managing director Nick Behunin [R1][R4][R6].
Status nowPermanently closed to surfing since 31 March/April 2011 after storm and boat-propeller damage; ASR Ltd went into liquidation September 2012; rebranded and reopened in stages (2014, then 2017) as a "Coastal Activity Park" for diving, snorkelling, windsurfing/kitesurfing and other non-surf water activities; by 2018 described as largely forgotten/neglected; debris from the structure was still washing ashore as late as Boxing Day 2017 [R1][R3][R4][R8].
Verdictfailed

sections.title: Motivation & who pushed for it
sections.html_or_text: Boscombe was a rundown 20th-century seaside suburb of Bournemouth in need of regeneration; the reef was one plank of a wider council-led seafront renewal that also refurbished Boscombe Pier and built new beachfront "pods" and flats [R1][R10]. A feasibility study was approved in 1999 and detailed plans approved in March 2003, with construction not starting until 2008 [R6][R1]. Financing was structured opportunistically around unrelated seafront property sales rather than a dedicated capital grant [R1][R4].

sections.title: Design as planned
sections.html_or_text: The reef was designed as a submerged, angled ramp of stacked geotextile sand containers that would intercept the dominant swell direction and reshape it into rideable peeling waves, rather than "creating" waves from nothing. ASR director Shaw Mead described the mechanism directly: "The reef doesn't actually create waves. It's angled to catch the mean wave direction, and it acts as a ramp which changes the way the waves break" [R10]. The design target was a "Grade 5" wave under good swell conditions, producing rides of roughly 75 m to the right and 35 m to the left, suited to bodyboarders and surfers [R10]. Eleven specific design/performance objectives were set, including materially increasing surf-day frequency (from ~77 to ~154 good surf days/yr) and beach-visit numbers (from ~5,000 to ~10,000/yr) [R1][R2].

sections.title: As built vs design
sections.html_or_text: The structure eventually installed — 55 sand-filled geotextile bags forming a ~1-hectare submerged mound ~13,000 m³ in volume — matched the general geotube concept, but construction ran roughly a decade behind the original 1999–2003 planning timeline and cost more than double the original £1.4 million estimate, landing at £3–3.2 million for the reef alone [R1][R2][R6]. Construction was repeatedly delayed and beset by "setbacks during building works" before the reef finally opened in November 2009 [R1]. Shaw Mead later blamed the outcome on "wrangling over funds, political in-fighting and bad project management decisions," distancing his own design/surf-science role from those problems [R8].

sections.title: Outcome
sections.html_or_text: A University of Plymouth interim evaluation (Dr Mark Davidson, published May 2010) found the reef met only 4 of its 11 original design objectives, stating: "The wave length is rather too intense and challenging [and it] is not quite as consistent as it should be" [R1][R2]. This evaluation is credited solely to Dr Mark Davidson in every source found; a claim (raised during a Gemini-survey cross-check) that the evaluation was co-authored by "Reeve" and "Medina" is not confirmed anywhere and is rejected — the only genuine Davidson co-authored paper found online is the separate, later Rendle & Davidson (2012, ICCE Proceedings) study on structural degradation, with a different co-author [R1]. In practice the reef worked best around low tide, with rides largely limited to steep, short sections, mainly ridden by bodyboarders rather than the standup surfers it was marketed to [R1]. A routine inspection in March 2011 found "substantial changes" to the reef's profile; it was closed for safety on 31 March 2011 [R1]. In April 2011 further damage was found, with one geo-container removed and another repaired, apparently after an unidentified boat's propeller struck the reef [R1][R9]. Repairs begun in August 2011 were suspended for winter and never satisfactorily completed [R1][R7]. ASR Ltd went into liquidation in September 2012 (one source: November 2012), owing the council roughly £14,800–£15,000; the council obtained a £306,531 insurance settlement in 2013 [R1][R4][R6]. A 2012 plan to repurpose the site as a dive/snorkel trail was itself abandoned [R5]. The site was rebranded in 2014 and again in 2017 as a "Coastal Activity Park," with surfing dropped as a priority [R1][R6]. Debris from the decaying structure was reported washing ashore as late as Boxing Day 2017 [R8].

sections.title: Why it worked / failed
sections.html_or_text: Shaw Mead's own later analysis concluded sand-filled geotextile bags were a structural dead end: "the sandbags were an evolutionary dead-end," and "as soon as even a single sand-filled container broke and lost sand, the whole structure changed shape due to the fluid nature of sand" — a design fundamentally vulnerable to point-impact damage [R8][R9]. The proximate damage cause was a boat-propeller strike, a mechanism Geosynthetics Magazine groups with damage at other ASR reefs elsewhere (anchor damage at Gold Coast, debris strikes at Kovalam, over-filling at Mount Maunganui) as evidence of a general geotextile-reef vulnerability pattern [R9]. Even before the propeller strike, the University of Plymouth's Davidson evaluation had already found the reef meeting only 4 of 11 design objectives, indicating the wave-shaping design itself, not only later physical damage, fell short [R1][R2]. Shaw Mead's own explanation for the broader project's failure also emphasises non-engineering causes — "wrangling over funds, political in-fighting and bad project management decisions" during a near-decade gap between 2003 planning approval and 2008 construction start [R8][R6][R1].

sections.title: Unexpected results
sections.html_or_text: The project drew media coverage in an estimated 60 countries around its 2009 opening, and local Boscombe hospitality businesses reported a real economic uplift regardless of the reef's technical shortcomings [R2]. Some media coverage carried headlines setting expectations the reef's actual short, steep, low-tide-only wave could not meet [R9]. The site was closed in 2011 over safety concerns involving hazardous undercurrents and gaps in the deteriorating structure, serious enough that local surfer/photographer Chris Skone-Roberts warned "it is just a question of time before someone dies" [R2]. Loose material and debris from the decaying geotextile bags continued washing ashore for years after closure, documented as late as Boxing Day 2017 [R8]. Dolphins were reported investigating the new structure shortly after construction, an unplanned/unmeasured ecological footnote [R10].

sections.title: What could have been done better
sections.html_or_text: Shaw Mead (ASR co-designer) concluded the material choice itself was wrong — sand-filled geotextile bags are "an evolutionary dead-end" for a structure that must survive years of surf-zone wave energy and occasional impacts — and moved ASR's subsequent multi-purpose-reef designs to rock construction instead [R8]. Geosynthetics Magazine's review implies the fix is structural redundancy: a single ruptured bag should not be able to reshape the whole reef, pointing toward either more failure-tolerant bag engineering or abandoning fabric containers for point-impact-prone sites like a boat channel [R9]. The University of Plymouth's own evaluation implies the wave-shaping geometry needed further hydrodynamic refinement even independent of material failure, since only 4 of 11 objectives were met while the structure was still intact [R1][R2]. Local critics, including councillor Ben Grower, framed the entire project as a governance and money failure rather than a fixable engineering detail [R2][R5].

sections.title: Relevance to Israel / Haifa
sections.html_or_text: Boscombe's tidal range is modest by UK Atlantic-coast standards (same-day check showed roughly 0.9–1.1 m high-to-low, illustrative only) [R12]; Haifa's Mediterranean coast is effectively micro-tidal, though no sourced numeric tidal-range figure for Haifa was found in this research [R14]. What transfers directly: Boscombe's central lesson is that geotextile-sandbag construction is vulnerable to point-impact damage (boat strikes, anchors, debris) and to cascading shape-change once any single bag ruptures, regardless of tidal regime [R8][R9]. Haifa's proposed reef site is assessed against real Shikmona-buoy wave data (significant wave height 0.45–0.8 m in the surfable window, occasional peaks to ~1.2 m), a much gentler wave-energy environment than the UK Channel/Atlantic-influenced south coast that shaped Boscombe's design — meaning less storm-wave loading, but underscoring that any Israeli project should still plan explicitly for boat-strike/anchor exposure in a working coastal-shipping and fishing environment [R14].

footprint.name: Boscombe Surf Reef
footprint.shape_type_notes: A single elongated, asymmetric angled bank/ramp ("the reef doesn't create waves...it acts as a ramp", R10) built from parallel geotextile tubes -- not a multi-armed chevron, V, or triangular delta. The already-verified aerial photo (raisedwaterresearch.com 'Boscombe-Arial') shows one coherent dark parallelogram-shaped patch with internal parallel stripes (individual container tubes), not two separate arms meeting at an apex.
footprint.coords: metres; origin = shoreline point directly onshore of the reef's photo-measured centroid; x = alongshore (positive toward east, i.e. toward Bournemouth Pier direction / away from Boscombe Pier, matching the card's '~240 m east of the pier' framing); y = offshore (positive seaward); shoreline approximated as the line y=0.

bbox_m.note: Axis-aligned envelope in the shore-parallel/shore-normal frame. This is much bigger than the structure's own along-ramp footprint (187.5 m x 58 m) because the ramp's long axis is tilted roughly 24 deg off the shore-normal (offshore) direction -- see derivation. Do not read 'length_alongshore' here as the reef's own long dimension.

name: Kovalam Reef (Lighthouse Beach)
year: As-built: December 2009 - February 2010 [R1][R10]; one source gives April 2010 instead [R3] - unresolved. (An earlier, differently-scoped version was proposed in 2005 but not built then [R5].)
type: Non-woven geotextile sand-filled containers ("Geotubes"/bags), built in ~30 m-long units [R1][R2][R10]
purpose: Primary: coastal-erosion protection (monsoon wave energy) [R1][R10]. Secondary: surfing/tourism amenity and ecological benefit [R1][R5][R10]
size: As-built total volume 4,800 m3, increased from an initial 3,000 m3 plan, shaped to produce a 100 m left-hand wave [R1][R10]. Crest/submergence depth: not found
financed_by: India's Tsunami Rehabilitation Project, under the Planning Commission, Government of India [R1][R10]. (The 2005 proposal predating this funding was to be jointly implemented by Kerala Tourism, the Centre for Earth Science Studies (CESS), and the Department of Harbour Engineering [R5].)
motivation: Kerala Tourism pushed the idea as early as 2005, citing tourist safety, boosting water-sports tourism, monsoon-season erosion prevention, beach widening, and fishing-community benefit [R5]. The project actually built several years later was funded through post-tsunami rehabilitation money and engaged international specialist firm ASR Ltd rather than the original state team [R1][R5][R10]
designer: ASR Ltd (New Zealand-based multi-purpose/surf-reef design-and-build firm), project leads Chris Jensen and Nick Behunin [R1]
contractor: Not separately named beyond ASR Ltd in sources found - not found
status_now: Reported non-functional: containers torn, deflated, and sunk such that "waves just roll over the reef now without even breaking" [R1]. No formal removal documented; reef instead degraded in place [R1]. A separate, later (2021) Rs 8.35 crore erosion-protection/walkway project addressed "recurring" erosion at Kovalam's Samudra, Sea Rock, and Lighthouse beaches, not confirmed as a direct repair/successor [R6]. Kerala tourism-marketing pages currently advertise an "Artificial Off Shore Coral Reef" attraction at Kovalam, claimed to reduce erosion and support marine life; its identity/relationship to the 2009-10 ASR structure could not be confirmed [R9]
hover_text: A 4,800 m3 geotextile-bag reef built 2009-10 for ~Rs 75M (~US$1.1M) under India's post-tsunami rehabilitation fund; it briefly produced praised 7-10s rides and reportedly widened the beach, but containers began tearing within weeks and by 2010-11 the sunken structure no longer broke waves at all [R1][R10].
design_as_planned: Two distinct designs exist from two project phases. 2005 proposal (not built as such): a 500 m-long submerged structure ~200 m offshore at Eve's Beach, 3-7 m water depth, non-woven geotextile bags filled with sand, engineered to block waves over 1 m and include a "tranquil basin" for fishing-boat movement while preserving the ecosystem [R5]; protection-first, closer to a detached breakwater/lagoon system. As-built ASR Ltd design (2009-10): a smaller, more surf-focused structure - 30 m geotextile bag units totalling 4,800 m3 (up from an initial 3,000 m3 plan), shaped to produce a 100 m left-hand surfable wave at Lighthouse Beach, promising "lefts that provided 7-10 second rides," "fun and open faced," with "occasional head dip opportunity" [R1][R10]. Coastal protection remained the primary stated purpose, with surf/ecology secondary [R1][R10]. No EIA/SIA/FIA was required before construction of the as-built reef [R1]
as_built_vs_design: Location shifted from the 2005 plan's Eve's/Hawah Beach to Lighthouse Beach [R1][R5][R10]. Scale shrank from a 500 m/200 m-offshore/3-7 m-deep structure [R5] to 4,800 m3 of material in 30 m units producing a 100 m wave [R1][R10], though no single directly comparable dimension confirms by how much the footprint shrank. The as-built project itself grew from an initial 3,000 m3 plan to 4,800 m3 during construction, a ~60% increase with no source explaining why [R1][R10]. Cost rose from the 2005 estimate of Rs 40.5M to the as-built Rs 75M (~US$1.1M), roughly 85% higher, though the two figures describe different-scope projects years apart [R1][R5][R10]. Design authority shifted from a Kerala Tourism/CESS/Harbour-Engineering effort to international firm ASR Ltd [R1][R5][R10]
outcome: Initial surfing quality was described positively - 7-10 second-ride lefts, "fun and open faced" - per the reef's own before/after monitoring [R1]. Surf journalist Sean Collins, in a piece dated 29 April 2010 (reposted on surfingindia.net), called the wave potentially "the best wave an artificial reef has ever created," possibly able to "host an ASP World Tour event" [R3]. This sits awkwardly against the failure timeline: Raised Water Research and an industry comparison site both state containers began tearing and washing ashore "less than two weeks" after inauguration, with the reef sinking so that by 2010-11 "waves just roll over the reef now without even breaking" (Jelle Rigole quote) [R1][R10]. A separate, unsigned Surfer.com piece of 6 May 2010 similarly quoted ASR Ltd's Chris Jensen, India Surf Club's Daruka Dasa, and an unnamed Kovalam Surf Club member, all positive about the reef in its first months [R4]. Sources found do not resolve this contradiction between contemporaneous positive surf-media coverage and rapid-failure accounts. Coastal protection: the reef's own monitoring showed the beach "remained wider" in both monsoon and non-monsoon seasons after installation, but this appears to describe only the initial period before structural failure [R1]. Ecology/fishing: local fishermen reported recovering "damaged portions of the artificial reef rather than more fish," the opposite of the project's stated fish-attraction goal [R1][R5]
why_worked_or_failed: Why it failed: an industry comparison source attributes Kovalam's container failures specifically to "debris strikes" [R2]. Coastal engineer Shaw Mead explains the underlying mechanism generally: "as soon as even a single sand-filled container broke and lost sand, the whole structure changed shape due to the fluid nature of sand" [R2] - a single puncture cascading into total reshaping. Once containers deflated, the structure sank deeper into the seabed, pushing its crest below the depth needed to break waves at all [R1]. No EIA, SIA, or FIA was required before construction [R1], meaning potential fisheries/community impacts were not formally assessed in advance. The task brief's own seed facts describe the failure as caused by "debris strikes/vandalism"; sources fetched confirm "debris strikes" [R2] but did not corroborate vandalism or intentional damage - unreferenced, needs source. Why the design promised what it did: the 100 m left-hand wave and multi-second ride times reflect a deliberate ASR Ltd wave-shaping design distinct from the more general, protection-first 2005 proposal [R1]
unexpected_results: Fishermen retrieving reef wreckage instead of catching more fish, a direct reversal of the project's stated fishing-community goal [R1][R5]. As surf and coastal-protection improvements visibly disappeared through 2010-2011, "coastal communities and civil society of Kerala demanded a judicial and scientific enquiry and social audit" [R1] - sources do not confirm whether any inquiry was actually convened. The coexistence of enthusiastic international surf-media accounts (Collins, R3; the separate Surfer.com piece, R4) with rapid-failure accounts from other sources [R1][R2][R10] suggests the story reaching international surf media diverged sharply from what was reportedly happening on the ground within the same window. Separately, India's broader 2023-announced national artificial-reef rollout (3,477 target fishing villages, ~937 approved as of Sept 2024, ~US$34.5M total) has drawn criticism over net entanglement, "ghost fishing," and erosion risk from poorly sited structures - echoing some of Kovalam's own failure modes [R8]
could_be_better: Shaw Mead's general point - that geotextile-bag reefs are fragile as a system, since a single puncture cascades into total reshaping - implies the core lesson is that this material/technology is inherently high-risk for exposed, high-energy, or debris-prone sites [R2]. The absence of an EIA/SIA/FIA before construction is flagged by Raised Water Research as notable; a proper impact assessment could plausibly have surfaced fisheries and community concerns before construction rather than after failure [R1]. The scale/scope mismatch between the 2005 proposal (500 m, protection-first, 3-7 m depth) and the eventual 100 m surf-focused build is not explicitly critiqued by any source found, but a structure re-scoped from a broad coastal-defence design to a narrower, surf-tuned design may have traded protective robustness for wave-shaping performance - this is this dossier's own inference, not a sourced expert claim [R5][R1][R10]
relevance_to_israel: No verified, sourced tide-range figure for Kovalam/Kerala was found - not found; qualitatively Kerala's Arabian Sea coast is a mixed, mesotidal-to-microtidal regime versus the microtidal Mediterranean at Haifa. Kovalam faces monsoon-driven swell seasons, a materially higher and more seasonal wave-energy environment than Israel's Mediterranean coast, relevant to why a transplanted geotextile-bag design might face structural loads and debris-strike risks not directly comparable to a Haifa site. Transferable lessons: (1) geotextile-bag reefs are reported across multiple sites (Kovalam, Boscombe, Mount Reef, Opunake) as prone to single-point-of-failure cascading damage once any one container is breached [R2] - relevant to any Haifa proposal considering the same Geotube technology already used at Ashkelon (per this project's own source note, 01_source_notes/jmse2023_bar_drimer_paper.md, which does not itself cover Kovalam); (2) the value of requiring an impact assessment (EIA/SIA/FIA) before construction, which Kovalam skipped [R1]; (3) the risk of scope/design drift between an original protection-first proposal and an eventual, differently-scoped as-built structure, as documented here between the 2005 and 2009-10 Kovalam designs [R5][R1][R10]

reviews.role: Founder of a local surf club
reviews.quote_or_summary: In the beginning, it was great. But after the first monsoon season, some of the bags that composed the reef came loose. The reef sank deeper into the sand so most of the waves just roll over the reef now without even breaking.

The wave could very well be the best wave an artificial reef has ever created and on the right swell, could even possibly host an ASP World Tour event; also called large-scale coastal-defence spending a gigantic bandaid that siphons millions of dollars from the economy on a regular cycle.
As soon as even a single sand-filled container broke and lost sand, the whole structure changed shape due to the fluid nature of sand.
Reported recovering damaged portions of the artificial reef rather than more fish from their nets.

reviews.who: Coastal communities and civil society of Kerala (collectively described)
reviews.quote_or_summary: Demanded a judicial and scientific enquiry and social audit as the reef's benefits visibly disappeared through 2010-2011.

Most importantly, the reef in India was designed to stabilize the beach... We then deployed monitoring instruments at the proposed site of the reef to get detailed data in order to design the reef to optimize the recreational component (surfing, fishing, diving).

We haven't visited Kovalam since they had the new reef built, but we plan to in the upcoming months (pre and post monsoon seasons)... It's also a great thing for Kovalam in helping them prevent coastal erosion. They were really starting to run out of beach.

Unfortunately, this year we had less surfable days because the reef only starts to work when the swell is above 3 feet, but when it works it throws up a sucking barrel. When it goes off Kovalam now offers a good quality reefbreak and the level of the kids grows gradually with every surf session.

sections.title: Quick facts
sections.html_or_text:
NameKovalam Reef (Lighthouse Beach)
PlaceKovalam, Kerala
CountryIndia
YearAs-built: December 2009 - February 2010 [R1][R10]; one source gives April 2010 instead [R3] - unresolved. (An earlier, differently-scoped version was proposed in 2005 but not built then [R5].)
TypeNon-woven geotextile sand-filled containers ("Geotubes"/bags), built in ~30 m-long units [R1][R2][R10]
PurposePrimary: coastal-erosion protection (monsoon wave energy) [R1][R10]. Secondary: surfing/tourism amenity and ecological benefit [R1][R5][R10]
SizeAs-built total volume 4,800 m3, increased from an initial 3,000 m3 plan, shaped to produce a 100 m left-hand wave [R1][R10]. Crest/submergence depth: not found
CostAs-built: Rs 75,000,000 [R1][R10]
Cost (approx. USD)1100000
Financed byIndia's Tsunami Rehabilitation Project, under the Planning Commission, Government of India [R1][R10]. (The 2005 proposal predating this funding was to be jointly implemented by Kerala Tourism, the Centre for Earth Science Studies (CESS), and the Department of Harbour Engineering [R5].)
DesignerASR Ltd (New Zealand-based multi-purpose/surf-reef design-and-build firm), project leads Chris Jensen and Nick Behunin [R1]
ContractorNot separately named beyond ASR Ltd in sources found - not found

No formal removal documented; reef instead degraded in place [R1]. A separate, later (2021) Rs 8.35 crore erosion-protection/walkway project addressed "recurring" erosion at Kovalam's Samudra, Sea Rock, and Lighthouse beaches, not confirmed as a direct repair/successor [R6]. Kerala tourism-marketing pages currently advertise an "Artificial Off Shore Coral Reef" attraction at Kovalam, claimed to reduce erosion and support marine life; its identity/relationship to the 2009-10 ASR structure could not be confirmed [R9]
Verdictmixed

sections.title: Motivation & who pushed for it
sections.html_or_text: Kerala Tourism pushed the idea as early as 2005, citing tourist safety, boosting water-sports tourism, monsoon-season erosion prevention, beach widening, and fishing-community benefit [R5]. The project actually built several years later was funded through post-tsunami rehabilitation money and engaged international specialist firm ASR Ltd rather than the original state team [R1][R5][R10]

sections.title: Design as planned
sections.html_or_text: Two distinct designs exist from two project phases. 2005 proposal (not built as such): a 500 m-long submerged structure ~200 m offshore at Eve's Beach, 3-7 m water depth, non-woven geotextile bags filled with sand, engineered to block waves over 1 m and include a "tranquil basin" for fishing-boat movement while preserving the ecosystem [R5]; protection-first, closer to a detached breakwater/lagoon system. As-built ASR Ltd design (2009-10): a smaller, more surf-focused structure - 30 m geotextile bag units totalling 4,800 m3 (up from an initial 3,000 m3 plan), shaped to produce a 100 m left-hand surfable wave at Lighthouse Beach, promising "lefts that provided 7-10 second rides," "fun and open faced," with "occasional head dip opportunity" [R1][R10]. Coastal protection remained the primary stated purpose, with surf/ecology secondary [R1][R10]. No EIA/SIA/FIA was required before construction of the as-built reef [R1]

sections.title: As built vs design
sections.html_or_text: Location shifted from the 2005 plan's Eve's/Hawah Beach to Lighthouse Beach [R1][R5][R10]. Scale shrank from a 500 m/200 m-offshore/3-7 m-deep structure [R5] to 4,800 m3 of material in 30 m units producing a 100 m wave [R1][R10], though no single directly comparable dimension confirms by how much the footprint shrank. The as-built project itself grew from an initial 3,000 m3 plan to 4,800 m3 during construction, a ~60% increase with no source explaining why [R1][R10]. Cost rose from the 2005 estimate of Rs 40.5M to the as-built Rs 75M (~US$1.1M), roughly 85% higher, though the two figures describe different-scope projects years apart [R1][R5][R10]. Design authority shifted from a Kerala Tourism/CESS/Harbour-Engineering effort to international firm ASR Ltd [R1][R5][R10]

sections.title: Outcome
sections.html_or_text: Initial surfing quality was described positively - 7-10 second-ride lefts, "fun and open faced" - per the reef's own before/after monitoring [R1]. Surf journalist Sean Collins, in a piece dated 29 April 2010 (reposted on surfingindia.net), called the wave potentially "the best wave an artificial reef has ever created," possibly able to "host an ASP World Tour event" [R3]. This sits awkwardly against the failure timeline: Raised Water Research and an industry comparison site both state containers began tearing and washing ashore "less than two weeks" after inauguration, with the reef sinking so that by 2010-11 "waves just roll over the reef now without even breaking" (Jelle Rigole quote) [R1][R10]. A separate, unsigned Surfer.com piece of 6 May 2010 similarly quoted ASR Ltd's Chris Jensen, India Surf Club's Daruka Dasa, and an unnamed Kovalam Surf Club member, all positive about the reef in its first months [R4]. Sources found do not resolve this contradiction between contemporaneous positive surf-media coverage and rapid-failure accounts. Coastal protection: the reef's own monitoring showed the beach "remained wider" in both monsoon and non-monsoon seasons after installation, but this appears to describe only the initial period before structural failure [R1]. Ecology/fishing: local fishermen reported recovering "damaged portions of the artificial reef rather than more fish," the opposite of the project's stated fish-attraction goal [R1][R5]

sections.title: Why it worked / failed
sections.html_or_text: Why it failed: an industry comparison source attributes Kovalam's container failures specifically to "debris strikes" [R2]. Coastal engineer Shaw Mead explains the underlying mechanism generally: "as soon as even a single sand-filled container broke and lost sand, the whole structure changed shape due to the fluid nature of sand" [R2] - a single puncture cascading into total reshaping. Once containers deflated, the structure sank deeper into the seabed, pushing its crest below the depth needed to break waves at all [R1]. No EIA, SIA, or FIA was required before construction [R1], meaning potential fisheries/community impacts were not formally assessed in advance. The task brief's own seed facts describe the failure as caused by "debris strikes/vandalism"; sources fetched confirm "debris strikes" [R2] but did not corroborate vandalism or intentional damage - unreferenced, needs source. Why the design promised what it did: the 100 m left-hand wave and multi-second ride times reflect a deliberate ASR Ltd wave-shaping design distinct from the more general, protection-first 2005 proposal [R1]

sections.title: Unexpected results
sections.html_or_text: Fishermen retrieving reef wreckage instead of catching more fish, a direct reversal of the project's stated fishing-community goal [R1][R5]. As surf and coastal-protection improvements visibly disappeared through 2010-2011, "coastal communities and civil society of Kerala demanded a judicial and scientific enquiry and social audit" [R1] - sources do not confirm whether any inquiry was actually convened. The coexistence of enthusiastic international surf-media accounts (Collins, R3; the separate Surfer.com piece, R4) with rapid-failure accounts from other sources [R1][R2][R10] suggests the story reaching international surf media diverged sharply from what was reportedly happening on the ground within the same window. Separately, India's broader 2023-announced national artificial-reef rollout (3,477 target fishing villages, ~937 approved as of Sept 2024, ~US$34.5M total) has drawn criticism over net entanglement, "ghost fishing," and erosion risk from poorly sited structures - echoing some of Kovalam's own failure modes [R8]

sections.title: What could have been done better
sections.html_or_text: Shaw Mead's general point - that geotextile-bag reefs are fragile as a system, since a single puncture cascades into total reshaping - implies the core lesson is that this material/technology is inherently high-risk for exposed, high-energy, or debris-prone sites [R2]. The absence of an EIA/SIA/FIA before construction is flagged by Raised Water Research as notable; a proper impact assessment could plausibly have surfaced fisheries and community concerns before construction rather than after failure [R1]. The scale/scope mismatch between the 2005 proposal (500 m, protection-first, 3-7 m depth) and the eventual 100 m surf-focused build is not explicitly critiqued by any source found, but a structure re-scoped from a broad coastal-defence design to a narrower, surf-tuned design may have traded protective robustness for wave-shaping performance - this is this dossier's own inference, not a sourced expert claim [R5][R1][R10]

sections.title: Relevance to Israel / Haifa
sections.html_or_text: No verified, sourced tide-range figure for Kovalam/Kerala was found - not found; qualitatively Kerala's Arabian Sea coast is a mixed, mesotidal-to-microtidal regime versus the microtidal Mediterranean at Haifa. Kovalam faces monsoon-driven swell seasons, a materially higher and more seasonal wave-energy environment than Israel's Mediterranean coast, relevant to why a transplanted geotextile-bag design might face structural loads and debris-strike risks not directly comparable to a Haifa site. Transferable lessons: (1) geotextile-bag reefs are reported across multiple sites (Kovalam, Boscombe, Mount Reef, Opunake) as prone to single-point-of-failure cascading damage once any one container is breached [R2] - relevant to any Haifa proposal considering the same Geotube technology already used at Ashkelon (per this project's own source note, 01_source_notes/jmse2023_bar_drimer_paper.md, which does not itself cover Kovalam); (2) the value of requiring an impact assessment (EIA/SIA/FIA) before construction, which Kovalam skipped [R1]; (3) the risk of scope/design drift between an original protection-first proposal and an eventual, differently-scoped as-built structure, as documented here between the 2005 and 2009-10 Kovalam designs [R5][R1][R10]

footprint.name: Kovalam Reef (Lighthouse Beach)
footprint.shape_type_notes: As-built structure appears to be an echelon/fan array of individual ~30 m geotextile bag units radiating from a focus near the rocky headland, producing a stepped/zigzag breaking line — NOT a single smooth curved crescent or delta wedge. Based on two independent photographic sources (S1/S2 ASR Ltd's own construction-phase aerial photo, and S3 Raised Water Research's traced wave-break outline). Medium confidence on typology; the exact number/angles of units is a schematic reconstruction (low confidence).
footprint.coords: metres; origin = shoreline point nearest the reef centroid (approximated at the base of the rocky headland/‘Lighthouse Point’ immediately updrift of the reef); x = alongshore, positive toward the southeast (from the headland toward the main Lighthouse Beach hotel frontage, matching the sense of ASR Ltd's own construction-phase aerial photo, S2) — the true compass bearing of this alongshore direction was not found in any source and this sense is inferred from photo geometry only; y = offshore, positive seaward; shoreline approximated as the line y=0
footprint.polygon_notes: SCHEMATIC RECONSTRUCTION, not an as-built survey polygon — no engineering drawing or GPS as-built survey of the Kovalam reef was found in any source (ours or Gemini's). Constructed as three ~30 m geotextile-tube units (matching the sourced '30 m units' fact, R1/R2/R10) chained in a staggered/echelon 'staircase' with a 12 m tube width (width itself not sourced for Kovalam; borrowed by analogy from comparable ASR Ltd geobag reef crest widths, e.g. Gold Coast/Mt Maunganui-family designs, and from Gemini's own unsourced 12 m crest-width assumption, which is plausible but likewise unverified). Verified closed and non-self-intersecting with shapely (is_valid=True, is_simple=True, first vertex == last vertex).
footprint.area_m2_notes: This is the footprint of the geobag tubes themselves (slender fan, ~12 m wide), not a filled solid wedge — substantially smaller than Gemini's candidate (3,800 m² gross / 2,245 m² by their own polygon-area audit) because we model the structure as an open fan of narrow tubes, consistent with the photographic evidence in S2, rather than a solid crescent/delta mass. Low confidence — order-of-magnitude estimate only.

crest_depth_m.notes: No source (ours, Gemini's cited sources, or this pass's independent search) states a crest/submergence depth for the as-built Kovalam reef. Gemini's 1.6 m value traces to two citations ('Kerala Harbour Engineering Dept Project Report 2011' and 'Thomas et al. 2012 Performance Assessment of Kovalam Multipurpose Reef') that could not be located or confirmed to exist under those titles/years in this pass's search (see gemini_comparison). By loose analogy, comparable ASR Ltd geotextile multi-purpose reefs (Mount Maunganui, Narrowneck) sit roughly 1.5–2.5 m below chart datum, but this is a generic analogy, not a Kovalam-specific figure, and is not asserted as fact.

distance_offshore_m.notes: Not published in any source. Our schematic polygon's inner edge sits ~34 m and outer edge ~76 m from the shoreline baseline (centroid ~55 m); this range is a low-confidence visual impression from the ASR Ltd construction-phase aerial photo (S2), where swimmers/snorkellers are shown very close to both the shore and the reef, suggesting a near-shore siting broadly compatible with, but not confirming, Gemini's specific 150 m figure. Gemini's 150 m could not be verified against any accessible source either.

footprint.orientation_notes: The unit fan appears to originate from a focus close to the rocky headland ('Eve's/Lighthouse Point' area) immediately updrift of Lighthouse Beach, with the geotextile-tube units fanning alongshore toward the main hotel-fronted beach and outward to sea (per S2's aerial photo, where a labelled 'Reef' shows several dark parallel/sub-parallel submerged tube-rows radiating from near the point). No compass bearing for the arms, the shoreline, or the incident swell was found specifically sourced for Kovalam; Gemini's swell-direction figure (200–240° SSW) is a generically plausible Arabian Sea SW-monsoon swell window but is not independently confirmed for this exact site in any source read this pass.
footprint.materials: Non-woven geotextile sand-filled containers ('Geotubes'/bags), built in ~30 m-long units [R1][R10]. R2 (Geosynthetics Magazine) discusses Kovalam only as an example of geotextile-bag failure ("debris strikes (Kovalam)") and does not itself state the 30 m unit length -- removed from this citation on re-verification (2026-09-25).

A generically SW-monsoon-driven swell climate at this coast is directionally plausible (not Kovalam-specific verified, but consistent with regional knowledge).

disagree.gemini: Curved crescent / delta wedge (smooth continuous curve, 9-vertex polygon)

disagree.why_ours: Two independent photographic sources (ASR Ltd's own construction-phase aerial photo, S2; Raised Water Research's traced wave-break outline, S3) both show straight-segment/staggered structure, not a smooth curve. Gemini's own methodology note ('9-vertex crescent polygon... centroid y=150.1m matches stated 150m exactly') shows the shape was drawn to fit an assumed 150 m distance, not read off any image or drawing — no image/drawing citation is given for the crescent shape itself.

disagree.ours: 1,083.5 m2 (schematic fan-of-tubes reconstruction)
disagree.why_ours: Gemini's own two files disagree with each other by ~70% (3,800 vs 2,245) with no reconciliation — an internal inconsistency, not just an unverified figure. Our lower figure reflects a slender-tube-fan interpretation, consistent with the photographic evidence, rather than a filled solid wedge.

disagree.gemini: 1.6 m, cited to 'Kerala Harbour Engineering Dept Project Report 2011' and 'Thomas et al. 2012 Performance Assessment of Kovalam Multipurpose Reef'
disagree.ours: not found (null)

The closest real, confirmable documents are: (a) ASR Ltd's own project brochure (client: 'Harbour Engineering Department, Government of Kerala' — plausibly the source of Gemini's garbled report title, but it contains no crest-depth figure); and (b) Mead, S.T. and Borrero, J.C. (2011) 'Multi-Purpose Reefs – A Decade of Application' (20th Australasian Coasts & Ports Conference) and a 2015 Ng/Thomas/Phillips et al. paper 'Multifunctional artificial reefs for small islands' (Ocean & Coastal Management) — neither of which could be read in full this pass (paywalled/gated), so neither could be confirmed to contain a Kovalam crest-depth figure either. Gemini's 1.6 m should be treated as unverified pending access to one of these real papers. Additionally (found on re-verification 2026-09-25): Gemini's own reef_footprints.json is internally inconsistent about this same number -- the top-level field states crest_depth_m=1.6, but the adjacent crest_depth_notes field for the same record says "crest at -1.5m CD" (1.6 vs 1.5), a small but real self-contradiction never reconciled in Gemini's own file.

disagree.gemini: scale_sketch_photo_alignment_audit.md, row 7: marks Kovalam "VERIFIED", "Discrepancy/Recommendation: None", justified by "Photo Alignment: The crescent wings explain the observed 22m sand salient and the A-frame peeling wave captured in surf school photos." Cites three of its own photos: kovalam-reef-india.jpg, _gallery1.jpg, _gallery2.jpg.
disagree.ours: Re-verified 2026-09-25 by opening all three of Gemini's own cited photos directly: kovalam-reef-india.jpg is a shoreline view of the lighthouse and headland (no water/reef visible at all); _gallery1.jpg and _gallery2.jpg are silhouette/sunset surfer photos with no visible submerged structure, outline, or aerial perspective. None of the three photos Gemini cites as its "Photo Alignment" evidence shows the reef's footprint, outline, or shape in any way.
disagree.why_ours: Gemini's own "VERIFIED" / "well-aligned with field evidence" verdict for Kovalam's shape is not actually supported by the photographic evidence it cites -- none of the three photos named in its own audit show the submerged structure's outline. This is a second, independent demonstration (alongside the centroid-matches-150m circularity already noted for distance_offshore_m) that Gemini's internal "audit" process marks entries VERIFIED without the cited evidence actually bearing on the claim being checked.

open_issues: No engineering drawing, GPS as-built survey, or dimensioned figure for the Kovalam reef was found in this pass (ours or Gemini's) — all footprint numbers here (ours and Gemini's) are estimates of varying rigor, not sourced as-built dimensions.

Gemini's two cited sources for crest depth/dimensions ('Kerala Harbour Engineering Dept Project Report 2011', 'Thomas et al. 2012') could not be located; they may be fabricated, badly mis-cited, or simply inaccessible online — flagged, not resolved.

Mead, S.T. and Borrero, J.C. (2011) 'Multi-Purpose Reefs – A Decade of Application' is very likely the actual technical source behind Raised Water Research's uncredited 'Mead and Borrero (2011)' reference and may contain real Kovalam performance/dimension data, but it sits behind ResearchGate/eCoast gates (eCoast requires an email-gated download) and could not be read this pass.

The 12 m tube/crest-width assumption used in our area estimate is not sourced for Kovalam specifically — borrowed by analogy from other ASR Ltd geobag reefs and from Gemini's own (also unsourced) assumption.
The compass bearing of the shoreline/alongshore direction and of the incident swell was not confirmed for this exact site in any source read this pass.

The 'Kovalam-Outline.jpg' hand-traced line could represent either the structure's crest outline or simply the visible foam/break-line pattern at one moment of one swell — sources do not label which, so its use here as shape evidence carries residual uncertainty.

Re-verification pass (2026-09-25) also opened three more images already hosted on the already-cited R1 page but not previously catalogued -- Kovalam-Geomat.jpg (a construction-beach photo of a large woven/mesh fabric sheet being hauled ashore with orange floats, headland visible offshore) and Kovalam-Reef-Underwater1.jpg / -Underwater2.jpg (close-range underwater shots of a smooth rounded mound with small fish, no scale reference) -- plus Gemini's own three cited photos (kovalam-reef-india.jpg, _gallery1.jpg, _gallery2.jpg). None of these six images contributed any new dimension or changed any number: the Geomat photo's exact role (base filter mat vs. the bag fabric itself) is not captioned or explained anywhere and is left unresolved; the underwater shots corroborate a smooth single-mound/tube-like structure at close range but carry no scale bar; Gemini's own three cited photos show no reef outline at all (see gemini_comparison, new finding).

verification.item: Bag-unit length 30 m
verification.evidence: Re-fetched R1 (raisedwaterresearch.com, 2026-09-25): "The bags measured 30m in length." Re-fetched R10 (coastalmanagement.com.au): "Geotextile sandbags (30m long)." Re-fetched R2 (geosyntheticsmagazine.com) and searched its full text for "Kovalam": it appears twice, once listing Kovalam among ASR's reefs and once as "debris strikes (Kovalam)" among failure causes -- R2 states NO unit length or dimension for Kovalam. R2 removed from the bag-unit-length citation (was wrongly co-cited) and from the materials field; kept only for the general fragility/failure-mode point it actually supports.

verification.item: As-built volume 4,800 m3
verification.evidence: Re-fetched R1: "Approximate volume: 4,800m3." Re-fetched R10: "Approximate volume: 4,800m3" (near-identical wording to R1, possibly a shared/copied source text, noted but not a red flag for the number itself).

verification.item: Number of chained units = 3 (schematic reconstruction)
verification.evidence: The volume/cross-section arithmetic checks out independently: 4800 m3 / 55 m2 assumed cross-section = 87.3 m of total tube length = 2.9 (~3) x 30 m units -- confirmed by recomputation. However, the claimed photographic corroboration ("S2 aerial photo shows ~4 visible dark parallel/sub-parallel submerged rows") is an overstatement: the PDF's aerial photo was downloaded and zoomed to high resolution (kovalam_page0_hires.png, 400 dpi) and at most 2 clearly discernible darker elongated submerged bands are visible (one with whitewater breaking along its seaward edge); the rest of the water shows diffuse texture that image compression and surface glare make impossible to confidently subdivide into 3 or 4 distinct bands. Wording corrected in the derivation table; the '3 units' conclusion itself is retained because it is primarily supported by the (disclosed, analogy-based) volume arithmetic, not by the photo count.

verification.item: Alongshore length (bbox) 87.9 m
verification.evidence: Recomputed independently with python/shapely from the stored polygon_m vertices: bbox x-span = 87.89 m, rounds to 87.9 m. Exact match.

verification.item: Cross-shore width (bbox) 41.6 m
verification.evidence: Recomputed independently: bbox y-span = 41.61 m, rounds to 41.6 m. Exact match.

verification.item: Footprint area 1,083.5 m2
verification.evidence: shapely.geometry.Polygon(polygon_m).area = 1083.31 m2 (vs. the stated 1083.5 m2, a 0.02% difference attributable to the stored vertices being rounded to 2 decimals rather than the original unrounded buffered-union polygon). Sanity cross-check: 3 tube segments x 30 m x 12 m = 1080 m2 (a flat-rectangle approximation) is consistent with the actual buffered/mitred-join polygon area of ~1083 m2. is_valid=True, exterior.is_simple=True, first vertex==last vertex (closed) -- all independently confirmed.

verification.item: max_dimension_m = 97.4
verification.evidence: Recomputed independently: the true maximum pairwise vertex-to-vertex distance within the actual (non-rectangular) polygon is 92.05 m (between vertices [-43.1, 34.31] and [39.01, 75.92]), not 97.4 m. The stated 97.4 m turns out to be the diagonal of the bounding BOX (sqrt(87.9^2 + 41.6^2) = 97.2-97.4 depending on rounding) -- a quantity the polygon's own vertices never actually reach, since the bbox's far corners are empty space outside the fan shape. Checked the convention used by sibling verified/researched footprint files (e.g. opunake, southern-ocean-surf-reef-albany, borth): max_dimension_m in every other file is the true max pairwise vertex distance of the actual polygon (<= bbox diagonal), never the bbox diagonal itself. Corrected to 92.1 m for consistency and accuracy.

verification.item: Shape typology: chevron / echelon fan (not smooth crescent)
verification.evidence: S3 (Kovalam-Outline.jpg) re-downloaded and viewed directly (2026-09-25): the hand-traced line is unambiguously a stepped zigzag polyline with at least 4 straight segments meeting at 3 sharp-angle vertices -- a staircase pattern, not a smooth curve. This is strong, clear, independently-viewed evidence for a staggered/chevron structure. S2 (ASR aerial photo) independently re-viewed at high resolution: shows a single elongated, gently-curved-to-irregular dark submerged patch with whitewater along its leading edge and at least 2 discernible darker bands (see 'number of chained units' item above) -- weaker support than originally claimed for '4 parallel rows fanning from the headland,' but still consistent with a non-smooth, multi-part structure rather than one continuous uniform crescent arc. Overall chevron/fan-over-crescent verdict CONFIRMED, resting primarily on S3, with S2 as weaker corroboration than the original draft implied.

verification.item: Crest depth: not found (null)
verification.evidence: R1, R2, R10, S1, S2 re-checked/re-fetched: none states a crest or submergence depth for Kovalam. Targeted web searches for Gemini's two cited sources ("Kerala Harbour Engineering Dept Project Report 2011", "Thomas et al. 2012 Performance Assessment of Kovalam Multipurpose Reef") returned no matching document under either title. A real 2015 paper by Ng, Thomas, Phillips et al. ("Multifunctional artificial reefs for small islands", Ocean & Coastal Management) does exist and does include a real author named Thomas -- a plausible source of the citation confusion -- but its title, year, and subject (small islands, not Kovalam-specific) do not match Gemini's citation, and it was not accessible to confirm or deny a Kovalam depth figure. Default-to-unsupported correctly applied; value remains null.

name: Borth coastal defence reef (incl. Wallog headland)
year: Feasibility study May 2004 [R10]; design from Oct 2009 [R1][R4]; construction started Jan 2011 [R1]; contractor's target completion Nov 2011 [R1][R9]; Coflein gives completion March 2012 [R3]; wider Phase-1 scheme described as 2011-2015 [R6]
type: Submerged rock (riprap) multi-purpose reef plus rock groynes, breakwaters and beach nourishment [R1][R4]
purpose: Primary: flood and erosion protection for Borth village, built on a mobile shingle bank whose 1970s timber-groyne defences were failing [R1][R2][R4]. Secondary/amenity: shape the reef so breaking swell also creates a surf wave, because the community explicitly rejected a hard sea wall in favour of keeping an open beach [R1][R2][R4]
size: Reef sited c.400 m offshore per the contractor (2011) [R1] / c.300 m per local/heritage sources (2013 press, Coflein) [R2][R3]; 275,000 t total material moved (84,500 t shingle replacement, 18,500 t Type-3 rock 0.3-1t, 16,200 t Type-1 rock 3-6t, 42,000 t Type-4 rock 6-10t, 500 t Type-6 rock 5-100kg) [R1]; Coflein separately states c.300,000 t of rock for the whole works [R3]
cost: Figures vary by source, not reconciled: Phase 1 funding envelope GBP 7M (FY2009/10-2010/11) [R4]; GBP 13.5M "first phase of the strategy" quoted in 2009 [R1]; BAM Nuttall's winning construction tender GBP 11.5M [R1]; full phased scheme costed at GBP 29M in 2011-2013 press [R1][R2]; Coflein gives completed reef/coastal-defence works at GBP 13M [R3]; Wikipedia gives GBP 12M for the 2011-2015 scheme [R6]
cost_usd_approx: Roughly GBP 12-13M is approximately US$15-17M, and GBP 29M is approximately US$36M, at approximate 2011-2013 GBP/USD rates of ~1.25-1.6 (rough conversion, not sourced to a specific FX reference)
financed_by: Coast Protection Grant from the Welsh Assembly Government (later Welsh Government) and Convergence funding from the Welsh European Funding Office (WEFO) / European Regional Development Fund [R4][R6]
motivation: Borth sits on a mobile shingle bank in Cardigan Bay; its 1970s timber groyne and breastwork sea defences were judged inadequate, with ordinary storms causing overtopping flooding through homes, per Borth councillor Ray Quant [R2]. A council feasibility study found existing defences within 10 years of failure with potentially catastrophic losses possible, triggering a 150-resident 2001 visioning meeting [R4]. Ceredigion County Council's coast and rivers engineer, Rhodri Llwyd, said the scheme had been 15 years in the making and that the community absolutely didn't want a wall, so the idea of a reef was born [R1][R2]
designer: Royal Haskoning (detailed design, appointed Oct 2009); specialist reef designer ASR (sub-consultant); physical modelling by HR Wallingford; environmental consultant Atkins [R1][R4]. Original feasibility study "Borth Multi-Purpose reef for Coastal Protection and Amenity" completed May 2004 for Ceredigion County Council (authors not confirmed; ResearchGate record blocked, content corroborated via Borth Community website) [R10][R4]
contractor: BAM Nuttall (site agent Ray Jones); plant from Norton Plant Hire [R1][R4]
status_now: Built and in service; as of December 2011 residents reported the new defences had already stopped two high tides from flooding their properties [R2][R3]. The wider Borth-to-Ynyslas coastal-protection programme was still being planned/phased in later business-case documents, implying more phases beyond the reef itself continued years after Phase 1 (details not found) [R4]
hover_text: A c.300-400 m offshore multi-purpose rock reef plus groynes and beach nourishment, built 2011-2012 for roughly GBP 12-13M (reported up to GBP 29M for the full phased scheme), financed by Welsh Government and EU (WEFO/ERDF) funding; it stopped flooding within months of substantial completion, but years later the surf-industry press still describes Borth only as "a proposed" reef site rather than crediting it with a reliable wave [R1][R2][R3][R7].
design_as_planned: The preferred option, chosen after comparing technical, economic, amenity, environmental and safety criteria, was "Rock Beach Control Structures with a Multi-Purpose Reef and Beach Nourishment" [R4][R10]. Phase 1 combined: a submerged multi-purpose reef near the Craig y Delyn cliffs at the beach's southern end (sited there so the community could keep an open beach and unobstructed views), two rock groynes and two rock breakwaters further along the frontage to retain shingle, and beach nourishment (originally 150,000 m3 of imported shingle) [R1][R4]. Designed to a 1-in-100-year storm standard while remaining adaptable to future climate change [R4]. The reef's role was explicitly dual: reduce wave energy to protect the beach from erosion and broaden the beach inshore, while also being shaped to help swell waves break as a secondary surfing amenity [R1][R2]. The team settled on "Option 9A" for outline design after comparing numerous layouts, with 3D physical wave-basin modelling by HR Wallingford used to size the rock armour [R1]
as_built_vs_design: Construction followed the planned reef/groynes/breakwaters/nourishment layout, but with two contractor-driven, budget-closing changes: the client's design already carried about GBP 1M of cost overrun after physical-model testing showed extra rock was needed, and BAM Nuttall's tender then came in a further GBP 1M over that inflated budget [R1]. BAM Nuttall closed the combined c.GBP 2M gap by (1) mining and reusing the beach's own existing shingle, bulked up with cheaper imported quarried material underneath and the original shingle put back on top, instead of importing the full 150,000 m3 specified, and (2) building a temporary rock causeway out to the reef site so land-based excavators and dumper trucks could be used instead of the originally tendered floating marine plant [R1]. The causeway was intended to be removed once the reef was finished [R9]. Construction ran on a tight tidal window (6am-9pm with a three-hour high-tide stoppage), with over 8,000 material deliveries made by September 2011 [R1][R2]
outcome: Coastal protection: residents reported the new defences had already stopped two high tides from flooding their properties by December 2011, while the works were still substantially under construction [R2][R3]. An unplanned side effect of the earthworks was the exposure of a prehistoric submerged forest (oak, pine, birch, willow and hazel stumps dated to roughly 1500 BCE) tied to the Welsh legend of Cantre'r Gwaelod, now visible at low tide [R6]. Surfing outcome is contested: press coverage at construction time promised the reef would provide excellent surf conditions and boost the local economy [R2], but the Stormrider Surf Guide, years after completion, still describes Borth as merely "a proposed" artificial reef site rather than a functioning named surf break [R7], and Surf-Forecast.com rates Borth's surf quality only 3.0/5 with beginner difficulty and no posted first-hand surfer reviews [R8]. No wave-height, ride-length or surfable-days measurement for the reef was found [R7][R8]
why_worked_or_failed: For coastal protection, the scheme functioned successfully in its early years, withstanding December-2011 storms without flooding the properties it protects within months of substantial completion [R2][R3]. Credited design choices: graded, multi-tonne rock armour (up to 10 t pieces) sized via HR Wallingford's 3D physical modelling before construction rather than off-the-shelf sizing [R1]; a reef+groyne+breakwater system working with beach nourishment instead of a rigid sea wall, chosen because the community rejected a wall [R1][R2]; and a construction sequencing (temporary causeway, tidal work windows) that let the contractor place rock accurately below the high-tide line [R1]. For the surfing function, no source found explains in engineering terms (crest depth, slope, wave-focusing geometry) why the wave has or hasn't performed; the continued "proposed" framing in the Stormrider guide is suggestive the amenity function has not been widely recognised as delivering a notable wave, but no direct technical post-mortem was located [R7]
unexpected_results: The exposure of the prehistoric petrified forest and its tie-in to the Cantre'r Gwaelod legend was an unplanned, publicised side effect of the earthworks [R6]. No sources found document fishing-pressure changes, ecological studies, rip-current safety incidents, litigation, or measurable tourism-economy impact specifically tied to the Borth reef (treated as a genuine gap, not confirmed absence of any such effect)
could_be_better: No source located offers an explicit engineers'/authors' retrospective critique of the Borth scheme's design or execution (unlike, e.g., Boscombe's published post-mortem). The one available critical signal is indirect: the Stormrider Surf Guide's continued description of Borth as merely "a proposed artificial reef site" years after completion implies the reef has not become a recognised, reliably rideable wave in the way pre-construction press promised [R7]; Surf-Forecast's low consistency/quality scores point the same way [R8], though neither source explains which design choice is responsible. From a cost-management perspective, the construction tender came in over budget on top of a design that had already grown by about GBP 1M after physical-model testing, and the contractor had to redesign its construction method and material sourcing specifically to close that gap, implying the original budget/design had under-priced the works as first specified [R1]
relevance_to_israel: Cardigan Bay/Aberystwyth (immediately adjacent to Borth) is macrotidal: spring tidal range is roughly 4.7-4.8 m (high spring tide c.5.4 m, low tide down to c.0.6 m) [R11]. This is drastically larger than the Israeli Mediterranean coast (Haifa/Ashkelon/Netanya etc.), which is effectively microtidal, with a tidal range on the order of tens of centimetres. A reef crest depth and rock-armour design tuned by HR Wallingford's physical modelling to work across a c.4.7 m tidal swing at Borth [R1] cannot be reused as-is on Israel's coast, since the same structure would sit permanently near a single water level in Israel rather than alternately surfacing and submerging by several metres, changing both wave-breaking performance and exposure/maintenance regime. What transfers conceptually: the core political lesson that a community explicitly chose a submerged multi-purpose reef over a hard sea wall specifically to keep an open, usable beach and views [R1][R2][R4], directly analogous to debates around geotubes/breakwaters at Ashkelon and Netanya. The value-engineering lesson (reusing existing shingle instead of full import, to control cost) is also directly transferable regardless of tidal regime [R1]
