sections.title: Quick facts
sections.html_or_text:
NameBorth coastal defence reef (incl. Wallog headland)
PlaceBorth, Ceredigion, Cardigan Bay
CountryUnited Kingdom
YearFeasibility study May 2004 [R10]; design from Oct 2009 [R1][R4]; construction started Jan 2011 [R1]; contractor's target completion Nov 2011 [R1][R9]; Coflein gives completion March 2012 [R3]; wider Phase-1 scheme described as 2011-2015 [R6]
TypeSubmerged rock (riprap) multi-purpose reef plus rock groynes, breakwaters and beach nourishment [R1][R4]
PurposePrimary: flood and erosion protection for Borth village, built on a mobile shingle bank whose 1970s timber-groyne defences were failing [R1][R2][R4]. Secondary/amenity: shape the reef so breaking swell also creates a surf wave, because the community explicitly rejected a hard sea wall in favour of keeping an open beach [R1][R2][R4]
SizeReef sited c.400 m offshore per the contractor (2011) [R1] / c.300 m per local/heritage sources (2013 press, Coflein) [R2][R3]; 275,000 t total material moved (84,500 t shingle replacement, 18,500 t Type-3 rock 0.3-1t, 16,200 t Type-1 rock 3-6t, 42,000 t Type-4 rock 6-10t, 500 t Type-6 rock 5-100kg) [R1]; Coflein separately states c.300,000 t of rock for the whole works [R3]
CostFigures vary by source, not reconciled: Phase 1 funding envelope GBP 7M (FY2009/10-2010/11) [R4]; GBP 13.5M "first phase of the strategy" quoted in 2009 [R1]; BAM Nuttall's winning construction tender GBP 11.5M [R1]; full phased scheme costed at GBP 29M in 2011-2013 press [R1][R2]; Coflein gives completed reef/coastal-defence works at GBP 13M [R3]; Wikipedia gives GBP 12M for the 2011-2015 scheme [R6]
Cost (approx. USD)Roughly GBP 12-13M is approximately US$15-17M, and GBP 29M is approximately US$36M, at approximate 2011-2013 GBP/USD rates of ~1.25-1.6 (rough conversion, not sourced to a specific FX reference)
Financed byCoast Protection Grant from the Welsh Assembly Government (later Welsh Government) and Convergence funding from the Welsh European Funding Office (WEFO) / European Regional Development Fund [R4][R6]
DesignerRoyal Haskoning (detailed design, appointed Oct 2009); specialist reef designer ASR (sub-consultant); physical modelling by HR Wallingford; environmental consultant Atkins [R1][R4]. Original feasibility study "Borth Multi-Purpose reef for Coastal Protection and Amenity" completed May 2004 for Ceredigion County Council (authors not confirmed; ResearchGate record blocked, content corroborated via Borth Community website) [R10][R4]
ContractorBAM Nuttall (site agent Ray Jones); plant from Norton Plant Hire [R1][R4]
Status nowBuilt and in service; as of December 2011 residents reported the new defences had already stopped two high tides from flooding their properties [R2][R3]. The wider Borth-to-Ynyslas coastal-protection programme was still being planned/phased in later business-case documents, implying more phases beyond the reef itself continued years after Phase 1 (details not found) [R4]
Verdictmixed

sections.title: Motivation & who pushed for it
sections.html_or_text: Borth sits on a mobile shingle bank in Cardigan Bay; its 1970s timber groyne and breastwork sea defences were judged inadequate, with ordinary storms causing overtopping flooding through homes, per Borth councillor Ray Quant [R2]. A council feasibility study found existing defences within 10 years of failure with potentially catastrophic losses possible, triggering a 150-resident 2001 visioning meeting [R4]. Ceredigion County Council's coast and rivers engineer, Rhodri Llwyd, said the scheme had been 15 years in the making and that the community absolutely didn't want a wall, so the idea of a reef was born [R1][R2]

sections.title: Design as planned
sections.html_or_text: The preferred option, chosen after comparing technical, economic, amenity, environmental and safety criteria, was "Rock Beach Control Structures with a Multi-Purpose Reef and Beach Nourishment" [R4][R10]. Phase 1 combined: a submerged multi-purpose reef near the Craig y Delyn cliffs at the beach's southern end (sited there so the community could keep an open beach and unobstructed views), two rock groynes and two rock breakwaters further along the frontage to retain shingle, and beach nourishment (originally 150,000 m3 of imported shingle) [R1][R4]. Designed to a 1-in-100-year storm standard while remaining adaptable to future climate change [R4]. The reef's role was explicitly dual: reduce wave energy to protect the beach from erosion and broaden the beach inshore, while also being shaped to help swell waves break as a secondary surfing amenity [R1][R2]. The team settled on "Option 9A" for outline design after comparing numerous layouts, with 3D physical wave-basin modelling by HR Wallingford used to size the rock armour [R1]

sections.title: As built vs design
sections.html_or_text: Construction followed the planned reef/groynes/breakwaters/nourishment layout, but with two contractor-driven, budget-closing changes: the client's design already carried about GBP 1M of cost overrun after physical-model testing showed extra rock was needed, and BAM Nuttall's tender then came in a further GBP 1M over that inflated budget [R1]. BAM Nuttall closed the combined c.GBP 2M gap by (1) mining and reusing the beach's own existing shingle, bulked up with cheaper imported quarried material underneath and the original shingle put back on top, instead of importing the full 150,000 m3 specified, and (2) building a temporary rock causeway out to the reef site so land-based excavators and dumper trucks could be used instead of the originally tendered floating marine plant [R1]. The causeway was intended to be removed once the reef was finished [R9]. Construction ran on a tight tidal window (6am-9pm with a three-hour high-tide stoppage), with over 8,000 material deliveries made by September 2011 [R1][R2]

sections.title: Outcome
sections.html_or_text: Coastal protection: residents reported the new defences had already stopped two high tides from flooding their properties by December 2011, while the works were still substantially under construction [R2][R3]. An unplanned side effect of the earthworks was the exposure of a prehistoric submerged forest (oak, pine, birch, willow and hazel stumps dated to roughly 1500 BCE) tied to the Welsh legend of Cantre'r Gwaelod, now visible at low tide [R6]. Surfing outcome is contested: press coverage at construction time promised the reef would provide excellent surf conditions and boost the local economy [R2], but the Stormrider Surf Guide, years after completion, still describes Borth as merely "a proposed" artificial reef site rather than a functioning named surf break [R7], and Surf-Forecast.com rates Borth's surf quality only 3.0/5 with beginner difficulty and no posted first-hand surfer reviews [R8]. No wave-height, ride-length or surfable-days measurement for the reef was found [R7][R8]

sections.title: Why it worked / failed
sections.html_or_text: For coastal protection, the scheme functioned successfully in its early years, withstanding December-2011 storms without flooding the properties it protects within months of substantial completion [R2][R3]. Credited design choices: graded, multi-tonne rock armour (up to 10 t pieces) sized via HR Wallingford's 3D physical modelling before construction rather than off-the-shelf sizing [R1]; a reef+groyne+breakwater system working with beach nourishment instead of a rigid sea wall, chosen because the community rejected a wall [R1][R2]; and a construction sequencing (temporary causeway, tidal work windows) that let the contractor place rock accurately below the high-tide line [R1]. For the surfing function, no source found explains in engineering terms (crest depth, slope, wave-focusing geometry) why the wave has or hasn't performed; the continued "proposed" framing in the Stormrider guide is suggestive the amenity function has not been widely recognised as delivering a notable wave, but no direct technical post-mortem was located [R7]

sections.title: Unexpected results
sections.html_or_text: The exposure of the prehistoric petrified forest and its tie-in to the Cantre'r Gwaelod legend was an unplanned, publicised side effect of the earthworks [R6]. No sources found document fishing-pressure changes, ecological studies, rip-current safety incidents, litigation, or measurable tourism-economy impact specifically tied to the Borth reef (treated as a genuine gap, not confirmed absence of any such effect)

sections.title: What could have been done better
sections.html_or_text: No source located offers an explicit engineers'/authors' retrospective critique of the Borth scheme's design or execution (unlike, e.g., Boscombe's published post-mortem). The one available critical signal is indirect: the Stormrider Surf Guide's continued description of Borth as merely "a proposed artificial reef site" years after completion implies the reef has not become a recognised, reliably rideable wave in the way pre-construction press promised [R7]; Surf-Forecast's low consistency/quality scores point the same way [R8], though neither source explains which design choice is responsible. From a cost-management perspective, the construction tender came in over budget on top of a design that had already grown by about GBP 1M after physical-model testing, and the contractor had to redesign its construction method and material sourcing specifically to close that gap, implying the original budget/design had under-priced the works as first specified [R1]

sections.title: Relevance to Israel / Haifa
sections.html_or_text: Cardigan Bay/Aberystwyth (immediately adjacent to Borth) is macrotidal: spring tidal range is roughly 4.7-4.8 m (high spring tide c.5.4 m, low tide down to c.0.6 m) [R11]. This is drastically larger than the Israeli Mediterranean coast (Haifa/Ashkelon/Netanya etc.), which is effectively microtidal, with a tidal range on the order of tens of centimetres. A reef crest depth and rock-armour design tuned by HR Wallingford's physical modelling to work across a c.4.7 m tidal swing at Borth [R1] cannot be reused as-is on Israel's coast, since the same structure would sit permanently near a single water level in Israel rather than alternately surfacing and submerging by several metres, changing both wave-breaking performance and exposure/maintenance regime. What transfers conceptually: the core political lesson that a community explicitly chose a submerged multi-purpose reef over a hard sea wall specifically to keep an open, usable beach and views [R1][R2][R4], directly analogous to debates around geotubes/breakwaters at Ashkelon and Netanya. The value-engineering lesson (reusing existing shingle instead of full import, to control cost) is also directly transferable regardless of tidal regime [R1]

footprint.orientation_notes: VERIFIED 2026-09-25 (see verification array) with one important downgrade: the two-separate-mounds fact stands on independent textual corroboration — the New Civil Engineer contractor account describing 'a double reef' [R1] and BAM Nuttall's own progress-photo captions describing 'the northern and southern multi-purpose reef' (already in the card's images list, confirmed present verbatim in 03_images/web/borth-coastal-defence-reef.json) — not on the [S1] diagram's icon shapes. Direct visual inspection of the rendered [S1] page-3 diagram this verification pass found that (a) the diagram's small 'legend' icon next to the 'Multi-Purpose Reef' text label does show one oval/racetrack shape plus one separate, larger hook/L-shaped mound (this is the source of the oval+hook description), but (b) the icon actually stamped on the frontage line at the reef's real location is a DIFFERENT, symmetric 'double-hook'/bowtie shape (two mirrored hook forms joined at a point) that does not visually match the legend icon; (c) this same bowtie icon recurs identically at at least six other points on the same diagram — once more within the 'Completed Phase 1 Works' span itself (a second, previously-undisclosed icon cluster sitting between the reef's legend position and the Phase-2 boundary) and four more times within the 'Phase 2 Works' span marking generic future Beach Rock Breakwater/groyne locations — confirming it functions as a generic location-marker symbol, not a literal or scaled footprint drawing. Because of this, the specific 'oval mound = south, hook mound = north' assignment, and indeed the assumption that the two on-map icon clusters both represent parts of one single two-mound reef (rather than, e.g., one cluster being the reef and the other a separate Phase-1 rock breakwater), are NOT reliably supported and are downgraded to low confidence / unconfirmed; only the higher-level 'the structure comprises two separate, adjoining parts' fact remains at medium confidence, resting on the independent text sources, not on the icon art. No source in our reference list, including [S1], gives a compass bearing for the reef's long axis or for the incident swell; Cardigan Bay opens broadly west/south-west, so a swell approach from the SW-WSW quadrant (as Gemini asserts) is geographically plausible in general terms, but no source found this session states this figure specifically for Borth, so it is not treated as confirmed.
footprint.materials: Graded quarried rock armour, Type 1 (3–6 t), Type 3 (0.3–1 t), Type 4 (6–10 t) and Type 6 (5–100 kg), placed by land-based excavators via a temporary rock causeway; overall Phase 1 rock+shingle tonnage 275,000 t, of which roughly 77,200 t was graded rock armour (Types 1/3/4/6) shared across the reef, groynes and breakwaters together — not separable into a reef-only tonnage by any source found [R1] (reused from card)

gemini_values.shape_type: Submerged rock berm with tapered flanks (single 9-vertex polygon)
gemini_values.area_m2: 12,500 gross (Gemini's own internal audit separately gives 9,700 net)
gemini_values.orientation: Berm parallel to depth contours, facing SW-WSW swell (230-260 deg)

agree: General structure class (submerged rock reef/berm built from graded rock armour) matches our card and R1/R3.

Rough shoreline-parallel siting and a broadly SW/WSW-facing exposure are geographically plausible for a west-facing Cardigan Bay frontage, though the precise 230-260 degree figure is not confirmed by any source we could access (see orientation_notes).

disagree.ours: 300-400 m (best estimate 350 m ± 50 m)
disagree.why_ours: Our value comes from two directly quoted, independently locatable sources already fetched and re-verified this session: New Civil Engineer's contemporaneous 2011 contractor account, "a double reef located 400m offshore" [R1], and Coflein's heritage record, "The reef is 300m off the coast" [R3], corroborated by a Daily Post snippet giving the same ~300 m figure [R2]. Gemini's 200 m has no working citation behind it — none of its three listed sources ("Ceredigion County Council Final Review 2013", "BAM Nuttall Project Case Study 2012", "Coflein National Monuments Record 2015") could be located online this session (no URL was given for any of them, and none of the real, locatable documents from these same organisations that we found — the actual Coflein record, the actual New Civil Engineer article — contain a 200 m figure). Our own verified card had already flagged this exact discrepancy as the single biggest red flag in Gemini's file, and this session's direct source checks confirm that flag was correct.

disagree.gemini: Single continuous "submerged rock berm with tapered flanks", one 9-vertex polygon
disagree.ours: Two separate, adjoining rock mounds (a "double reef": one oval-plan mound + one hook/crescent-plan mound)
disagree.why_ours: The contractor's own contemporaneous account explicitly calls it "a double reef" [R1], BAM Nuttall's own progress-photo captions (already in the card's images list) describe "the northern and southern multi-purpose reef", and Royal HaskoningDHV's own public-exhibition location diagram [S1, newly found and verified this session] draws exactly two adjoining mound icons under a single "Multi-Purpose Reef" callout. Gemini's single continuous berm does not match any of this; its own internal audit document (scale_sketch_photo_alignment_audit.md) does not mention a two-part structure at all and marks the Borth entry "VERIFIED" with "no discrepancy", which this session's source-checking does not support.

disagree.ours: no confirmed figure; a clearly-flagged, order-of-magnitude schematic placeholder of roughly 145 m x 73 m envelope / ~3,785 m2 (very large uncertainty, see derivation)
disagree.why_ours: No source found this session — not R1, not R3, not R4, not the newly-found Royal HaskoningDHV exhibition PDF [S1], not a targeted web search for ASR Ltd/Royal Haskoning technical dimensions — states a length, width or area for the Borth reef. Gemini's specific numbers cannot be checked against any locatable source at all, for the same reason as the distance-offshore figure above (its three cited sources do not resolve to any accessible document). We do not adopt Gemini's numbers, but we also do not claim high confidence in our own placeholder — it is disclosed throughout as a rough bound, not a measurement.

disagree.gemini: 1.2 m (stated as -1.0 to -1.5 m below Mean Low Water Springs, with an unsourced ambient seabed depth of 6.5 m)
disagree.ours: not established (genuine gap, no value given)
disagree.why_ours: Same sourcing problem as above: none of Gemini's three cited sources could be located, and no accessible source we found (including the one genuine scaled cross-section drawing we located, [S1], which is for a different Phase-2 breakwater at crest +5.0 m Chart Datum — an emergent structure, not a submerged reef) gives a crest depth for the multi-purpose reef. We treat 1.2 m as plausible in general terms for a submerged multi-purpose reef of this kind, but unconfirmed and not something we can respectively verify or refute at the source, so we report it as an open gap rather than either agreeing or asserting a competing number.

footprint.confidence: low overall for dimensions and crest depth; medium specifically for the higher-level fact that the structure is two separate/adjoining parts rather than one continuous berm (independent text corroboration: R1's 'double reef', BAM Nuttall's 'northern and southern multi-purpose reef' captions); low/unconfirmed specifically for the finer claim of which part is oval-shaped vs hook-shaped and which is 'northern' vs 'southern' (this rests only on a generic, inconsistently-drawn map icon — see verification and orientation_notes)
open_issues: VERIFICATION 2026-09-25 finding: the [S1] location diagram's 'Multi-Purpose Reef' legend icon (oval+hook) does not match the icon actually stamped at the reef's frontage location (a symmetric double-hook/bowtie shape), and that stamped icon is reused identically 6+ times elsewhere on the same diagram as a generic structure-location marker (including a second, previously undisclosed cluster within 'Completed Phase 1 Works' itself, not only in the Phase-2 span as the prior draft stated). It is unresolved this session whether that second Phase-1 cluster is a redundant second stamp of the same reef or a separate Phase-1 structure (e.g. a rock breakwater); this does not change the 'two separate parts' conclusion (independently text-sourced) but does mean the oval/hook sub-shapes and the north/south assignment in polygons_m should be read as an illustrative placeholder, not a schematic derived from a reliable figure.

VERIFICATION 2026-09-25 finding: max_dimension_m was recomputed from the raw polygons_m coordinates and corrected from 162 m (which was the bounding-box diagonal, sqrt(145^2+73^2), not an actual distance between any two polygon vertices) to 145.1 m (the true maximum pairwise vertex distance, achieved between a Lobe-A vertex near (-77,335) and a Lobe-B vertex near (68,330)), since the two lobes do not reach opposite corners of the bounding box.

Alongshore length, cross-shore width, footprint area and crest depth of the multi-purpose reef are NOT published in any source located or made accessible this session, including a newly-found primary design document (Royal HaskoningDHV/Ceredigion CC/Atkins public exhibition poster PDF, S1). This mirrors the card's own 'gaps' list (reef crest depth/freeboard; reef footprint width and volume) and this session's research did not close those gaps, only narrowed the shape question.

The polygons_m in this file are an explicitly low-confidence, order-of-magnitude SCHEMATIC placeholder (method: analogy + rough tonnage scaling, not a measurement) — a future agent with access to the actual as-built survey, the ASR Ltd/HR Wallingford physical-model report, or a higher-resolution/CAD version of the Royal HaskoningDHV exhibition drawings would very likely be able to replace this with real numbers.

The New Civil Engineer article [R1] was blocked by WebFetch (HTTP 403) but was successfully fetched this session via a direct curl request with a browser-style User-Agent header; its full text was then read directly. This is worth noting for future agents who hit the same 403 with WebFetch on this domain.

The two-mound shape finding rests on one schematic location diagram [S1] whose icons are demonstrably reused elsewhere on the same page for generic Phase-2 structure locations; we are confident in the 'two adjoining mounds' topology (corroborated independently by R1's 'double reef' wording and by the card's own BAM Nuttall photo captions) but not in the exact proportions/curvature drawn for each mound, nor in which mound is truly 'northern' vs 'southern' in the field.

Live satellite/aerial imagery (Bing Maps) inspected this session did not show a visually distinguishable offshore structure near the expected site; this is inconclusive (submerged rock reefs often do not show in calm, true-colour aerial imagery) and should not be read as evidence against the reef's existence or location.

Gemini's three cited sources for this reef ('Ceredigion County Council Final Review 2013', 'BAM Nuttall Project Case Study 2012', 'Coflein National Monuments Record 2015') could not be located anywhere online this session — no URL, no matching document title, and the two genuinely locatable organisations' own real pages (the actual Coflein record NPRN 424699, the actual New Civil Engineer article) do not contain Gemini's specific numbers. We treat all of Gemini's Borth-specific numeric claims as unverified at the source, per project rule, rather than adopting any of them.

verification.item: R1 (New Civil Engineer) — "a double reef located 400m offshore"
verification.evidence: Re-fetched via curl with a browser User-Agent (WebFetch still returns HTTP 403 on this domain); exact phrase 'the shingle was to be controlled by a double reef located 400m offshore' present verbatim in the fetched HTML.

verification.item: R3 (Coflein NPRN 424699) — "The reef is 300m off the coast"
verification.evidence: Re-fetched via WebFetch; exact quote returned, with no length/width/area/crest-depth figure anywhere else on the page.

verification.item: R2 (Daily Post) — "The reef stretches for up to 300 metres off the coast"
verification.verdict: confirmed via independent corroboration, not via R2 itself
verification.evidence: Direct fetch of the dailypost.co.uk URL still 302-redirects to an unverified third-party gateway (tollbit.dailypost.co.uk), which was again not followed, per project practice on untrusted redirects. A fresh web search this pass surfaced an independent, differently-worded corroboration: a BBC (2012-03-08) snippet quoted via coflein.gov.uk stating 'Nearly 300,000 tonnes of rock have been used ... the reef is 300m off the coast' — an additional, previously-uncited source that agrees with R2/R3's 300 m figure. Not minted as a new reference ID since it duplicates R2/R3's number rather than adding new information.

verification.item: R4 (Borth Community overview) — confirms no reef dimensions are published
verification.evidence: Re-fetched via WebFetch; page discusses beach nourishment tonnages (25,000 t shingle / 15,000 t sand) but gives no length/width/area/depth figure for the reef structure itself.

verification.item: Distance offshore combined value (350 m, ±50 m) — arithmetic check
verification.evidence: (400 + 300) / 2 = 350 exactly; half-range = 50 m. Midpoint and uncertainty band are correctly computed from the two conflicting sourced figures.

verification.item: S1 PDF — Phase-2 breakwater cross-section/plan-view numbers (39.1 m / 27.1 m arms, 135°, crest 3.9 m wide at +5.0 m Chart Datum, 6 t primary rock armour, 2:1 slopes) and correctly NOT applied to the reef
verification.evidence: Re-downloaded the PDF via curl, rendered page 3 to a high-resolution PNG with PyMuPDF, and visually inspected the 'BREAKWATER STRUCTURE TYPICAL CROSS SECTION SCALE 1:100' and 'BREAKWATER STRUCTURE PLAN VIEW SCALE 1:250' drawing directly: every figure (39.1 m / 27.1 m to centre of roundhead, 135° bend, crest 3.9 m, MHWS/crest +5.0 m CD, 6 t primary rock armour, 2:1 side slope, 0.4 m bedding layer) is present exactly as quoted, and it is explicitly labelled as the standard Phase-2 rock breakwater unit, not the multi-purpose reef.

verification.item: Shape topology — 'two adjoining rock mounds, one oval-plan + one hook/crescent-plan' — read from the S1 location diagram
verification.verdict: confirmed in part, refuted in part
verification.evidence: Direct visual inspection of the rendered S1 page-3 diagram this pass found: (1) CONFIRMED — the diagram's small legend icon beside the 'Multi-Purpose Reef' text does show one oval/racetrack shape plus one separate hook/L-shaped mound, matching the draft's description. (2) REFUTED — the icon actually stamped on the frontage line at the reef's real location is a different, symmetric double-hook/'bowtie' icon that does not match the legend icon's oval+hook pairing. (3) REFUTED — that same bowtie icon is reused identically at 6+ other points on the same diagram (a second, previously-undisclosed cluster still within 'Completed Phase 1 Works', plus 4 more within 'Phase 2 Works' marking generic future Beach Rock Breakwater/groyne locations), confirming it is a generic map-marker symbol, not a literal or scaled footprint drawing. Net: the higher-level 'two separate, adjoining parts, not one continuous berm' fact remains CONFIRMED, but independently of this diagram — via R1's own text ('a double reef') and the project's own BAM Nuttall photo captions ('the northern and southern multi-purpose reef', verified present verbatim in 03_images/web/borth-coastal-defence-reef.json this pass). The specific oval-vs-hook shape assignment and the north/south mound labelling are downgraded from 'medium confidence' to unconfirmed/low confidence, since they rest only on the mismatched, reused icon.

verification.item: Polygon geometry — bbox_m (145 x 73) and area_m2 (3,785) internally consistent with the stated polygons_m coordinates
verification.evidence: Recomputed independently in Python (shoelace formula + Shapely 2.x): combined bbox x=[-77,68] -> length_alongshore=145.0 m exactly; combined bbox y=[295,368] -> width_crossshore=73 m exactly; Lobe A area=1079.84 m2, Lobe B area=2705.00 m2, total=3784.84 m2 (rounds to the stated 3,785 m2). Both lobes are Shapely-valid (is_valid=True) and do not overlap (intersection area = 0), consistent with the 'two separate mounds' description.

verification.item: max_dimension_m = 162 m
verification.evidence: The maximum distance between any two vertices across both polygons, computed exhaustively over all vertex pairs, is 145.09 m (between a Lobe-A vertex near (-77, 335) and a Lobe-B vertex near (68, 330)), not 162 m. 162 m equals sqrt(145^2 + 73^2), the diagonal of the bounding box — but no actual polygon vertex sits at the opposite corners needed to realise that diagonal, since the two lobes are offset rather than diagonally opposed. Fixed in the JSON to 145.1 m.

verification.item: Crest depth — 'not established', genuine unresolved gap
verification.evidence: This pass additionally searched for a technical paper ('Borth Multi-Purpose reef for Coastal Protection and Amenity', ResearchGate) that might contain a design crest level; the ResearchGate page returned HTTP 403 (paywalled/blocked, consistent with the prior draft's account) and no other accessible source (R1-R4, S1, or further targeted web searches) gives a crest depth or level for the reef itself. The +5.0 m Chart Datum figure remains correctly attributed only to the unrelated Phase-2 breakwater (see above). Gap confirmed genuine, not an oversight.

verification.item: Gemini comparison table — fairness and accuracy of quoted Gemini values
verification.evidence: Read Gemini's own 02_world_reefs_data/reef_footprints.json (structures[] entry id='borth') and scale_sketch_photo_alignment_audit.md (row 8) directly. Every value attributed to Gemini in our comparison table matches verbatim: distance_offshore_m=200, dimensions 200.0 x 65.0 m, footprint_area_m2=12500.0 (audit table separately gives 9,700 m2 net), crest_depth_m=1.2 with crest_depth_notes 'crest at -1.0m to -1.5m below Mean Low Water Springs (MLWS)', incident_swell_direction_deg '230°-260° (SW to WSW)', shape_typology 'Submerged Rock Berm with Tapered Flanks', and the three sources 'Ceredigion County Council: Borth Coastal Defense Scheme Final Review (2013)', 'BAM Nuttall Project Case Study: Borth Coastal Defense (2012)', 'Coflein National Monuments Record of Wales: Craig y Delyn Reef (2015)' — none of which resolve to any locatable document, matching our card's finding. The audit row marks Borth 'VERIFIED' with 'Discrepancy / Recommendation: None', accurately characterised as such in our file.

verification.item: No number in the derivation table lacks a source or an explicit estimation method
verification.evidence: Every derivation-table row carries either a source_ref with a quote/URL (distance-offshore rows, shape topology) or an explicit 'method: estimated, not derived from any Borth-specific published figure' / 'not established, no estimate ventured' label (bbox/area/max-dimension row; crest-depth row). No orphan numbers found.

name: Bunbury Airwave
year: Installation attempted December 2019 (failed during install); concept development began ~2008-2009 [R2]
type: Inflatable dome-shaped rubber (Hypalon) 'air bladder' artificial surf reef, anchored with sand ballast and filled with air/sand, glued (not welded) seams [R3][R9][R8]
purpose: Create a reliable, rideable wave at a beach with swell but poor bathymetry ('closeouts'); position Bunbury as a surfing destination alternative to nearby Margaret River, attract competitions/tourism, give local surfers a place to progress [R1][R2][R6]
size: Base diameter 12 m (≈40 ft) [R1][R2][R3][R6]; height above seabed given as 2 m in most sources but 1.6 m at its highest point in one dedicated preview article [R1][R2][R3][R6][R9]; sited ~30–45 m offshore in ~1 m of water at low tide [R2][R3][R9]; filled with washed coarse beach sand (140 tonnes) plus air [R9][R8]
cost: City of Bunbury committed A$75,000 as a council sponsorship (approved June 2019) [R1][R2]; total project cost reported as ~US$400,000 including installation by one source and ~US$350,000 by another — sources disagree on the total figure [R3][R10]
cost_usd_approx: ~350,000–400,000 (total project, disputed between sources); A$75,000 (~US$50,000) of that was the confirmed City of Bunbury contribution [R1][R2][R3][R10]
financed_by: City of Bunbury council sponsorship (A$75,000, approved June 2019) [R1][R2]; an August 2018 Kickstarter crowdfunding campaign by Waveco failed to raise enough [R3]; remainder via Waveco/Bottegal investors [R5]
motivation: Bunbury sits near Margaret River, a premier surf destination, but Back Beach had swell without the bathymetry to shape it into rideable waves [R1][R2][R6]. Waveco founder Troy Bottegal had spent roughly a decade developing the inflatable-bladder concept and wanted a real-world test site [R2][R10]; the City of Bunbury under Mayor Gary Brennan saw it as a low-cost way to brand the town as a surfing destination and draw competitions and tourism [R2].
designer: Troy Bottegal, inventor and sole patent holder, director of Waveco Pty Ltd (Dunsborough, WA); conceived the idea after watching a dome-shaped ('oyster') light fitting create ripples in a bathtub [R6][R10]
contractor: Waveco Pty Ltd; installation used three divers and a boat [R9]; fabrication was originally overseas, later moved to a Western Australian manufacturer after the 2019 failure [R5][R8]
status_now: Torn along a glued seam during installation, ~90% complete, mid-December 2019; the partially-inflated bladder was removed from the water within about three days per most sources, though one source (Bottegal, 2020-07-09) separately says it was removed in half a day — the two figures conflict [R1][R5][R8][R18]. A second Airwave prototype install, needing a further ~A$300,000, was being planned for December 2020 [R18]; no source confirms whether it happened or succeeded. A 2022-03-22 article quotes Bottegal saying the Airwave would be 'back in the water in time for Summer, 2024' after relocating fabrication to a WA manufacturer [R8]. A Waveco Instagram post from June 2024 shows an active Bunbury Back Beach surf-cam [R11]. By September 2025, Waveco's own site/Instagram show its active Bunbury proposal has shifted to a 'granite artificial reef' (rock) design at a dedicated project site (bunburyartificialreef.info), framed around coastal-erosion protection rather than surf amenity [R20] — no source confirms the original inflatable Airwave was ever successfully reinstalled; status as of research date is unconfirmed for the inflatable Airwave specifically, and Waveco's current Bunbury-facing project appears to be a different (granite) technology [R8][R11][R18][R20]
hover_text: A 12 m inflatable rubber 'air bladder' surf reef (A$75,000 council funding; total project ~US$350–400,000, disputed) that tore along a glued seam during its December 2019 installation off Bunbury Back Beach, WA, and was pulled from the water within days: it failed, because it was never completed and no independent source documents rideable waves on it [R1][R3][R8][R18]. The developer calls it 'not a failure' and says it 'successfully created peeling waves', but its own page misdates the install to 2018 and no independent report supports the wave claim [R21]; by 2025 its Bunbury proposal is a different (granite/rock) design [R20].
design_as_planned: A 12 m-diameter, dome-shaped inflatable rubber bladder anchored to the seabed with sand ballast, filled with air/sand/water, sited ~30–45 m offshore in ~1 m of water at low tide [R2][R3][R9]. It was meant to 'lift, peak, and hold the swell to create a concave, tapered wall of water that retains its shape as it peels toward the beach' [R19], producing an A-frame peak with left and right breaks where there had previously only been closeouts [R3]. Bottegal modelled the intended wave on Thunderbomb, a wave in Nicaragua [R4]. It was designed to work across roughly 2–8 ft swell, with expected ride length ~40 m / 26 seconds, over an estimated 150 rideable-swell days per year [R2][R3][R9]. A hard-wired webcam and a planned 12-month University of Western Australia scientific study were part of the design [R9]. The reversibility/removability of the inflatable design (not ecological habitat creation) was the explicit environmental/cost pitch — 'if they don't do what you want them to do... they take half a day to move' [R10].
as_built_vs_design: Construction was reported 'halfway complete' in October 2019 against a November 2019 install target [R4]; installation slipped to December 2019, and divers/boat crew got the bladder to ~90% complete (deployed but not fully anchored) when an unexpectedly large, deep offshore swell drove strong undertow through the line-up during the final fill/anchoring phase, tearing a glued seam [R1][R5][R6]. The tear was along the seam, not the rubber itself [R1]; the underlying cause was the choice of Hypalon rubber, which could not be welded and so had to be glued — a joint that could not withstand pump pressure during the final fill [R8]. The bladder was removed within about three days (one conflicting account says half a day) [R1][R5][R8][R18]. The reef therefore was never completed to its designed, fully-anchored, surfable state.
outcome: Installation was not completed: the bladder tore and was pulled from the water, unsurfable in its intended form [R1][R5][R8]. During the brief period it was partially in the water, Bottegal later reported that 'a wave did break on it... peeled nearly all the way to the beach... created a 0.75 metre wave' — the only quantified wave-performance data found, describing a small, uncontrolled result rather than a validated trial [R8]. No formal UWA study results were found; the planned 12-month study appears never to have started [R9]. A second prototype installation was being planned for December 2020 with a further A$300,000 [R18], but no source confirms it happened or succeeded. A 2022 article promised a Summer 2024 relaunch after moving fabrication to WA [R8]; a June 2024 Instagram post shows an active surf-cam [R11]; but by September 2025 Waveco's active Bunbury-facing project had shifted to a different, granite (rock) reef design aimed at coastal-erosion protection [R20]. No source found confirms the inflatable Airwave was ever successfully completed and operating as a surf reef at Bunbury.
why_worked_or_failed: Failure mechanism (installation, Dec 2019): an unexpectedly deep offshore swell during the final anchoring/fill phase generated strong undertow that flexed the bladder, concentrating stress on a glued seam [R1][R5][R6]. The underlying materials cause was the use of Hypalon rubber, which cannot be welded; the glued seams used instead could not withstand pressure reached during the final pump/fill stage [R8]. This was a materials/fabrication-method failure compounded by an installation-timing/weather-window problem, rather than a wave-performance or siting failure — the reef never reached a state where its surf-shaping performance could be properly judged.
unexpected_results: The one recorded moment of the Airwave functioning — before the tear forced its removal — reportedly produced a wave that 'peeled nearly all the way to the beach' and reached about 0.75 m, an unplanned, brief glimpse of the concept working, per Bottegal's later account [R8]. No sources document fishing-pressure effects, ecological colonization, rip-current changes, safety incidents, or litigation connected to this installation — plausible given the structure was never operational for an extended period. Local news noted reputational 'deflation' for Bunbury when the trial failed on a high-profile install day [R1].
could_be_better: From Waveco/the designer's own account: the identified fix was materials and fabrication method — move away from glued Hypalon seams (relocating manufacture to a WA-based manufacturer) and secure fresh investment before re-attempting installation [R8]. Bottegal framed the setback as a timing/weather issue (an unplanned deep swell during the vulnerable, partially-anchored install phase) rather than a fundamental design flaw, maintaining '100 percent' confidence the concept would work [R6]. Detailed surfer/commentator critique was not found in the sources successfully retrieved for this research [see dossier for blocked forum sources].
relevance_to_israel: Bunbury sits on a microtidal WA coast (tidal range roughly ~1 m or less) [R13], broadly comparable in scale to the Mediterranean's small tidal range at Haifa — not itself a factor implicated in the Bunbury failure, but relevant to sizing an Israeli pilot in a similarly low-tide setting. Wave climate differs in kind: Bunbury/SW WA faces Southern Ocean groundswell (~150 rideable-swell days/year) [R9], far more energetic than the Eastern Mediterranean's short-period, wind-driven seas off Haifa. What transfers: (1) the low-cost, rapidly-removable inflatable concept is attractive for a wave-poor, low-tidal-range coast like Israel's, avoiding large capital commitment before wave performance is proven; (2) the documented failure mode — glued (not welded) seam material failing under dynamic swell/undertow loading during the vulnerable partially-anchored installation phase — is a fabrication/installation-window risk any Israeli inflatable-reef pilot would need to solve first, independent of local wave/tide conditions; (3) because Israel's swell energy is much lower than SW Australia's, a device sized for Bunbury's 2–8 ft face range may be oversized for Haifa's smaller everyday waves and would need dedicated re-sizing/modelling, not found in any source reviewed here.

developer_account.who: Waveco Pty Ltd (the developer; Troy Bottegal, CEO & founder)
developer_account.page: All About Us - The Story of Behind the Airwave (About page), section 'The Path to Discovery' > 'The Bunbury Deployment'
developer_account.page_dates: WordPress REST API (page id 53654): created 2019-08-11, last modified 2025-12-22; the Bunbury passage itself carries no date
developer_account.quote: In 2018, we deployed a 150-tonne sand-slurry bladder at Bunbury’s Back Beach. While it successfully created peeling waves, a final-day overpressure event led to a seam split. It wasn't a failure—it was the catalyst for our next breakthrough.
developer_account.quote_check: verified verbatim in the raw page HTML on 2026-10-05 (the page uses a curly apostrophe in Bunbury’s and an em dash)
developer_account.independence: self-published by the developer; promotional; not independent
developer_account.adjacent_text: 'Post-2018, we pivoted. We designed and patented a modular concrete version of the Airwave... Simultaneously, we developed a conventional Granite ASR design.' (same page) [R21]

checks.independent_record: Installation was attempted in December 2019: it began the week of 9 Dec, a diver spotted the seam tear on the afternoon of Fri 13 Dec, and it was reported on Mon 16 Dec [R1][R5][R6][R7][R15]. Before that it had not been deployed: ABC (2019-06-13) said it was set to be installed in November [R2]; Tracks (2019-08-12) described a trial planned for mid-November and a crowd-funding campaign 'last year' [R23]; Raised Water Research (2019-10-14) said construction was half-way [R4]; Tracks (2019-11-15) said the live trial was 'some time in the next couple of months' [R9]; RWR's spot page says it was installed in December 2019 [R3]; ABC listen (2022-10-07) says 'In 2019 ... attempted to install' [R24]. The only 2018 events found are Waveco's failed Aug 2018 Kickstarter [R3] and a 'may be installed' preview [R19]. One outlier: the 2022 Bunbury Mail intro says 'four years since' and captions a supplied photo 'The original Bunbury Airwave in 2018' [R8]; that conflicts with every dated 2019 report above.

Sand-slurry fill is corroborated: Tracks 2019 ('washed, coarse beach sand... for that slurry') [R9]; Bottegal in the Bunbury Mail ('irrigate the sandslurry') [R8]; RWR ('partially filling it with sand', the rest water and air) [R3]; a local observer on Swellnet saw a slurry pump and hoses on the beach on 7 Dec 2019 [R15]. ABC and SurferToday call it 'filled with air' [R1][R7]; Tracks 2019 says 'a mixture of sand and air' [R9]; the card's 'air bladder anchored with sand ballast' fits all of these. The mass has no independent source: 140 tonnes in Tracks 2021 and the Bunbury Mail 2022, both reporting Bottegal [R22][R8]; '150T' in a forum summary of his Feb 2020 conference talk [R15]. So 140-150 t, developer-sourced only; the 7% gap is inside the developer's own statements.
checks.assessment: material and bladder type consistent; mass is developer-only, 140-150 t (card keeps 140 t)

checks.claim: 'While it successfully created peeling waves' (wave performance)
checks.independent_record: No independent report, photograph or video of surfable waves on the reef was found. ABC (2019-12-16) reports only the tear; it paraphrases a tourist as 'looking forward to riding whatever wave the Airwave produced' and beach-goers were told to keep away [R1]. RWR, SurferToday and The Inertia report no wave [R5][R6][R7]. The ABC video 11804314 shows the bladder on the seabed with a diver and no wave (card video notes). Tracks 2021 says the plan to webcast 'perfectly peeling waves' 'didn't quite play that way' [R22]; the webcam was not live for the install [R15]. The wave claim comes from the developer alone: Bottegal told the Bunbury Mail in 2022 that 'a wave did break' just before the tear, a 'lone wave' that 'peeled for about thirty metres' and 'created a 0.75 metre wave' seen by onlookers [R8] (his recollection 27 months later; no footage or named witness cited). Second-hand only: a Swellnet user quoting Waveco's Dec 2019 Instagram says the redesign reflects 'small wave action' observed during install, and a forum summary of his Feb 2020 talk lists 'Small Wave Peak' among positives [R15].
checks.assessment: not independently supported: at most ONE small wave (about 0.75 m, about 30 m long) reported by the developer himself, while the bladder was about 90% installed and not anchored; no ride by anyone, no footage found

checks.claim: 'a final-day overpressure event led to a seam split' (failure mechanism)
checks.independent_record: Seam split: confirmed; the tear was along a glued seam, not through the rubber [R1][R5][R8]. 'Final-day': the tear was spotted on about the fifth day of the install week (Fri 13 Dec) when, per ABC reporting Bottegal, it was '90 per cent complete' but 'not completely anchored' [R1][R7]; a local observer saw it 'partially filled' that afternoon [R15]. It never operated as a finished reef. 'Overpressure': this is the developer's own later explanation, and it changes. Dec 2019: an unexpected deep swell and undertow flexed the airbag against the seam [R1][R5][R7]. Oct 2021 (Tracks): sand pumped too heavily into one quadrant put too much pressure on one section of the skin, and the new valves avoid 'the same over pressurization problem' [R22]. Mar 2022 (Bunbury Mail): glued overlapped Hypalon seams plus 'full pump pressure applied to a confined space in the final fill phase' caused a tear in the back quadrant [R8]. No independent engineering report exists.
checks.assessment: partly supported: seam split true; 'overpressure' matches his 2021-22 accounts but not his 2019 one; 'final-day' makes an unfinished install sound like a completed deployment

checks.independent_record: Bottegal told the Bunbury Mail in Mar 2022 the prototype installation 'certainly was not a failure' [R8]. But Tracks (2021-10-08) writes that he 'readily admits that the first trial of his Airwave was a failure' (Tracks' paraphrase, not a direct quote) [R22]. Facts on record: the bladder tore during installation and was removed within days (reports range from about 5 hours to 3 days) [R8][R18][R15]; no completed trial and the planned 12-month UWA study never started [R9]; a second prototype (planned Dec 2020, about A$300,000 more needed) is not confirmed built [R18][R8]; the redesign has only been tank-tested [R22]; by 2025 Waveco's Bunbury proposal is a granite reef [R20]; and its own page says it 'pivoted' away from the rubber Airwave after 2018 [R21].
checks.assessment: a judgement, not a checkable fact; the record supports 'learning prototype' as the developer's framing but not 'success'

developer_account.overall: Of the four factual claims, one is contradicted (2018), one is consistent but developer-only on mass (150 t vs 140 t elsewhere), one is partly supported (seam split yes; 'final-day overpressure' reframes an unfinished install), and one has no independent support (successfully created peeling waves). The card verdict stays 'failed'.

verdict_reason: The structure tore along a glued seam during installation (spotted Fri 13 Dec 2019, about 90% installed and not fully anchored), was removed within days, and never operated as a completed reef [R1][R5][R8][R18]. No independent report, photo or video documents rideable waves on it; the only wave claim is the developer's own later account of one lone 0.75 m wave seen during installation [R8][R21]. The developer's page says the trial 'wasn't a failure' [R21], but it misdates the deployment to 2018 (it was December 2019), Tracks reported in 2021 that Bottegal 'readily admits' the first trial was a failure [R22], no second install is confirmed [R18][R8], and by 2025 Waveco's Bunbury proposal is a different (granite) design [R20]. Verdict kept as 'failed' after checking the developer's account (2026-10-05).

hover.outcome: A 12 m inflatable rubber 'air bladder' surf reef (A$75,000 council funding; total project ~US$350–400,000, disputed) that tore along a glued seam during its December 2019 installation off Bunbury Back Beach, WA, and was pulled from the water within days: it failed, because it was never completed and no independent source documents rideable waves on it [R1][R3][R8][R18]. sections.title: Quick facts
sections.html_or_text:
NameBunbury Airwave
PlaceBunbury Back Beach, Western Australia
CountryAustralia
YearInstallation attempted December 2019 (failed during install); concept development began ~2008-2009 [R2]
TypeInflatable dome-shaped rubber (Hypalon) 'air bladder' artificial surf reef, anchored with sand ballast and filled with air/sand, glued (not welded) seams [R3][R9][R8]
PurposeCreate a reliable, rideable wave at a beach with swell but poor bathymetry ('closeouts'); position Bunbury as a surfing destination alternative to nearby Margaret River, attract competitions/tourism, give local surfers a place to progress [R1][R2][R6]
SizeBase diameter 12 m (≈40 ft) [R1][R2][R3][R6]; height above seabed given as 2 m in most sources but 1.6 m at its highest point in one dedicated preview article [R1][R2][R3][R6][R9]; sited ~30–45 m offshore in ~1 m of water at low tide [R2][R3][R9]; filled with washed coarse beach sand (140 tonnes) plus air [R9][R8]
CostCity of Bunbury committed A$75,000 as a council sponsorship (approved June 2019) [R1][R2]; total project cost reported as ~US$400,000 including installation by one source and ~US$350,000 by another — sources disagree on the total figure [R3][R10]
Cost (approx. USD)~350,000–400,000 (total project, disputed between sources); A$75,000 (~US$50,000) of that was the confirmed City of Bunbury contribution [R1][R2][R3][R10]
Financed byCity of Bunbury council sponsorship (A$75,000, approved June 2019) [R1][R2]; an August 2018 Kickstarter crowdfunding campaign by Waveco failed to raise enough [R3]; remainder via Waveco/Bottegal investors [R5]
DesignerTroy Bottegal, inventor and sole patent holder, director of Waveco Pty Ltd (Dunsborough, WA); conceived the idea after watching a dome-shaped ('oyster') light fitting create ripples in a bathtub [R6][R10]
ContractorWaveco Pty Ltd; installation used three divers and a boat [R9]; fabrication was originally overseas, later moved to a Western Australian manufacturer after the 2019 failure [R5][R8]
Status nowTorn along a glued seam during installation, ~90% complete, mid-December 2019; the partially-inflated bladder was removed from the water within about three days per most sources, though one source (Bottegal, 2020-07-09) separately says it was removed in half a day — the two figures conflict [R1][R5][R8][R18]. A second Airwave prototype install, needing a further ~A$300,000, was being planned for December 2020 [R18]; no source confirms whether it happened or succeeded. A 2022-03-22 article quotes Bottegal saying the Airwave would be 'back in the water in time for Summer, 2024' after relocating fabrication to a WA manufacturer [R8]. A Waveco Instagram post from June 2024 shows an active Bunbury Back Beach surf-cam [R11]. By September 2025, Waveco's own site/Instagram show its active Bunbury proposal has shifted to a 'granite artificial reef' (rock) design at a dedicated project site (bunburyartificialreef.info), framed around coastal-erosion protection rather than surf amenity [R20] — no source confirms the original inflatable Airwave was ever successfully reinstalled; status as of research date is unconfirmed for the inflatable Airwave specifically, and Waveco's current Bunbury-facing project appears to be a different (granite) technology [R8][R11][R18][R20]

sections.title: Motivation & who pushed for it
sections.html_or_text: Bunbury sits near Margaret River, a premier surf destination, but Back Beach had swell without the bathymetry to shape it into rideable waves [R1][R2][R6]. Waveco founder Troy Bottegal had spent roughly a decade developing the inflatable-bladder concept and wanted a real-world test site [R2][R10]; the City of Bunbury under Mayor Gary Brennan saw it as a low-cost way to brand the town as a surfing destination and draw competitions and tourism [R2].

sections.title: Design as planned
sections.html_or_text: A 12 m-diameter, dome-shaped inflatable rubber bladder anchored to the seabed with sand ballast, filled with air/sand/water, sited ~30–45 m offshore in ~1 m of water at low tide [R2][R3][R9]. It was meant to 'lift, peak, and hold the swell to create a concave, tapered wall of water that retains its shape as it peels toward the beach' [R19], producing an A-frame peak with left and right breaks where there had previously only been closeouts [R3]. Bottegal modelled the intended wave on Thunderbomb, a wave in Nicaragua [R4]. It was designed to work across roughly 2–8 ft swell, with expected ride length ~40 m / 26 seconds, over an estimated 150 rideable-swell days per year [R2][R3][R9]. A hard-wired webcam and a planned 12-month University of Western Australia scientific study were part of the design [R9]. The reversibility/removability of the inflatable design (not ecological habitat creation) was the explicit environmental/cost pitch — 'if they don't do what you want them to do... they take half a day to move' [R10].

sections.title: As built vs design
sections.html_or_text: Construction was reported 'halfway complete' in October 2019 against a November 2019 install target [R4]; installation slipped to December 2019, and divers/boat crew got the bladder to ~90% complete (deployed but not fully anchored) when an unexpectedly large, deep offshore swell drove strong undertow through the line-up during the final fill/anchoring phase, tearing a glued seam [R1][R5][R6]. The tear was along the seam, not the rubber itself [R1]; the underlying cause was the choice of Hypalon rubber, which could not be welded and so had to be glued — a joint that could not withstand pump pressure during the final fill [R8]. The bladder was removed within about three days (one conflicting account says half a day) [R1][R5][R8][R18]. The reef therefore was never completed to its designed, fully-anchored, surfable state.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.html_or_text: Installation was not completed: the bladder tore and was pulled from the water, unsurfable in its intended form [R1][R5][R8]. During the brief period it was partially in the water, Bottegal later reported that 'a wave did break on it... peeled nearly all the way to the beach... created a 0.75 metre wave' — the only quantified wave-performance data found, describing a small, uncontrolled result rather than a validated trial [R8]. No formal UWA study results were found; the planned 12-month study appears never to have started [R9]. A second prototype installation was being planned for December 2020 with a further A$300,000 [R18], but no source confirms it happened or succeeded. A 2022 article promised a Summer 2024 relaunch after moving fabrication to WA [R8]; a June 2024 Instagram post shows an active surf-cam [R11]; but by September 2025 Waveco's active Bunbury-facing project had shifted to a different, granite (rock) reef design aimed at coastal-erosion protection [R20]. No source found confirms the inflatable Airwave was ever successfully completed and operating as a surf reef at Bunbury.

sections.title: Why it worked / failed
sections.html_or_text: Failure mechanism (installation, Dec 2019): an unexpectedly deep offshore swell during the final anchoring/fill phase generated strong undertow that flexed the bladder, concentrating stress on a glued seam [R1][R5][R6]. The underlying materials cause was the use of Hypalon rubber, which cannot be welded; the glued seams used instead could not withstand pressure reached during the final pump/fill stage [R8]. This was a materials/fabrication-method failure compounded by an installation-timing/weather-window problem, rather than a wave-performance or siting failure — the reef never reached a state where its surf-shaping performance could be properly judged.

sections.title: Unexpected results
sections.html_or_text: The one recorded moment of the Airwave functioning — before the tear forced its removal — reportedly produced a wave that 'peeled nearly all the way to the beach' and reached about 0.75 m, an unplanned, brief glimpse of the concept working, per Bottegal's later account [R8]. No sources document fishing-pressure effects, ecological colonization, rip-current changes, safety incidents, or litigation connected to this installation — plausible given the structure was never operational for an extended period. Local news noted reputational 'deflation' for Bunbury when the trial failed on a high-profile install day [R1].

sections.title: What could have been done better
sections.html_or_text: From Waveco/the designer's own account: the identified fix was materials and fabrication method — move away from glued Hypalon seams (relocating manufacture to a WA-based manufacturer) and secure fresh investment before re-attempting installation [R8]. Bottegal framed the setback as a timing/weather issue (an unplanned deep swell during the vulnerable, partially-anchored install phase) rather than a fundamental design flaw, maintaining '100 percent' confidence the concept would work [R6]. Detailed surfer/commentator critique was not found in the sources successfully retrieved for this research [see dossier for blocked forum sources].

sections.title: Relevance to Israel / Haifa
sections.html_or_text: Bunbury sits on a microtidal WA coast (tidal range roughly ~1 m or less) [R13], broadly comparable in scale to the Mediterranean's small tidal range at Haifa — not itself a factor implicated in the Bunbury failure, but relevant to sizing an Israeli pilot in a similarly low-tide setting. Wave climate differs in kind: Bunbury/SW WA faces Southern Ocean groundswell (~150 rideable-swell days/year) [R9], far more energetic than the Eastern Mediterranean's short-period, wind-driven seas off Haifa. What transfers: (1) the low-cost, rapidly-removable inflatable concept is attractive for a wave-poor, low-tidal-range coast like Israel's, avoiding large capital commitment before wave performance is proven; (2) the documented failure mode — glued (not welded) seam material failing under dynamic swell/undertow loading during the vulnerable partially-anchored installation phase — is a fabrication/installation-window risk any Israeli inflatable-reef pilot would need to solve first, independent of local wave/tide conditions; (3) because Israel's swell energy is much lower than SW Australia's, a device sized for Bunbury's 2–8 ft face range may be oversized for Haifa's smaller everyday waves and would need dedicated re-sizing/modelling, not found in any source reviewed here.

footprint.name: Bunbury Airwave
footprint.shape_type_notes: Not a V/delta/chevron/linear/crescent/L shape -- a single circular inflatable dome ('mound') with no arms or directional geometry.
footprint.coords: metres; origin = shoreline point nearest the reef centroid; x = alongshore (positive toward north, approximate -- Back Beach's coastline trends roughly N-S; no source gives an exact shoreline azimuth); y = offshore (positive seaward); shoreline approximated as the line y=0. Orientation is moot for a circle.

crest_depth_m.datum: below the water surface at low tide (LAT, approximate)

footprint.crest_depth_alt_note: Structure height above seabed is reported as 2 m in most contemporaneous sources (R1,R2,R3,R6) but as 1.6 m in one 2022 retrospective (R8); the 1.0 m crest-depth figure is a directly stated quote independent of which height figure is used.

disagree.why_ours: R3 (raisedwaterresearch.com, re-fetched 2026-09-25) states directly: 'at low tide, the shallow point is about 1m under the surface of the water.' No source supports 1.8 m. Traced Gemini's own working: its `reef_footprints.json` gives `coastal_context.ambient_seabed_depth_m = 3.8` and `crest_depth_m = 1.8` with the note 'Dome inflated to 2m height; crest submerged 1.8m' -- i.e. Gemini computed 3.8 - 2.0 = 1.8, but the 3.8 m 'ambient seabed depth' input is not sourced anywhere in Gemini's own files or ours; it appears to be an assumed/invented figure, not a cited one. Gemini's own two cited sources for this reef (a 2019 'project brief' and a 2020 Surfer Magazine review) do not appear anywhere in our reference list or in the pages we located, so they could not be independently checked.

R3 states a 30-45 m design-target range, not a single figure; R2 was re-checked 2026-09-25 and does not mention any offshore distance at all (an earlier draft of this file incorrectly cited R2 alongside R3 for this number). Gemini's 38 m happens to fall inside R3's range but is not itself sourced anywhere we could find (Gemini's own polygon in `reef_footprints.json` is simply centered at y=38, matching its stated value with no separate citation); we report the documented range's midpoint (37.5 m) instead of an unsourced point estimate.

open_issues: The reef was never completed (installation reached ~90% before a glued seam tore and the bladder was removed within days); every figure here is an as-designed value, not an as-installed/as-surveyed one.

Height above seabed is inconsistently reported: 2 m (R1,R2,R3 contemporaneous) vs 1.6 m (1 later retrospective, R8); R6's imperial 'about 7-feet' is an approximate corroboration only, not an independent precise measurement.

R3 and R9 in the verified card cite the same raisedwaterresearch.com URL under two different reference ids -- likely a minor duplication in the card, noted here but not corrected (out of scope for this footprint-only task).
No exact installed lat/lon or surveyed offshore distance exists; 30-45 m is the pre-installation design target, sourced to R3 only (R2 does not mention offshore distance).
Volume (117.3 m3) is our own geometric estimate, not a published figure; offered only as a sand-tonnage plausibility check.

Gemini's two cited sources for this reef ('Bottegal 2019 Project Brief', 'Surfer Magazine Trial Review 2020') could not be located or verified; treat Gemini's crest-depth and offshore-distance figures as unverified. Traced the specific mechanism of Gemini's 1.8 m crest-depth figure: it equals Gemini's own (unsourced) 3.8 m 'ambient seabed depth' input minus the 2.0 m height -- an internally consistent but externally unsupported calculation.

Attribution note: the earlier draft of this file's claim that Bunbury 'matches the flag already in Gemini's own suspicious notes' was imprecisely worded -- that 'suspicious' annotation ('one of the better-matched reefs') actually lives in OUR project's own intermediate extract file (07_scale/00_gemini_footprints_extract.json), not inside the Gemini folder itself. Gemini's own self-audit file (scale_sketch_photo_alignment_audit.md, row 11) independently marks Bunbury 'VERIFIED' with no discrepancy flagged. Both statements are substantively accurate; only the attribution of which file the note lives in has been corrected here.

Three citation errors found and fixed during 2026-09-25 adversarial verification: (1) R2 (ABC 2019-06-13) was wrongly cited alongside R3 for the 12 m diameter and the 30-45 m offshore distance -- re-fetched twice with targeted prompts and confirmed R2 states ONLY the 2 m height, nothing else; (2) R1's diameter quote was wrongly given the '(40 feet)' parenthetical that actually belongs to R3 -- R1's real text is metric-only ('two-metre-high, 12-metre-wide'); (3) R6 (The Inertia) was quoted as giving a precise '6.5 feet' height when the actual (Wayback-Machine-verified, since the live URL 403s) text says 'about 7-feet high' -- a looser rounding. None of these fixes changed any headline number (12 m, 2 m, 1.0 m, 30-45 m all still hold on corrected citations), but the reference attributions have been corrected throughout. A fourth fix: the fill-material quote 'washed, coarse beach sand' was not actually found on the R3 page and has been replaced with the verbatim R3 quote (sand + water + air).

name: Palm Beach Reef
year: Concept design 2013; detailed design 2013–2014; construction Apr/May–Oct 2019; finalised and certified Sept 2019 [R1][R3][R5]
type: Submerged rock (quarried boulder) reef, 4–8 t boulders on individual sourcing (up to 8 t per most sources), NOT geotextile sand containers — a deliberate contrast with Narrowneck [R2][R4][R7][R16]
purpose: Multipurpose, in order of priority: (1) coastal-erosion protection for a narrow, storm-vulnerable beach; (2) surf amenity (a right-hand wave), explicit in the design brief from the start, unlike Narrowneck; (3) marine habitat, unquantified [R3][R8][R12][R13][R16]
size: 160 m long × 80 m wide "core" per most sources, vs Royal HaskoningDHV's own page giving 144 m wide (unresolved); ~270 m offshore per most sources vs Royal HaskoningDHV's 330 m (unresolved); crest 1.5 m below MSL at highest point, 60 cm at lowest astronomical tide; ~25,000 m³ of rock (~60,000 tonnes of boulders) [R2][R4][R5][R6][R7][R9][R13][R15]
cost: AU$18.2 million per most sources, vs AU$18.3 million per ICM's technical comparison (both cited, unresolved) [R2][R4][R7][R8][R9][R12][R13][R16]
cost_usd_approx: ~US$12.5 million (Raised Water Research's own stated conversion, ~2019 rate) [R2]
financed_by: City of Gold Coast (local council), under its Ocean Beaches Strategy (adopted 2015); no state/federal co-funding found in any source checked [R8][R12]
motivation: Palm Beach is the Gold Coast's most erosion-prone beach, with the coastal road running close to the shore [R11][R16]. An earlier 2004 reef proposal near 21st Avenue was defeated by a community 'no reef' campaign and never built [R10][R16]. The successful 2013–2019 project is Phase 2 of the Palm Beach Shoreline Project, following a 2017 sand-nourishment Phase 1, and was pushed forward by a run of severe storms (2013 storm damage, a 2014 Climate Council sea-level-rise report, the 2015 Ocean Beaches Strategy, and Cyclone Oma battering Palm Beach in early 2019) [R5][R8][R12]. Mayor Tom Tate was the principal political champion throughout [R8][R12][R16].
designer: Disputed/multi-party, unreconciled across sources: DHI Australia (lead, principal engineer Simon Mortensen, won the Concept Design Study by open tender in 2013) [R3][R18]; Royal HaskoningDHV (design reference report, hydrodynamic modelling, environmental assessment, construction-phase QA, final engineering certification) [R5]; Bluecoast Consulting Engineers (core consultancy team, construction QA, as-built certification) [R1]. No source lays out how these three roles fit together.
contractor: HC2 joint venture — Hall Contracting Pty Ltd (AU) and Heron Construction Company (NZ); built using a backhoe dredge for precise rock placement, rock sourced from South-East Queensland quarries and barged from the Port of Brisbane [R4][R16]
status_now: Operational as of the most recent source checked (ICM article, updated Feb 2025, still describes it in the present tense); no removal, decommissioning, or major structural-damage report found for this reef specifically in any source fetched, including a targeted (unsuccessful) search for Cyclone Alfred (March 2025) impact [R13]
hover_text: A 160×80 m submerged boulder reef built 2019 for AU$18.2M by the City of Gold Coast to fight erosion at Palm Beach, with a right-hand surf wave designed in from the start; it retained roughly 550,000 m³ of sand in its first two years and delivers a modest, workable (not world-class) wave, though a narrow shallow-to-deep tidal window draws local complaints [R2][R9][R15].
design_as_planned: DHI Australia (lead designer Simon Mortensen) combined empirical surf knowledge — Mortensen personally surfing Palm Beach and reference breaks — with numerical modelling (DHI's MIKE 21 SM shoreline module using 30 years of wave/current data, a 3D VOF model in OpenFOAM, in-house OptiSurf surf-simulation software) and physical wave-tank testing for rock sizing [R3][R18]. The reef was deliberately sited 'in the lee of a natural reef' offshore to exploit an existing natural wave-focusing zone, targeting a right-hand wave 'suitable for average [to advanced] surfers with accessible takeoffs and extended wall length,' with a secondary short, more intense left on larger swells [R3][R13][R15][R17]. Rock (not geotextile, as used at Narrowneck) was chosen for its 100+-year coastal-engineering track record, precise shape control, expected habitat value, and to avoid geotextile bags' documented tearing/removal-cost problems [R3]. Design freeboard was set at a minimum 1.5 m below mean sea level, 60 cm at lowest astronomical tide, based on six years of local swell data [R2][R15]. Mortensen himself framed it as 'always a compromise... especially since the main focus was coastal protection' [R3].
as_built_vs_design: The built reef matches the planned footprint and dominant right-hand wave, but execution surfaced issues not evident in the design promise. Swellnet's July 2019 first-look (at ~50% completion) reported the reef 'alarmingly shallow, with one rock even breaking the surface,' and a forum commenter described it going 'from too shallow to too deep really quickly' across the tide cycle — a narrower-than-hoped surfable tidal window [R15]. The timeline held essentially to plan rather than beating it: Swellnet's own 23 Aug 2019 update reported the reef only ~50% complete and 'still on track for an October finish,' and the project was finalised/certified in September 2019 — consistent with, not ahead of, the original target [R1][R5][R17]. Cost and dimension figures vary slightly by source (AU$18.2M vs AU$18.3M; 80 m vs 144 m width; 270 m vs 330 m offshore), plausibly rounding/measurement-basis differences between the council's headline figures and individual consultants' own project pages, though no source explains the gap [R2][R4][R5][R7][R9][R13].
outcome: Surfing: on its first meaningful swell test (July 2019, reef ~50% built) it broke 4–5 ft waves with rides up to ~30 m; at completion it produced a consistent right with a short, thick left on bigger swells, handling at least double-overhead SE swells [R6][R15][R17]. The Inertia groups Palm Beach with Cable Station and Burkitts Reef among Australian stone reefs delivering 'modest, measurable improvements in the quality of waves' without becoming world-class breaks [R18]. Coastal protection: ABC News reported approximately 550,000 m³ of sand retained over the reef's first two years of operation — the clearest quantitative protection outcome found [R9]. Coastal engineer Evan Watterson argued such structures compare favourably to plain beach nourishment 'over a 30-year period' [R9]. Ecology: marine-habitat creation is claimed by both Bluecoast and Raised Water Research but with zero ecological survey data found in any source fetched [R1][R2]. Longevity: no storm-damage, structural-failure, or removal reports were found for this reef specifically [R13][R17]. Awards: IPWEAQ 2019 Excellence Award for Innovation and a 2020 Excellence Award for Coastal Engineering [R5].
why_worked_or_failed: Sources repeatedly credit the rock-over-geotextile material choice as the key differentiator from failed reef projects elsewhere — rock's long engineering track record, precise shape-control, and habitat value versus geotextile bags' history of tearing and expensive removal [R3][R13][R18]. Siting the reef behind an existing natural reef to pre-focus wave energy is credited with helping it punch above its size for surf quality [R3][R13]. The tuned crest depth/freeboard (1.5 m below MSL / 60 cm at LAT) balanced rideable wave height against safety, but the resulting narrow, fast-changing tidal window drew user complaints [R15]. Lead designer Simon Mortensen's own stated regret was about process, not physical design: 'we would have been more realistic in our budgeting on how long it would actually take to work on this reef. The City got a good deal' [R3]. ICM's own comparison attributes Palm Beach's stronger wave outcome (versus Narrowneck) to its surf-first design brief at a materially higher unit cost (~AU$700/m³ vs ~AU$30/m³ at Narrowneck): 'when the objective is surfing, the design can be more focused and effective' [R13].
unexpected_results: Rock breaking the surface at low tide, flagged by Swellnet as a possible safety/design concern locals questioned [R15]. A single joking Swellnet forum comment about a shark sighting ('Predatory Pirate Shark circles Palmy Reef') was not corroborated by any other source and is not treated here as a real trend [R17]. Crowding complaints: because the reef breaks predominantly as a right-hander in a region already dominated by right-hand points, some surfers criticised it for adding to an existing imbalance and concentrating crowds [R17]. The pre-existing 2004 'no reef' community backlash that killed an earlier reef proposal at the same beach is itself a notable data point about local social license, given the later, larger 2019 project proceeded with comparatively less reported opposition [R10][R16].
could_be_better: Simon Mortensen's own retrospective criticism concerns process, not the built structure: the consultancy underestimated how long the multi-year design phase would take [R3]. Outside civil engineer Shane Abel (not on the design team) argued before construction that 'whatever they build in the ocean should be removable and 8 tonnes of rock isn't,' proposing a removable design instead of the fixed boulder approach [R16]. The Palm Beach Board Riders Club (Mike Gifford) felt stakeholder consultation with surfers was inadequate ahead of construction [R16]. Post-construction surfer commentary focused on the tide-sensitivity problem — the narrow window between 'too shallow' and 'too deep' — suggesting a design tweak to crest depth or profile might have produced a more forgiving tidal window [R15]. Some surfers also felt the community would have been better served by a different wave shape (e.g. a left or a peak) given the Gold Coast's existing abundance of right-hand points [R17].
relevance_to_israel: Tide range: Palm Beach is microtidal (~1.5 m illustrative weekly range per a live tide check), broadly consistent with the reef's own 1.5 m/60 cm freeboard spec; Haifa's Mediterranean coast is essentially micro-tidal to negligible-tidal, which means Palm Beach's core challenge — keeping a fixed-crest structure inside a workable 'not too shallow, not too deep' window across the tide cycle — would be more forgiving at Haifa, since Haifa's tide swing is smaller [R14][R15]. Wave climate: Palm Beach's design leaned on six years of dominant east-to-southeast Pacific ocean swell arriving at a site with an existing natural offshore reef to pre-focus it; Haifa's Mediterranean wave climate is smaller and less consistent, meaning a Haifa reef would likely need to actively increase wave height rather than merely reshape already-large incoming swell [R3][R15]. What transfers: (1) the rock-over-geotextile durability and shape-control lesson is directly transferable regardless of wave climate; (2) siting behind/near an existing natural feature to pre-focus energy is a transferable design principle, though Haifa may lack an equivalent natural offshore reef; (3) the tide-window lesson is less of a constraint for Haifa given its smaller tidal range, giving more freedom in crest-depth choice; (4) the cost lesson — Palm Beach's much higher per-m³ cost than Narrowneck reflects the premium of prioritising surf quality in the design brief — is directly relevant to budgeting a Haifa reef if surf quality is a primary goal [R13].
