sections.title: Quick facts
sections.html_or_text:
NamePalm Beach Reef
PlacePalm Beach, Gold Coast, Queensland
CountryAustralia
YearConcept design 2013; detailed design 2013–2014; construction Apr/May–Oct 2019; finalised and certified Sept 2019 [R1][R3][R5]
TypeSubmerged rock (quarried boulder) reef, 4–8 t boulders on individual sourcing (up to 8 t per most sources), NOT geotextile sand containers — a deliberate contrast with Narrowneck [R2][R4][R7][R16]
PurposeMultipurpose, in order of priority: (1) coastal-erosion protection for a narrow, storm-vulnerable beach; (2) surf amenity (a right-hand wave), explicit in the design brief from the start, unlike Narrowneck; (3) marine habitat, unquantified [R3][R8][R12][R13][R16]
Size160 m long × 80 m wide "core" per most sources, vs Royal HaskoningDHV's own page giving 144 m wide (unresolved); ~270 m offshore per most sources vs Royal HaskoningDHV's 330 m (unresolved); crest 1.5 m below MSL at highest point, 60 cm at lowest astronomical tide; ~25,000 m³ of rock (~60,000 tonnes of boulders) [R2][R4][R5][R6][R7][R9][R13][R15]
CostAU$18.2 million per most sources, vs AU$18.3 million per ICM's technical comparison (both cited, unresolved) [R2][R4][R7][R8][R9][R12][R13][R16]
Cost (approx. USD)~US$12.5 million (Raised Water Research's own stated conversion, ~2019 rate) [R2]
Financed byCity of Gold Coast (local council), under its Ocean Beaches Strategy (adopted 2015); no state/federal co-funding found in any source checked [R8][R12]
DesignerDisputed/multi-party, unreconciled across sources: DHI Australia (lead, principal engineer Simon Mortensen, won the Concept Design Study by open tender in 2013) [R3][R18]; Royal HaskoningDHV (design reference report, hydrodynamic modelling, environmental assessment, construction-phase QA, final engineering certification) [R5]; Bluecoast Consulting Engineers (core consultancy team, construction QA, as-built certification) [R1]. No source lays out how these three roles fit together.
ContractorHC2 joint venture — Hall Contracting Pty Ltd (AU) and Heron Construction Company (NZ); built using a backhoe dredge for precise rock placement, rock sourced from South-East Queensland quarries and barged from the Port of Brisbane [R4][R16]
Status nowOperational as of the most recent source checked (ICM article, updated Feb 2025, still describes it in the present tense); no removal, decommissioning, or major structural-damage report found for this reef specifically in any source fetched, including a targeted (unsuccessful) search for Cyclone Alfred (March 2025) impact [R13]
Verdictpartly worked

sections.title: Motivation & who pushed for it
sections.html_or_text: Palm Beach is the Gold Coast's most erosion-prone beach, with the coastal road running close to the shore [R11][R16]. An earlier 2004 reef proposal near 21st Avenue was defeated by a community 'no reef' campaign and never built [R10][R16]. The successful 2013–2019 project is Phase 2 of the Palm Beach Shoreline Project, following a 2017 sand-nourishment Phase 1, and was pushed forward by a run of severe storms (2013 storm damage, a 2014 Climate Council sea-level-rise report, the 2015 Ocean Beaches Strategy, and Cyclone Oma battering Palm Beach in early 2019) [R5][R8][R12]. Mayor Tom Tate was the principal political champion throughout [R8][R12][R16].

sections.title: Design as planned
sections.html_or_text: DHI Australia (lead designer Simon Mortensen) combined empirical surf knowledge — Mortensen personally surfing Palm Beach and reference breaks — with numerical modelling (DHI's MIKE 21 SM shoreline module using 30 years of wave/current data, a 3D VOF model in OpenFOAM, in-house OptiSurf surf-simulation software) and physical wave-tank testing for rock sizing [R3][R18]. The reef was deliberately sited 'in the lee of a natural reef' offshore to exploit an existing natural wave-focusing zone, targeting a right-hand wave 'suitable for average [to advanced] surfers with accessible takeoffs and extended wall length,' with a secondary short, more intense left on larger swells [R3][R13][R15][R17]. Rock (not geotextile, as used at Narrowneck) was chosen for its 100+-year coastal-engineering track record, precise shape control, expected habitat value, and to avoid geotextile bags' documented tearing/removal-cost problems [R3]. Design freeboard was set at a minimum 1.5 m below mean sea level, 60 cm at lowest astronomical tide, based on six years of local swell data [R2][R15]. Mortensen himself framed it as 'always a compromise... especially since the main focus was coastal protection' [R3].

sections.title: As built vs design
sections.html_or_text: The built reef matches the planned footprint and dominant right-hand wave, but execution surfaced issues not evident in the design promise. Swellnet's July 2019 first-look (at ~50% completion) reported the reef 'alarmingly shallow, with one rock even breaking the surface,' and a forum commenter described it going 'from too shallow to too deep really quickly' across the tide cycle — a narrower-than-hoped surfable tidal window [R15]. The timeline held essentially to plan rather than beating it: Swellnet's own 23 Aug 2019 update reported the reef only ~50% complete and 'still on track for an October finish,' and the project was finalised/certified in September 2019 — consistent with, not ahead of, the original target [R1][R5][R17]. Cost and dimension figures vary slightly by source (AU$18.2M vs AU$18.3M; 80 m vs 144 m width; 270 m vs 330 m offshore), plausibly rounding/measurement-basis differences between the council's headline figures and individual consultants' own project pages, though no source explains the gap [R2][R4][R5][R7][R9][R13].

sections.title: Outcome
sections.html_or_text: Surfing: on its first meaningful swell test (July 2019, reef ~50% built) it broke 4–5 ft waves with rides up to ~30 m; at completion it produced a consistent right with a short, thick left on bigger swells, handling at least double-overhead SE swells [R6][R15][R17]. The Inertia groups Palm Beach with Cable Station and Burkitts Reef among Australian stone reefs delivering 'modest, measurable improvements in the quality of waves' without becoming world-class breaks [R18]. Coastal protection: ABC News reported approximately 550,000 m³ of sand retained over the reef's first two years of operation — the clearest quantitative protection outcome found [R9]. Coastal engineer Evan Watterson argued such structures compare favourably to plain beach nourishment 'over a 30-year period' [R9]. Ecology: marine-habitat creation is claimed by both Bluecoast and Raised Water Research but with zero ecological survey data found in any source fetched [R1][R2]. Longevity: no storm-damage, structural-failure, or removal reports were found for this reef specifically [R13][R17]. Awards: IPWEAQ 2019 Excellence Award for Innovation and a 2020 Excellence Award for Coastal Engineering [R5].

sections.title: Why it worked / failed
sections.html_or_text: Sources repeatedly credit the rock-over-geotextile material choice as the key differentiator from failed reef projects elsewhere — rock's long engineering track record, precise shape-control, and habitat value versus geotextile bags' history of tearing and expensive removal [R3][R13][R18]. Siting the reef behind an existing natural reef to pre-focus wave energy is credited with helping it punch above its size for surf quality [R3][R13]. The tuned crest depth/freeboard (1.5 m below MSL / 60 cm at LAT) balanced rideable wave height against safety, but the resulting narrow, fast-changing tidal window drew user complaints [R15]. Lead designer Simon Mortensen's own stated regret was about process, not physical design: 'we would have been more realistic in our budgeting on how long it would actually take to work on this reef. The City got a good deal' [R3]. ICM's own comparison attributes Palm Beach's stronger wave outcome (versus Narrowneck) to its surf-first design brief at a materially higher unit cost (~AU$700/m³ vs ~AU$30/m³ at Narrowneck): 'when the objective is surfing, the design can be more focused and effective' [R13].

sections.title: Unexpected results
sections.html_or_text: Rock breaking the surface at low tide, flagged by Swellnet as a possible safety/design concern locals questioned [R15]. A single joking Swellnet forum comment about a shark sighting ('Predatory Pirate Shark circles Palmy Reef') was not corroborated by any other source and is not treated here as a real trend [R17]. Crowding complaints: because the reef breaks predominantly as a right-hander in a region already dominated by right-hand points, some surfers criticised it for adding to an existing imbalance and concentrating crowds [R17]. The pre-existing 2004 'no reef' community backlash that killed an earlier reef proposal at the same beach is itself a notable data point about local social license, given the later, larger 2019 project proceeded with comparatively less reported opposition [R10][R16].

sections.title: What could have been done better
sections.html_or_text: Simon Mortensen's own retrospective criticism concerns process, not the built structure: the consultancy underestimated how long the multi-year design phase would take [R3]. Outside civil engineer Shane Abel (not on the design team) argued before construction that 'whatever they build in the ocean should be removable and 8 tonnes of rock isn't,' proposing a removable design instead of the fixed boulder approach [R16]. The Palm Beach Board Riders Club (Mike Gifford) felt stakeholder consultation with surfers was inadequate ahead of construction [R16]. Post-construction surfer commentary focused on the tide-sensitivity problem — the narrow window between 'too shallow' and 'too deep' — suggesting a design tweak to crest depth or profile might have produced a more forgiving tidal window [R15]. Some surfers also felt the community would have been better served by a different wave shape (e.g. a left or a peak) given the Gold Coast's existing abundance of right-hand points [R17].

sections.title: Relevance to Israel / Haifa
sections.html_or_text: Tide range: Palm Beach is microtidal (~1.5 m illustrative weekly range per a live tide check), broadly consistent with the reef's own 1.5 m/60 cm freeboard spec; Haifa's Mediterranean coast is essentially micro-tidal to negligible-tidal, which means Palm Beach's core challenge — keeping a fixed-crest structure inside a workable 'not too shallow, not too deep' window across the tide cycle — would be more forgiving at Haifa, since Haifa's tide swing is smaller [R14][R15]. Wave climate: Palm Beach's design leaned on six years of dominant east-to-southeast Pacific ocean swell arriving at a site with an existing natural offshore reef to pre-focus it; Haifa's Mediterranean wave climate is smaller and less consistent, meaning a Haifa reef would likely need to actively increase wave height rather than merely reshape already-large incoming swell [R3][R15]. What transfers: (1) the rock-over-geotextile durability and shape-control lesson is directly transferable regardless of wave climate; (2) siting behind/near an existing natural feature to pre-focus energy is a transferable design principle, though Haifa may lack an equivalent natural offshore reef; (3) the tide-window lesson is less of a constraint for Haifa given its smaller tidal range, giving more freedom in crest-depth choice; (4) the cost lesson — Palm Beach's much higher per-m³ cost than Narrowneck reflects the premium of prioritising surf quality in the design brief — is directly relevant to budgeting a Haifa reef if surf quality is a primary goal [R13].

footprint.name: Palm Beach Reef
footprint.coords: metres; origin = shoreline point nearest the reef centroid (approx. 19th Avenue, Palm Beach); x = alongshore (positive toward north, the predominant sand-transport / downdrift direction per the City of Gold Coast's own explainer video [S1]); y = offshore (positive seaward); shoreline approximated as the line y=0

crest_depth_m.datum: below mean sea level at the reef's highest point (≈0.6 m below lowest astronomical tide)

distance_offshore_m.measured_from: shoreline near 19th Avenue, Palm Beach (exact measurement point — near edge, far edge, or centroid — not specified by any source; we placed the polygon centroid at y=270 as a simplifying assumption, see derivation/open_issues)

footprint.orientation_notes: Elongated, rounded, asymmetric rock mound. Read off the two available plan-view graphics (the labelled aerial/schematic diagrams on Cru Collective's site, sourced from the project team) and cross-checked against the visible rock-shadow patch in the ABC News aerial photo, the mound tapers to a narrower, rounded point on its shoreward (near-shore) side and broadens to a blunter, rounded mass on its seaward (offshore) side — the opposite taper direction from Gemini's assumed 'apex seaward' chevron (see gemini_comparison). Long axis (160 m) treated as alongshore, short axis (80 m) as cross-shore, matching the conventional reading of '160 m long × 80 m wide' in every source, though no source explicitly labels which figure is alongshore vs cross-shore (flagged in open_issues). The reef sits in the lee of Palm Beach's natural offshore reef [R3], targeting dominant east-to-southeast swell [R2][R15], with sand naturally transported north along this stretch of coast [S1] — hence x-positive is defined as north. No source gives a numeric shoreline bearing or swell-approach angle; Gemini's '345° NNW shoreline / 090–110° swell' figures are not supported by any source we found and are not reproduced here.
footprint.materials: Quarried rock boulders, up to 8 t each (max individual weight, stated directly by S1, R4, R7, R16; re-verified 2026-09-25) — R2 separately describes a design-evolution note, "The rock size was increased from 3 tons to 5 and 8 ton rocks," implying discrete size classes rather than a continuous range; no source states a minimum boulder weight or a formal "X–8 t" range. [Verification 2026-09-25: an earlier draft of this file stated "4–8 t each" and attributed the range to R16; R16 was re-fetched and found to state only "up to eight tonne," with no minimum — the "4 t" figure was unsupported and has been removed.] Total ~60,000 tonnes [R7, R9 — both state "60,000 tonnes" directly; R2/R4/R16 do not give a total-tonnage figure], ~25,000 m³ by volume [R13]; rock type (e.g. basalt/granite) is not specified in any source we found [R2][R4][R7][R9][R13][R16]

open_issues: Width (80 m vs Royal HaskoningDHV's own 144 m) and distance offshore (270 m vs Royal HaskoningDHV's own 330 m) remain unresolved across every source checked, including this one — carried forward unchanged from the card [R5].

No source explicitly states which published figure (160 m or 80 m) is the alongshore dimension vs the cross-shore dimension; we assumed 160 m = alongshore and 80 m = cross-shore, matching the conventional reading and Gemini's own assumption, but this is an inference, not a stated fact.

The point from which '270 m offshore' is measured (near edge, far edge, or centroid) is not specified by any source; we assumed centroid for simplicity, which shifts the true near/far edges by roughly ±40-45 m depending on which convention the original designers used.

Verification 2026-09-25 flags an internal tension: our own reading of the Cru Collective schematic (images_relied_on #1) concludes the '270m' arrow visually lands on the reef's near/shoreward edge, not its centroid — yet the polygon below places the centroid (not the near edge) at y=270. If the near-edge reading is right, the whole polygon should sit roughly 40m further offshore than drawn (shoreward tip near y=266 instead of y=226, centroid near y=310 instead of y=270). This was not corrected in the polygon itself (doing so would require a new speculative construction, which this adversarial-check task's scope does not extend to), but is flagged here as an unresolved self-consistency issue for a future revision.

No true as-built CAD drawing or bathymetric survey of the constructed reef was found publicly (despite Gemini's citation, which does not correspond to any real accessible document); our polygon's exact vertex geometry is a qualitative estimate from a non-scaled marketing schematic plus a real aerial photo, not a measurement, and should be treated as illustrative of shape family (elongated, rounded, shoreward-tapered mound) rather than a precise outline.
Precise lat/lon of the reef structure itself (as opposed to the 19th Avenue onshore reference point) was not found in any source.
Net footprint area (~9,678 m2 here) is a geometric consequence of our assumed polygon shape, not an independently published or measured figure; treat as low-confidence.

verification.evidence: Re-verified S1 against the on-file transcript (i6k6WN2GtWI.txt): "it will be 160 metres long and up to 80 metres wide." Re-fetched R2 ("roughly 160m long and 80m wide"), R4 ("approximately 160m long and 80m wide"), R7 ("160 metres long and 80 metres wide") via WebFetch/curl+grep — all confirm verbatim.

verification.evidence: Confirmed by S1 transcript, R2 ("approximately 270 m off shore"), R4 ("270 metres offshore from Palm Beach"), R7 ("Located approximately 270 metres offshore from Nineteenth Avenue"). R9 re-checked with a full-text search for '270', 'metres offshore' and distance figures -- confirmed R9 does NOT mention any offshore distance; removed from this row's citation (previously wrongly included).

verification.evidence: Re-fetched R5 (haskoning.com) directly: "The 144-metre-wide reef has been built 330 metres offshore." No length figure given on that page. Conflict against the majority 80 m / 270 m value is real and remains unresolved, exactly as the card states.

verification.item: Volume of rock 25,000 m3
verification.evidence: Re-fetched R13 (coastalmanagement.com.au) directly, exact quote: "Quarried rock approx 25,000m3."

verification.item: Total tonnage ~60,000 t
verification.evidence: Re-fetched R7 ("constructed using 60,000 tonnes of rock") and R9 ("made up of 60,000 tonnes of boulders") -- both state the total directly. R2, R4 and R16 were re-checked and only give a per-boulder MAX weight (up to 8 t), not a total-tonnage figure; the materials field and R4's reference entry were corrected to stop implying R4 supports a total-tonnage number.

verification.item: Boulder weight: 'up to 8 t' vs the card's former '4-8 t range'
verification.evidence: Re-fetched/re-grepped R16 (curl + raw-text search) -- the page states only "up to eight tonne" boulders in three separate mentions; no minimum weight or '4-8 t' range appears anywhere on the page. The '4-8 t' figure in the prior draft, attributed to R16, was therefore unsupported and has been removed. Separately, R2 was re-read directly via browser (WebFetch's own summary of R2 had hallucinated a nonexistent quote, "the rocks vary in size from 4 to 8 tons each" -- this was checked against the live rendered page and does NOT appear there); R2's actual text instead reads "The rock size was increased from 3 tons to 5 and 8 ton rocks," a design-evolution note describing discrete size classes, not a stated continuous range. The materials field has been rewritten to reflect only what is actually stated: max weight up to 8 t (S1, R4, R7, R16), plus R2's 3/5/8-ton design-history note; no source gives an authoritative minimum.

verification.item: Polygon bbox, area, validity
verification.evidence: Recomputed independently with python + shapely: bounding box exactly 160.0 m (x) x 80.0 m (y); shoelace/shapely area = 9677.65 m2, matching the stated 9677.6 m2; polygon is closed, is_valid=True, exterior.is_simple=True (no self-intersections); area-weighted centroid = (0.031, 270.005), matching the stated design target of centroid at (0.03, 270.0).

verification.item: Plan-view shape / taper direction (narrow shoreward, broad seaward)
verification.evidence: Downloaded and directly viewed all three cited images (Completion2.jpg, Completion.jpg, ABC aerial) at high zoom. Completion2.jpg does show a shape narrower/pointed at the arrow (shoreward) end and blunter/wider at the far (seaward) end, consistent with the card's claim, and the '270m' arrow visually lands on the icon's near tip, not its center -- but the icon itself is a generic stock-style 3D rock graphic, not a purpose-drawn technical plan, so this is weak evidence. Completion.jpg's icon is too small/low-res to independently confirm taper direction. The ABC aerial photo's dark patch is elongated and roughly consistent with the claimed taper, but the active dredger sits at the patch's near/broad end, so dredging turbidity may be inflating that end's apparent width -- a confound not previously flagged. Net: the taper-direction call remains the best-supported reading available (better than Gemini's citation-free opposite claim) but should be read as plausible, weakly-evidenced qualitative shape family, not a confirmed geometric fact -- consistent with (and now more explicitly caveated than) the card's existing 'High uncertainty' label.

verification.item: Near-edge vs. centroid placement of '270 m offshore' in the polygon
verification.evidence: The card's own image analysis (images_relied_on #1) concludes the 270m arrow lands on the reef's near/shoreward edge, not its centroid -- yet the polygon construction placed the CENTROID at y=270. This is an internal inconsistency not caught in the original draft. Not corrected in the polygon geometry itself (would require a new speculative construction, out of adversarial-check scope) but added to open_issues for a future revision.

verification.item: Gemini comparison table (all rows)
verification.evidence: Read Gemini's actual files directly: reef_footprints.json (structures[], id 'palm_beach') confirms shape_typology 'Sculptured Asymmetric Rock Chevron / Trapezoid', a 9-vertex bounding_polygon with its single highest-y (most-seaward) vertex at (15,310) -- matching the card's 'apex seaward' description exactly; area_m2=12800.0; shoreline_orientation_deg=345, incident_swell_direction_deg='090-110' -- both match. scale_sketch_photo_alignment_audit.md (row 9, Palm Beach) contains, verbatim, 'Matches the 42,000-tonne basalt rock blueprint' and 'the documented 38 m sand salient fronting the 11th Avenue SLSC tower' -- both quoted accurately in the card. images/scale/palm_beach.png was opened directly and is confirmed to be an auto-generated chart (axis-labelled plot, a legend box repeating the same L/W/area/volume/crest/offshore numbers, a drawn '100 METERS' scale bar) -- not a scan or reproduction of any real bathymetric survey, exactly as the card describes.

verification.item: Overall confidence rating
verification.evidence: All five headline numbers (160 m, 80 m, 1.5 m below MSL, 270 m, 25,000 m3) were independently re-confirmed at their primary sources and are unchanged by this pass. What changed were citation-hygiene errors (R6/R9 wrongly cited for dimensions/distance, R16 wrongly cited for a '4-8 t' range, R4 wrongly summarized as giving 'tonnage') and additional caveats on the already-low-confidence shape/taper and area estimates -- none of which raises or lowers confidence in the headline dimensions, so 'medium' is retained rather than changed.

name: Southern Ocean Surf Reef ("Midds Reef")
year: Construction began ~Oct 2024 (quarry establishment); main rock placement Jan-Mar 2025; officially opened 16 July 2025 [R1][R2][R3]
type: Submerged rock-berm surf reef, ~70,000 t of layered granite in three graded layers (belly, core, Class 1 armour), no geotextile [R2][R3][R1]
purpose: Surfing amenity / tourism / youth retention - the reef's sole and primary stated design objective; unlike most artificial surf reefs, coastal erosion protection was not a driver [R3][R8][R9]
size: Length 165 m; width up to 110 m; crest at -1.0 m AHD; total volume 62,800 t (belly D50 0.16 m/12,400 t, core D50 0.49 m/23,600 t, armour D50 0.94 m/26,800 t); reef sits ~140 m offshore [R3]
cost: City of Albany 'Total Committed Funds' AUD $11.75 million; Wikipedia/ABC/Beachgrit report project cost as approximately AUD $13 million [R3][R1][R7]
cost_usd_approx: ~USD $7.6-8.5 million at an approximate, unsourced AUD->USD conversion of ~0.65-0.72 (indicative only, not independently sourced) [R3][R1][R7]
financed_by: Commonwealth (Australian) Government $4.75M; WA State Government (DPIRD) $5M; City of Albany $1.995M; Albany Boardriders club $5,000. WA state pledge from both major parties in the 2017 election; federal pledge from both major parties in 2022 [R3][R2][R6]
motivation: Middleton Beach produced 'unreliable and unsurfable waves for much of the year' despite being closest to central Albany; ~30 years of local-surfer advocacy (led by Peter Bolt from 1990) sought a consistent, surfable wave to build youth surf access, tourism, and economic development for Albany - not a response to erosion or a port-mitigation problem [R1][R6][R3][R8]
designer: Bluecoast Consulting Engineers, lead design engineer Evan Watterson (principal engineer at Bluecoast per the firm's own bio; 'Principal Coastal Engineer / Director' per a separate CV) [R3][R16]
contractor: Heron Construction Limited (main contractor; marine personnel crew mobilised from New Zealand); Stantec (project superintendent); Spinifex Crushing & Screening Services (rock supplier, quarry at Mindijup Rd, Palmdale); marine plant (backhoe dredge, barges/tugs) mobilised via Darwin and Adelaide [R3][R2][R6][R17]
status_now: Built and operating since July 2025. As of March 2026, the City of Albany repositioned 18 rocks on the reef, at a cost of more than AUD $20,000, in response to a spate of user injuries [R3][R11][R8]
hover_text: 165 m long, 62,800-tonne rock reef built for AUD ~$13M (opened July 2025) that delivers a widely praised, better-than-design surf break - but its shallow, permeable rock crest caused repeated surfer injuries, forcing an 18-rock, $20,000+ safety 'detuning' in March 2026 [R1][R2][R3][R11].
design_as_planned: The 2015 Feasibility Study's objective was 'the creation of a consistent, surfable wave, which maximises available swell conditions' for Albany's economic and demographic benefit [R3]. The Detailed Design (executive summary by 2020) targeted a left-hand break, rides up to 100 m, and surfable waves 41% of the year, aimed at beginner-to-intermediate surfers per EPA WA [R3][R2][R9]. Design used 'thorough numerical, physical and conceptual modelling', with a 2018 BMT Environmental Impact Assessment reportedly finding no significant coastal-process impact and predicting shoreline widening in the reef's lee [R3][R8]. Business-case modelling projected NPV $57.9M / BCR 6.69, driven by ~10 annual surfing events and ~3,500 extra overnight visitors/year (an earlier May-2023 interim figure gave NPV $19.4M / BCR 3.25) [R3][R15].
as_built_vs_design: The built reef matches the design specification closely on paper: 165 m long, up to 110 m wide, crest at -1.0 m AHD, 62,800 t of rock in three graded layers [R3]. Construction ran from ~Oct 2024 (quarry establishment) through March 2025 (survey/practical completion), with main placement in Jan-Mar 2025 by a New Zealand marine crew using precision geospatial placement equipment [R3][R2][R8]. Once open, the reef performed 'far higher' than the 41% design-surfability target, though no source gives a precise revised percentage [R2][R6]. The most significant post-opening change came in March 2026: the City of Albany spent more than AUD $20,000 repositioning 18 rocks, described by the Albany Advertiser as a 'successful bid to reduce user injuries' [R11].
outcome: Widely reported as a rare unambiguous artificial-surf-reef success on wave quality: Swellnet says 'the reef performs far better than expectations' [R8]; Peter Bolt calls it 'intermediate-to-advanced on most days' as swell grows [R6][R2]; local surfer Cameron Warburton calls it 'a really high-performance wave' [R2]. Raised Water Research describes 0.8-1.3 m faces, 100-120 m rides, breaking on the reef proper ~40% of the year [R10]. But a persistent forum question (Aug-Oct 2025, user 'steveb') is whether it breaks well on the small (<1 m) everyday swells that dominate the local climate; local 'soggydog' answered 'No, but it has created reliable banks either side when it's too small for the reef proper' [R8]. No monitoring data, beach-width surveys, storm-damage, or fisheries/ecology results were found in sources fetched, beyond the single 2018 EIA citation [R8].
why_worked_or_failed: Sources attribute the reef's relative success to layered, precision-placed rock construction rather than geotextile sand bags, which 'failed due to the bags splitting, shifting, or settling' at earlier reefs worldwide [R8][R3][R6]. Engineer 'steveb' (Swellnet) argues rock reefs cannot match a sand-formed bank's contour accuracy because armour rock must be massive for stability, so shallow enough placement to break small swells 'compromises user safety'; rock permeability also means small swells 'surge into the reef rather than shoal and break', while larger swells ride over imperfections and shoal further up - explaining why the reef performs much better on bigger swells [R8]. He contrasts Albany's shallow crest (-1.0 m AHD, chosen partly 'to maximise wave breaking') unfavourably with Palm Beach (Gold Coast), which mitigated injury risk with a deeper crest [R8][R3]. Mayor Greg Stocks frames the injuries more as a behavioural issue: 'inexperienced surfers taking on quite elite waves...the temptation to go there above your skill level is probably contributing to some of that' [R7].
unexpected_results: Injuries began within weeks of opening: Swellnet forum posts from Albany locals describe 'a good face injury', sharp rocks cutting feet, and (per 'Baldhead') 'a number of injuries - broken bones, gashes, concussion' [R8]. By October 2025 the reef was being considered for 'detuning' ('busting up a couple of the rocks in the shallower part of the wave') following a 'spate of injuries on beginner surfers who can't handle its juice' [R7]. By March 2026 the City had repositioned 18 rocks at a cost of more than AUD $20,000 [R11]. 'steveb' argued this represented a public-liability/facility-design failure, comparing the reef to a council-managed playground where 'public safety is the number one priority' [R8]. Positive unplanned effects include reliable secondary sand-bank breaks either side of the reef on small swells, and youth/community access described by Peter Bolt watching 'the kids come down here before school, in the dark, to get a wave before they go to school' [R8][R2]. Shark risk is raised as a live community concern (no confirmed incident found) [R8].
could_be_better: Engineer 'steveb' (Swellnet) proposes that rock-dumped reefs inherently trade wave-shape accuracy against user safety, and argues a fully prefabricated reef structure - built onshore, floated out, and installed by controlled submergence - could achieve 'accurate shape and level, no subsidence, no settlement, no sharp edges, no possible entrapment points', citing materials with a 'safe working life in excess of 100 years', and points to Palm Beach's deeper, safer crest as a precedent for the safety/wave-quality trade-off Albany did not take [R8][R3]. Most surfer sentiment in the sources is not calling for a safer/easier wave - several posters push back on 'detuning' as inherent to a legitimately world-class wave - but there is a recurring, unanswered request for clearer information on how reliably the reef breaks on the small, sub-1 m swells that make up most of Middleton Beach's actual wave climate [R7][R8].
relevance_to_israel: King George Sound (Albany) is micro-tidal (mean range 0.4 m, spring 1.1 m), broadly comparable to the Mediterranean at Haifa, which is also effectively micro-tidal, though no fetched source gives a numeric Haifa tidal-range figure [R5][R10]. Albany's wave climate (consistent, long-period 12-16s Southern Ocean groundswell) is fundamentally more energetic than Haifa's, where Lior's own Shikmona-buoy measurements define 'minimum surfable' at only 0.45-0.6 m / 6-8s within a narrow WNW swell window [R10][R12]. Albany's problem was reshaping abundant swell into a rideable, non-closeout wave; Haifa/Israel's problem is swell scarcity ('less than 1 day/week' naturally surfable per Lior's Haifa proposal) [R13]. What transfers: (1) rock-vs-geotextile construction lesson; (2) the shallow-crest/wave-quality vs deeper-crest/safety trade-off any Haifa project would also face; (3) the multi-decade, multi-level-government (federal/state/city/club) financing pattern; (4) because Haifa is swell-starved rather than closeout-prone, Albany is a better precedent for safe rock-reef engineering than for wave-energy requirements, where Lior's own Gold Coast/Narrowneck comparison may be more directly analogous [R8][R3][R13].

reviews.role: long-time Albany surfer, lead advocate for ~30 years
reviews.quote_or_summary: We just felt that's where we needed the juniors to have something decent to surf... in town where they can get access to it.
It's a really high-performance wave, and the reef is creating a culture around town that's really good.

reviews.role: self-identified Albany local, Swellnet forum poster
reviews.quote_or_summary: Visitor had a good face injury yesterday. The rocks are sharp, feet are pretty cut up... It's not a beginner wave. There are dangers. But it's pretty fucking epic when you get a good one.
There's been a number of injuries - broken bones, gashes, concussion. There's a hardy crew on it.
Well done Albany council! Proper tubey take-off, big open face section to carve off too... Good vibes in the line-up too (for now anyhow).
Mixed report: on a given swell 'it didn't seem to be breaking very well, quite full and inconsistent,' while nearby beach breaks were closing out well that day.

reviews.role: Swellnet forum poster, self-identified public-recreation-facility engineer
reviews.quote_or_summary: The potential for far more serious injuries seems high... can artificial surfing reefs be made safer and better?
A much-loved local asset and a source of pride for surfers, families and the wider community, crediting passion, persistence and community support.

[The surf reef] does perform very well at different times, and the temptation to go there above your skill level is probably contributing to some of that... surfers acknowledge that there's risk, and all the surfing community that I've spoken to are delighted with the surf reef.

sections.title: Quick facts
sections.html_or_text:
NameSouthern Ocean Surf Reef ("Midds Reef")
PlaceMiddleton Beach, Albany, Western Australia
CountryAustralia
YearConstruction began ~Oct 2024 (quarry establishment); main rock placement Jan-Mar 2025; officially opened 16 July 2025 [R1][R2][R3]
TypeSubmerged rock-berm surf reef, ~70,000 t of layered granite in three graded layers (belly, core, Class 1 armour), no geotextile [R2][R3][R1]
PurposeSurfing amenity / tourism / youth retention - the reef's sole and primary stated design objective; unlike most artificial surf reefs, coastal erosion protection was not a driver [R3][R8][R9]
SizeLength 165 m; width up to 110 m; crest at -1.0 m AHD; total volume 62,800 t (belly D50 0.16 m/12,400 t, core D50 0.49 m/23,600 t, armour D50 0.94 m/26,800 t); reef sits ~140 m offshore [R3]
CostCity of Albany 'Total Committed Funds' AUD $11.75 million; Wikipedia/ABC/Beachgrit report project cost as approximately AUD $13 million [R3][R1][R7]
Cost (approx. USD)~USD $7.6-8.5 million at an approximate, unsourced AUD->USD conversion of ~0.65-0.72 (indicative only, not independently sourced) [R3][R1][R7]
Financed byCommonwealth (Australian) Government $4.75M; WA State Government (DPIRD) $5M; City of Albany $1.995M; Albany Boardriders club $5,000. WA state pledge from both major parties in the 2017 election; federal pledge from both major parties in 2022 [R3][R2][R6]
DesignerBluecoast Consulting Engineers, lead design engineer Evan Watterson (principal engineer at Bluecoast per the firm's own bio; 'Principal Coastal Engineer / Director' per a separate CV) [R3][R16]
ContractorHeron Construction Limited (main contractor; marine personnel crew mobilised from New Zealand); Stantec (project superintendent); Spinifex Crushing & Screening Services (rock supplier, quarry at Mindijup Rd, Palmdale); marine plant (backhoe dredge, barges/tugs) mobilised via Darwin and Adelaide [R3][R2][R6][R17]
Status nowBuilt and operating since July 2025. As of March 2026, the City of Albany repositioned 18 rocks on the reef, at a cost of more than AUD $20,000, in response to a spate of user injuries [R3][R11][R8]
Verdictmixed

sections.title: Motivation & who pushed for it
sections.html_or_text: Middleton Beach produced 'unreliable and unsurfable waves for much of the year' despite being closest to central Albany; ~30 years of local-surfer advocacy (led by Peter Bolt from 1990) sought a consistent, surfable wave to build youth surf access, tourism, and economic development for Albany - not a response to erosion or a port-mitigation problem [R1][R6][R3][R8]

sections.title: Design as planned
sections.html_or_text: The 2015 Feasibility Study's objective was 'the creation of a consistent, surfable wave, which maximises available swell conditions' for Albany's economic and demographic benefit [R3]. The Detailed Design (executive summary by 2020) targeted a left-hand break, rides up to 100 m, and surfable waves 41% of the year, aimed at beginner-to-intermediate surfers per EPA WA [R3][R2][R9]. Design used 'thorough numerical, physical and conceptual modelling', with a 2018 BMT Environmental Impact Assessment reportedly finding no significant coastal-process impact and predicting shoreline widening in the reef's lee [R3][R8]. Business-case modelling projected NPV $57.9M / BCR 6.69, driven by ~10 annual surfing events and ~3,500 extra overnight visitors/year (an earlier May-2023 interim figure gave NPV $19.4M / BCR 3.25) [R3][R15].

sections.title: As built vs design
sections.html_or_text: The built reef matches the design specification closely on paper: 165 m long, up to 110 m wide, crest at -1.0 m AHD, 62,800 t of rock in three graded layers [R3]. Construction ran from ~Oct 2024 (quarry establishment) through March 2025 (survey/practical completion), with main placement in Jan-Mar 2025 by a New Zealand marine crew using precision geospatial placement equipment [R3][R2][R8]. Once open, the reef performed 'far higher' than the 41% design-surfability target, though no source gives a precise revised percentage [R2][R6]. The most significant post-opening change came in March 2026: the City of Albany spent more than AUD $20,000 repositioning 18 rocks, described by the Albany Advertiser as a 'successful bid to reduce user injuries' [R11].

sections.title: Outcome
sections.html_or_text: Widely reported as a rare unambiguous artificial-surf-reef success on wave quality: Swellnet says 'the reef performs far better than expectations' [R8]; Peter Bolt calls it 'intermediate-to-advanced on most days' as swell grows [R6][R2]; local surfer Cameron Warburton calls it 'a really high-performance wave' [R2]. Raised Water Research describes 0.8-1.3 m faces, 100-120 m rides, breaking on the reef proper ~40% of the year [R10]. But a persistent forum question (Aug-Oct 2025, user 'steveb') is whether it breaks well on the small (<1 m) everyday swells that dominate the local climate; local 'soggydog' answered 'No, but it has created reliable banks either side when it's too small for the reef proper' [R8]. No monitoring data, beach-width surveys, storm-damage, or fisheries/ecology results were found in sources fetched, beyond the single 2018 EIA citation [R8].

sections.title: Why it worked / failed
sections.html_or_text: Sources attribute the reef's relative success to layered, precision-placed rock construction rather than geotextile sand bags, which 'failed due to the bags splitting, shifting, or settling' at earlier reefs worldwide [R8][R3][R6]. Engineer 'steveb' (Swellnet) argues rock reefs cannot match a sand-formed bank's contour accuracy because armour rock must be massive for stability, so shallow enough placement to break small swells 'compromises user safety'; rock permeability also means small swells 'surge into the reef rather than shoal and break', while larger swells ride over imperfections and shoal further up - explaining why the reef performs much better on bigger swells [R8]. He contrasts Albany's shallow crest (-1.0 m AHD, chosen partly 'to maximise wave breaking') unfavourably with Palm Beach (Gold Coast), which mitigated injury risk with a deeper crest [R8][R3]. Mayor Greg Stocks frames the injuries more as a behavioural issue: 'inexperienced surfers taking on quite elite waves...the temptation to go there above your skill level is probably contributing to some of that' [R7].

sections.title: Unexpected results
sections.html_or_text: Injuries began within weeks of opening: Swellnet forum posts from Albany locals describe 'a good face injury', sharp rocks cutting feet, and (per 'Baldhead') 'a number of injuries - broken bones, gashes, concussion' [R8]. By October 2025 the reef was being considered for 'detuning' ('busting up a couple of the rocks in the shallower part of the wave') following a 'spate of injuries on beginner surfers who can't handle its juice' [R7]. By March 2026 the City had repositioned 18 rocks at a cost of more than AUD $20,000 [R11]. 'steveb' argued this represented a public-liability/facility-design failure, comparing the reef to a council-managed playground where 'public safety is the number one priority' [R8]. Positive unplanned effects include reliable secondary sand-bank breaks either side of the reef on small swells, and youth/community access described by Peter Bolt watching 'the kids come down here before school, in the dark, to get a wave before they go to school' [R8][R2]. Shark risk is raised as a live community concern (no confirmed incident found) [R8].

sections.title: What could have been done better
sections.html_or_text: Engineer 'steveb' (Swellnet) proposes that rock-dumped reefs inherently trade wave-shape accuracy against user safety, and argues a fully prefabricated reef structure - built onshore, floated out, and installed by controlled submergence - could achieve 'accurate shape and level, no subsidence, no settlement, no sharp edges, no possible entrapment points', citing materials with a 'safe working life in excess of 100 years', and points to Palm Beach's deeper, safer crest as a precedent for the safety/wave-quality trade-off Albany did not take [R8][R3]. Most surfer sentiment in the sources is not calling for a safer/easier wave - several posters push back on 'detuning' as inherent to a legitimately world-class wave - but there is a recurring, unanswered request for clearer information on how reliably the reef breaks on the small, sub-1 m swells that make up most of Middleton Beach's actual wave climate [R7][R8].

sections.title: Relevance to Israel / Haifa
sections.html_or_text: King George Sound (Albany) is micro-tidal (mean range 0.4 m, spring 1.1 m), broadly comparable to the Mediterranean at Haifa, which is also effectively micro-tidal, though no fetched source gives a numeric Haifa tidal-range figure [R5][R10]. Albany's wave climate (consistent, long-period 12-16s Southern Ocean groundswell) is fundamentally more energetic than Haifa's, where Lior's own Shikmona-buoy measurements define 'minimum surfable' at only 0.45-0.6 m / 6-8s within a narrow WNW swell window [R10][R12]. Albany's problem was reshaping abundant swell into a rideable, non-closeout wave; Haifa/Israel's problem is swell scarcity ('less than 1 day/week' naturally surfable per Lior's Haifa proposal) [R13]. What transfers: (1) rock-vs-geotextile construction lesson; (2) the shallow-crest/wave-quality vs deeper-crest/safety trade-off any Haifa project would also face; (3) the multi-decade, multi-level-government (federal/state/city/club) financing pattern; (4) because Haifa is swell-starved rather than closeout-prone, Albany is a better precedent for safe rock-reef engineering than for wave-energy requirements, where Lior's own Gold Coast/Narrowneck comparison may be more directly analogous [R8][R3][R13].

footprint.name: Southern Ocean Surf Reef ("Midds Reef")
footprint.coords: metres; origin = shoreline point nearest the reef centroid (Middleton Beach, near the 'Surfer's Beach' car park); x = alongshore (positive toward north — assumed from the apparent north-up orientation of the Bluecoast/ASR design figure [R3], which shows dunes/land to the west and open water to the east, consistent with Middleton Beach's real north-south shoreline trend; no explicit north arrow is printed on the figure, so this is an inference, see open_issues); y = offshore (positive seaward); shoreline approximated as the line y=0

crest_depth_m.datum: below AHD (Australian Height Datum, ≈ mean sea level); ≈0.74 m below mean low water, ≈1.34 m below mean high water

distance_offshore_m.measured_from: shoreline / landward toe of the reef, per the Bluecoast/ASR concept-design table ('Cross-shore position: 140m from landward toe') reproduced on the City of Albany project page; our polygon's near (shoreward) tips sit at y=140-145 and its centroid sits at y≈189

footprint.orientation_notes: The Bluecoast/ASR 'Final Reef Design' table (reproduced as a figure on R3, filename design.jpg) specifies 'Crest orientation: Curved, 270°N-305°N... Maximises breaking and creates waves that peel evenly along the reef.' This is the bearing of the reef's own curved crest/wave-break line (a ~35 degree arc), not a stated swell-approach azimuth — no source we found gives a numeric swell-approach bearing (contrary to Gemini's invented '160-190 deg SSE-S', see gemini_comparison). The design table also specifies 'Surfing direction: Left-hander' and a 'Take-off area' at the more offshore, wider end of the reef (per the same figure), with the wave peeling toward the narrower, more shoreward end, matching R3's text 'the design provides surfing rides of up to 100m'. Our polygon therefore tapers to a point at its shoreward/updrift-adjacent end and bulges to its maximum ~110 m cross-shore width at the offshore 'take-off' end, per this figure — but the figure's own two dimension-arrow annotations (110 m and 140 m) do not share a consistent pixel scale (see derivation row 8), so this reading is topological/qualitative only, not a scaled tracing.
footprint.materials: Submerged rock-berm surf reef; ~62,800 t of layered granite in three graded layers — belly (D50 0.16 m, 12,400 t, 18%), core (D50 0.49 m, 23,600 t, 36%), Class 1 armour (D50 0.94 m, 26,800 t, 46%); no geotextile [R3]

open_issues: No true as-built plan-view CAD drawing or bathymetric survey was found publicly. The only plan-view figure available (design.jpg, legend 'ASR Design') is a pre-final concept sketch whose own two printed dimension arrows (110 m and 140 m) scale inconsistently by ~37% when pixel-measured — it was therefore used only for qualitative shape/taper topology, never for scaled vertex coordinates.

The design.jpg figure combines the physical reef outline with a separate wave-refraction/peel-line fan; distinguishing the two required close visual inspection and there remains some residual uncertainty about exactly where the rock structure's own edge lies versus the illustrative wave lines.

The two real aerial construction photos (R10, R2) are both dated/captioned May 2025, i.e. mid-construction — they may show a partially-built extent rather than the completed footprint, so were used only to corroborate general taper direction, not final size.

Exact polygon vertices are a low-confidence synthetic estimate, constrained only by the sourced 165 m x 110 m bounding envelope and the qualitative crescent curvature described in the design table; treat the polygon as illustrative of shape family, not a precise outline.
area_m2 (9,720) is not a published figure — it is a geometric consequence of our assumed polygon and should be treated as low-confidence, same caveat as Gemini's own area figures.

The x-axis 'positive = north' convention is inferred from the apparent north-up orientation of the design figure (land west, water east, coast trending N-S) rather than from an explicit stated bearing or printed north arrow — flagged as an assumption.

Distance offshore has a documented range across sources (120 m per Wikipedia/R4, 140 m per the current R3 page, ~145 m per a 2023 FAQ/R15) reflecting design evolution over time; we used the current page's 140 m figure as primary, consistent with the card.

Reef volume (34,000 m3) comes from an earlier 2017-bathymetry concept-stage table on the same figure as the shape sketch and may not equal the final as-built volume; only the final tonnage (62,800 t) is well corroborated across sources.

name: Xala Reef (Costalegre artificial surf reef)
place: Xala development, Costalegre coast, Jalisco (between Puerto Vallarta and Manzanillo)
year: Unclear/phased: boulder surf break reported built by April 2025 [R3][R4]; Raised Water Research calls it 'newly completed' and unveiled it 31 Mar–16 Apr 2026 [R1]
type: Rock/boulder reef — 3,000 truckloads of quarried boulders, not geotextile sand tubes [R3][R4]
purpose: Dual: (1) private members'-only high-performance surf break for Xala's owners/guests; (2) coastal protection/beach restoration, engineered to 'restore the beach, not flatten it' [R3][R4][R5]
size: Not disclosed — no length, width, crest depth, or fill volume found in any source this sweep [R1][R3][R4][R5]
cost: Not disclosed for the reef specifically [R3][R5]
financed_by: Xala development by Activos Turísticos de México (ACTUR), led by Ricardo Santa Cruz and Jerónimo Bremer; Richard Gere is a co-founder/backer; Six Senses (IHG) will operate the resort hotel. No source itemizes who specifically paid for the reef construction [R3][R4][R5]
motivation: Positioned as part of a 'regenerative,' low-density luxury development contrasted with conventional Mexican coastal resorts; developer Ricardo Santa Cruz frames the project around ecological restraint over density and a buyer base (largely Californian tech-wealth) that doesn't want a conventional resort [R3][R4]
designer: Simon Brandi Mortensen, Principal Coastal Engineer and Managing Director, DHI Seaport (MSc Coastal Engineering, TU Denmark; 19 years in coastal projects; designer of Australia's Palm Beach Reef) [R1][R6]
status_now: Complete and operational per Raised Water Research; publicly unveiled 16 April 2026 at a California Surf Club event in Redondo Beach, CA. Access is private/limited — Xala caps built units at 93 against an approved 4,500 [R1][R3][R4]
hover_text: A private, members'-only rock/boulder surf reef (3,000 truckloads of quarried boulders) built inside the Xala luxury resort development on Mexico's Costalegre coast, Jalisco; cost and exact build date undisclosed, unveiled publicly 16 April 2026 — too new for any independent outcome data to exist yet [R1][R3][R4].
design_as_planned: No detailed design brief (target wave height, period, break type, or beach-width promise) was found. Documented: quarried rock/boulder construction (3,000 truckloads), not geotextile sand-filled tubes [R3][R4], consistent with designer Simon Mortensen's stated philosophy that geotextile reefs suffer from bags 'breaking, shifting or sinking' with removal costs sometimes exceeding placement costs, whereas rock is 'natural and provides many small crevasses for marine habitat' [R12]. Stated intent: coastal protection/beach nourishment combined with a 'consistently great wave,' explicitly contrasted with reef designs that would 'flatten' rather than 'restore' the beach [R3][R4][R5]. No public engineering report, EIS, or design paper was located this sweep.
as_built_vs_design: Not enough independent material was found to compare as-designed vs as-built — no construction-progress reporting, as-built drawings, or named contractor were located. The only construction detail available (3,000 truckloads of quarry boulders) is presented in press coverage as the finished description, not a revised design target [R3][R4]. A roughly one-year gap between the reef being described as part of Xala's built amenities (April 2025 [R3][R4]) and Raised Water Research's 'newly completed'/unveiling framing (March–April 2026 [R1]) is unresolved in sources found — possibly phased construction, or the reef was substantially built by 2025 and only formally unveiled in 2026.
outcome: No independent surf report, wave-height measurement, or session footage description was found; Raised Water Research withheld even the reef's exact location until the 16 April 2026 event and promised 'never-before-seen footage,' implying essentially no public track record as of the unveiling [R1]. Coastal-protection performance (before/after beach-profile or erosion data) is not measured/reported in any source found. Ecology is not reported for the reef structure itself, though the wider Xala site includes a leatherback/Olive Ridley/green sea-turtle sanctuary and Ramsar-listed estuaries as separate conservation features [R5][R10]. Access/longevity/damage-event data does not yet exist given the very recent (April 2026) public unveiling.
why_worked_or_failed: No outcome data exists yet to assess this directly. The only available engineering signal is designer pedigree: Simon Mortensen led the design of Australia's Palm Beach Reef (Gold Coast; design 2013–2014, construction April–September 2019 [R6][R7]; ~$18.2M AUD/~$12.5M USD, financed by the City of Gold Coast; 4–8 tonne rock boulders plus 470,000 m³ of beach-nourishment sand), which Raised Water Research assesses as a design success — 'the reef appears to be a success,' producing a consistent ~60 m right-hander and a shorter left in bigger swell [R7]. This is background on the designer's method only, not evidence about Xala's own performance — no source directly ties Palm Beach's outcome data to the Xala build.
unexpected_results: Nothing Xala-specific was found (no litigation, safety incidents, fishing pressure, rip currents, or tourism-surge reporting). One indirect signal: an unrelated online repost of the Hollywood Reporter piece on a political/finance forum drew at least one favorable outside comment calling the whole project 'a neat idea/project,' but this concerns the development in general, not the reef, and is a single anonymous forum post [R4].
could_be_better: No source offers a critique of the Xala reef specifically (too new; no engineering post-mortem or surfer complaint thread was found). Generic rock-reef trade-off to watch for once surf reports exist: rock-bottom reefs (versus sand-bottom breaks) have drawn 'harder surface' complaints at other sites such as Palm Beach Reef — flagged here only as a general risk category, not a documented Xala complaint. No author/expert or surfer view was found for Xala specifically; the site's private/members-only access model may itself suppress independent public reviews for some time.
relevance_to_israel: Tide range and local wave climate at the Xala/Costalegre site were not found this sweep. What transfers conceptually, independent of Xala's own unverified outcome: (1) Material choice precedent — the designer's shift toward quarried rock/boulder construction (also used at Palm Beach Reef, 4–8 t boulders) rather than geotextile sand-filled tubes is directly comparable to the geotube-vs-rock materials question already live in this project's Israel dossiers (e.g. Ashkelon's 2018 geotube) — a rock-reef alternative is one materials option Israeli planners could weigh against documented geotube failure modes (undersized tubes, sand burial). (2) Governance-model contrast — Xala's reef is privately financed and privately accessed (members-only resort), unlike Israel's public-agency-funded structures (e.g. Ashkelon, Michmoret), a useful contrast case for 'who pays / who gets access' framing, though not a coastal-engineering transfer.

disagree.ours: 160 m (explicitly labeled as a Palm-Beach-analogy estimate, not a Xala measurement)
disagree.why_ours: We re-fetched all 4 of Gemini's own cited sources (Indelicato/Raised Water Research unveiling article, Romeyn/Hollywood Reporter via its Yahoo syndication, the freerepublic repost, and Hospitality Net) on 2026-09-25 and confirmed none contains any length, width, area, or footprint figure for Xala - only the boulder-truckload count. Gemini's Key Technical Specifications section presents '~140 x 75 m' with a tilde but with zero citation tying it to any of the 4 listed references, none of which is an engineering drawing or contains a number close to 140 or 75. The number cannot be derived from Gemini's own source list. Our own value (160m) is at least traceable to a real, cited, quoted figure - Palm Beach Reef's published dimension - and is labeled throughout as an unverified analogy, not a Xala fact.

disagree.ours: 80 m (Palm-Beach-analogy estimate)
disagree.why_ours: Same as above - no cited source supports 75 m for Xala. 75 m is suspiciously close to Palm Beach's real 80 m, supporting our own card's 'suspicious' note that Gemini likely performed the same Simon-Mortensen/Palm-Beach analogy internally without disclosing it or citing Palm Beach as the source.

disagree.gemini: ~1.0-1.5 m below MSL
disagree.ours: 1.5 m below MSL (Palm-Beach-analogy estimate, single value not a range)
disagree.why_ours: Palm Beach Reef's crest depth is documented as exactly 1.5 m below MSL (Raised Water Research spot page, quoted above). Gemini's range brackets this exact figure but, again, cites only the 4 Xala-specific sources, none of which mentions a crest depth at all. We present a single analogy value with an explicit large-uncertainty caveat rather than a bare range with no stated method.

disagree.ours: 270 m (Palm-Beach-analogy estimate)
disagree.why_ours: Palm Beach Reef sits ~270 m offshore per its own spot page. None of Gemini's 4 cited Xala sources states any offshore distance. Gemini's lower range (180-250 m) may reflect an independent guess or a partial/rounded version of the same analogy; either way it is uncited and we cannot verify it against any source.

disagree.gemini: Not drawn; described only in prose as a 'non-linear Boussinesq refraction wedge' with 'peeling left and right shoulders'
disagree.ours: shape_type 'other' (undetermined footprint envelope only); orientation explicitly flagged as unknown
disagree.why_ours: The 'peeling left and right shoulders' description is not supported by any Xala-specific source; our own verified card's Outcome section states no independent surf report of Xala exists at all, so we do not know if it produces one wave direction or two. This phrase looks like it was generalized from Palm Beach Reef's documented behavior (a right-hander plus a shorter left in bigger swell) or from generic surf-reef design language, not from anything published about Xala.

open_issues: No source found by either this project's exhaustive card/dossier sweep (2026-09-24) or this footprint task's re-check (2026-09-25) discloses any Xala-specific length, width, area, crest depth, or offshore distance.

No aerial photo, plan-view figure, engineering drawing, permit filing, or CAD/scale asset for Xala exists in this project's media indexes, in Gemini's media indexes, or in Gemini's reef_footprints.json (confirmed by direct grep - the Gemini slug 'xala-reef-mexico' has no entry in the structures array at all).

The only two verified images of Xala (both already in the card's `images` list) are close-range, water-level surf action photos with no shoreline, scale reference, or plan view visible - confirmed by direct visual inspection this task.

This entire footprint record is therefore a labeled DESIGN-ANALOGY PLACEHOLDER (to the designer's only other published reef, Palm Beach), not a Xala measurement or a figure-based estimate. It should be replaced the moment a real design paper, permit drawing, or aerial photo of Xala's reef becomes available.
Exact reef coordinates and shoreline orientation are undisclosed, so the coordinate frame's alongshore-positive direction is arbitrary and cannot be tied to a compass heading.

Whether Xala's reef is symmetric, single-armed, or a chevron/V like Palm Beach is completely unconfirmed; the polygon supplied here is a symmetric envelope specifically to avoid asserting an unconfirmed asymmetric/chevron shape.
